# Product status

This page is the map of what exists today, what has been QA-certified, what's
actively being built, and what's still on the roadmap. Nothing below is
aspirational unless it sits under **Roadmap**.

!!! info "What Secrets Bridge is"
    Secrets Bridge is a **unified secrets control plane** for governing secrets
    across external providers **without storing secret values in the control
    plane**.

    It **does not replace** HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key
    Vault, GCP Secret Manager, or Kubernetes External Secrets. It governs
    **access, workflows, approvals, audit, and agent execution** around them.
    The values stay in your provider.

## Implemented features

Everything in this section is built and running.

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Provider connections** | Manage external secret-provider connections and bind them to projects / environments. |
| **Agent onboarding** | Outbound-only agent enrollment with **one-time enrollment tokens** bound to one provider connection. The enrollment at pod start with a PVC is being replaced before the first release by the operator-side flow listed under [In progress](#in-progress). |
| **Direct reveal** | Controlled non-prod secret reveal with **MFA step-up**, **TTL**, **single-shot wraps**, and a **server-anchored countdown**. |
| **Prod protection** | Direct reveal is **hard-blocked for prod** environments and the refusal is audited (metadata-only). |
| **Cross-team secret request flow** | Requester submits destination keys → value provider fills values → approver verifies → agent executes the provider write. |
| **Destination key enforcement** | Destination keys are validated at the **submit, fill, and execute** boundaries. |
| **Metadata-only audit trail** | Records actions, IDs, statuses, reasons, and timestamps; **never** plaintext values, tokens, or wrap bodies. |
| **Agent fleet visibility** | Admin / provider agent list, `provider_connection_id` binding, active / stale / revoked status, revoke flow, and heartbeat. |
| **Security model** | No secret values in Postgres, Redis, audit logs, browser storage, or control-plane logs. |

## QA-certified

The following flows have passed a focused QA cycle and are tracked as a
release / demo candidate. "PASS" means verified end-to-end, not merely merged.

| Certification | Status |
|---|---|
| Project access (RBAC + environment scoping) | ✅ PASS |
| Direct reveal end-to-end + TTL | ✅ PASS |
| Prod reveal refusal | ✅ PASS |
| Cross-team backend / API lifecycle | ✅ PASS |
| Cross-team UI drawer submit | ✅ PASS |
| Approver verify-panel context | ✅ PASS |
| Plaintext-leakage sweep | ✅ PASS |
| Agent Onboarding API (earlier single-step enrollment; the two-step flow under In progress has not been through QA) | ✅ PASS / CLOSED |

## In progress

Being built now; not yet live or certified. Do not depend on these yet.

- **Stateless agent with a customer-owned key** (first-release requirement,
  [skills#116](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/skills/issues/116)): an
  operator runs `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` inside their boundary, which
  generates the X25519 wire-encryption key locally, proves possession
  through a sealed challenge and receives `agent_id` and `agent_secret` once.
  The bundle goes to AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or a Kubernetes Secret; the
  agent reads it from a read-only Secret (`identity.existingSecret`, mounted
  `0400` at `/etc/secrets-bridge/agent`) and writes nothing. The control plane
  stores only the public key and a hash of the secret. Every agent request
  carries its key fingerprint, there is no public-key overwrite route, and the
  key rotates through an audited flow with a fresh second factor. The PVC and
  enrollment at pod start are removed with no compatibility mode. Being built
  across the api, agent, console and chart; not merged, not through QA. See
  [Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/).
- **Richer agent fleet dashboard (UI)**: the agent management API exists; the
  full fleet UI view is next.
- **Object storage for media**: project and team logos move from Postgres to
  a private S3 or S3-compatible bucket, served through the api with the
  existing authorization. Secret values never go to object storage.
  Implemented in the api and the chart, not yet through QA. See
  [Object storage](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/object-storage/).
- **Signed releases**: every image and chart is signed with cosign by the
  workflow that built it, and images carry an SBOM and build provenance.
  All repos release together under one shared version; the first release
  has not been tagged yet. See
  [Verifying images and charts](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/verifying-releases/).
- **Sign in with Google, with admin approval**: an admin connects a Google
  Workspace from the console. Accounts are bound by Google's issuer and
  subject, the `hd` claim must be in the allowed domains, and new accounts
  wait for an admin to approve them with a role and scope. Existing
  accounts connect Google from their profile. The worker can post one
  webhook message per run about waiting accounts. Merged in the api,
  console and worker, not yet through QA. See
  [Sign in with Google](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/).
- **Gateway, Release 1 (Argo CD)**: an optional, outbound-only, read-only
  component that runs in your boundary and reports Argo CD rollout state as
  metadata. Merged, not yet through QA:
    - the Gateway binary (Argo CD connector only, signed image) and its Helm
      chart (no RBAC, no service-account token, egress-only NetworkPolicy);
    - the Argo CD privilege probe: at boot and at every recheck (5 minutes
      by default) the Gateway asks Argo CD's can-i, for each allowed
      AppProject and each static target it has read, whether its token can
      write, exec, read logs, write ApplicationSets or change the AppProject,
      and refuses to run on any `yes`. A read probe (`applications get` on
      `*/*`) reports the connector `degraded` when the token can read every
      AppProject. An Argo CD outage at boot makes the pod crash-loop, and the
      refusal names the failed check. Resource-action grants are not visible
      to can-i and stay the integrator's policy review.
      See [Argo CD privilege checks](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#argo-cd-privilege-checks);
    - Application identity: the Gateway pins each target's `metadata.uid`
      (optionally fixed in the values as `applications[].uid`), answers
      `target_identity_changed` when it changes, and sends only a scoped
      digest of it, in evidence and in its catalog. The control plane pins
      the first digest for each target; a different one suspends the
      target's bindings until a platform admin re-confirms it. See
      [Application identity](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#application-identity);
    - the control-plane registry: enrollment, heartbeat, catalog, connector
      approval, bindings, disable, enable, revoke and the `gateway.*`
      permissions;
    - observation tasks: a change that reaches `executed` in an environment
      whose observation source is `gateway` gets a task per binding, which the
      Gateway claims, leases and answers with metadata-only evidence that the
      control plane checks against the task's target before it computes the
      verdict. Tasks are not dispatched for a connector that a replica
      reported `over_privileged` in the last 10 minutes;
    - the per-environment observation source (`gateway` or `none`, the
      default) and the request's evidence at
      `GET /requests/:id/observations`;
    - the worker sweepers for leases, deadlines, stale Gateways and old
      replica rows (`SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED`);
    - the console: Admin → Gateways, the Observation column on a project's
      environments, and the Argo CD panel on the request page.

    - the cutover ([gateway#13](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/issues/13)):
      the Gateway is the only component that talks to Argo CD. The control
      plane's Argo CD poller, its endpoint and app-mapping routes and the
      stored Argo CD tokens are removed, along with the console's
      Integrations pages. `GET /requests/:id/gitops` serves the old poller
      rows as read-only history, shown on the request page as context only.
      See
      [Gateway cutover](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway-cutover/).

    Argo CD `Healthy` and `Synced` are operational state, never proof that a
    secret reached a workload: a Release 1 task ends `unverified`
    (`context_only`), never `verified`, and a Gateway that is offline or late
    leaves it `pending` and then `timed_out`, never failed. See
    [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/).

## Live vs Roadmap

### Live / implemented

- AWS Secrets Manager provider connection
- Outbound agent (execution inside your boundary)
- Direct reveal (non-prod, MFA-gated, single-shot)
- Cross-team request → fill → approve → execute workflow
- Metadata-only audit trail
- Provider-bound agent onboarding (one-time enrollment tokens). The stateless, customer-key flow that replaces enrollment at pod start is in progress
- Agent revoke / list / status
- Non-prod reveal protection
- Prod reveal refusal (audited)

### Retired

- Control-plane Argo CD observation (the worker's GitOps poller,
  `SB_GITOPS_ENABLED`, Argo CD endpoints and app mappings). Argo CD state now
  comes only from a [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/). Old observations stay
  readable as history, labelled context only.

### Roadmap / coming later

*Listed here because they are **not** live yet. Do not read these as shipped.*

- Azure Key Vault provider
- GCP Secret Manager provider
- HashiCorp Vault advanced flows
- Deeper Kubernetes External Secrets integration
- Flux integration
- Gateway Release 2: External Secrets Operator sync and Deployment rollout
  observation (in the gateway code, off by default and not supported for
  production)
- Gateway Argo CD discovery and AppProject-scoped bindings (ADR 0002,
  [gateway#25](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/issues/25)): the
  Gateway would list the Applications in its allowed AppProjects, and a
  binding would cover a project instead of one named target. The transport
  rule for the list read exists; discovery itself is not built
- Signed Gateway evidence ([gateway#7](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/issues/7)),
  required before Gateway evidence is used as compliance evidence
- Agent connection-scoped job claim
- Richer agent fleet dashboard

## Security model at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph people [" "]
        A["Admin / Developer / Approver"]
    end
    A -->|"session auth (HTTPS)"| CP["Secrets Bridge Control Plane<br/>(metadata • workflow • audit • RBAC)"]
    CP -->|"outbound jobs only"| AG["Secrets Bridge Agent<br/>(inside your boundary)"]
    AG -->|"read / write values"| P["External Provider<br/>AWS SM · Vault · Azure KV · GCP SM · Kubernetes"]
```

- The **agent is outbound-only**: it opens connections to the control plane and
  to its local provider; it never accepts inbound connections.
- The agent **accepts no inbound connections** for control-plane or user
  traffic. Its only listener serves health probes and metrics; the Helm
  chart binds it on the pod IP for kubelet and its NetworkPolicy denies all
  ingress.
- The agent has **no Postgres and no Redis** dependency, and **no Kubernetes API
  access** to read or write Secrets. With the in-progress stateless flow it
  also keeps no durable state and reads its credential and key from a
  read-only Secret.
- The **control plane stores metadata only**, never plaintext values.
- **Secrets remain in the provider.** Secrets Bridge governs access around them.
- Values move only through **controlled, wrapped, single-shot** flows
  (KMS-wrapped envelopes, consumed exactly once, short TTL).
- **Audit is metadata-only**: actions, IDs, statuses, reasons, timestamps; no
  values, tokens, or wrap bodies.

See the [full architecture](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/architecture/) and the
[threat model](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/) for how each boundary is enforced.

## The guarantees we hold

- **Outbound-only agent**: no inbound listener apart from the probe and
  metrics port, no cluster-API dependency.
- **Metadata-only audit**: append-only at the schema layer (Postgres triggers).
- **No plaintext persistence**: not in Postgres, Redis, logs, or the browser.
- **MFA-gated reveal**: non-prod reveals require an MFA step-up.
- **Prod reveal hard-block**: refused and audited, not merely discouraged.
- **One-time enrollment tokens**: hash-only, short-TTL, returned once, spent once.
- **Provider-bound agents**: an enrolled agent is bound to a single provider
  connection.
- **Revocation**: an agent can be revoked; its heartbeats and job polling stop
  being accepted immediately.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/architecture/

# Architecture

The platform splits into three loosely-coupled tiers and one
metadata index. Each tier holds one type of trust: the Control
Plane decides; the Agent executes; the Providers own the values.
An optional [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/) observes: it runs next to
the workloads, reads Argo CD rollout state without changing anything, and
reports metadata to the Control Plane over its own outbound connection.
Release 1 of the Gateway is in progress; see
[Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/#in-progress).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph user_plane ["User / Dev plane"]
        UI["UI SPA"]
        Dev["Developer"]
        Approver["Approver"]
        Dev --> UI
        Approver --> UI
    end

    subgraph control_plane ["Control Plane (Secrets Bridge)"]
        API["api (Fiber v3)"]
        Postgres[("Postgres<br/>append-only audit")]
        Redis[("Redis<br/>locks, cache,<br/>rate limit")]
        Worker["worker<br/>sweepers"]
        KMS["KMS backend<br/>local / vault-transit / aws-kms"]
    end

    subgraph workload ["Workload network (per cluster)"]
        Agent["agent<br/>outbound only"]
        Gateway["gateway (optional)<br/>outbound only, read-only"]
        ArgoCD["Argo CD"]
        Vault[("HashiCorp Vault")]
        AWSSM[("AWS Secrets Manager")]
        AzureKV[("Azure Key Vault")]
        GCPSM[("GCP Secret Manager")]
    end

    UI <--> API
    API <--> Postgres
    API <--> Redis
    API <--> KMS
    Worker <--> Postgres
    Worker <--> Redis
    Agent -->|"outbound HTTPS"| API
    Agent --> Vault
    Agent --> AWSSM
    Agent --> AzureKV
    Agent --> GCPSM
    Gateway -->|"outbound HTTPS"| API
    Gateway -->|"GET only"| ArgoCD
```

## Trust boundaries: what holds what

| Component | What it holds | What it must never hold |
|---|---|---|
| **UI** | Nothing that authenticates: the browser holds the HttpOnly `sb_session` cookie, which page scripts can't read | Any provider credential, any plaintext value beyond the reveal-once modal lifetime |
| **API** | KMS-wrapped envelopes (single-shot, TTL'd), audit rows, policy rules, role catalogs | Raw plaintext values, provider master credentials |
| **Postgres** | Hashes + envelopes + metadata + append-only audit | The decryption key, which lives in the KMS backend, *outside* Postgres |
| **Redis** | Idempotency tokens, distributed locks, rate-limit windows, pub/sub messages | Any value-bearing payload (the `runtime` package doesn't even expose a generic `Set()` ) |
| **Worker** | The same Postgres + Redis access as the API | Provider credentials, plaintext values |
| **Agent** | Provider credentials *for its own network boundary*, plaintext values for the duration of one request, and its own `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and X25519 private key as read-only files from a Secret in its boundary | Anything from another cluster / account; any durable state (no PVC, no writable identity file, no Kubernetes Secret write); no inbound listener; no Postgres / Redis client |
| **Gateway** (optional) | Its own credential for the Control Plane and a read-only Argo CD token, both as read-only files in its own boundary | Secret values, provider credentials, Kubernetes RBAC on Secrets, any write access; no inbound listener except loopback health; no Postgres / Redis client; no path to the agent |
| **Providers** | The actual secret values | n/a (these are unchanged systems) |

## The four request lifecycles

=== "Read"

    ```mermaid
    sequenceDiagram
        participant Dev
        participant UI
        participant API
        participant Approver
        participant Agent
        participant Vault

        Dev->>UI: Submit read request<br/>(prod/db/password, justification)
        UI->>API: POST /requests/read
        API->>API: Resolve policy → workflow
        API-->>UI: status: pending
        Approver->>UI: Click Approve
        UI->>API: POST /requests/:id/approve
        API->>API: Enqueue read job
        API-->>UI: status: approved
        Agent->>API: POST /jobs/claim
        API-->>Agent: read job payload
        Agent->>Vault: GetValue prod/db/password
        Vault-->>Agent: bundle with DB_PASSWORD
        Agent->>API: POST /agents/:id/wraps<br/>(envelope-encrypted)
        Agent->>API: POST /jobs/:id/complete (succeeded)
        API-->>Agent: 204
        Dev->>UI: Click Reveal (one-time)
        UI->>API: GET /requests/:id/wraps/:wrap_id<br/>?user_id=dev
        API->>API: Atomic consume + KMS decrypt
        API-->>UI: plaintext (base64, single-shot)
        UI->>UI: Show in modal, clear on close
    ```

=== "Patch"

    ```mermaid
    sequenceDiagram
        participant Dev
        participant UI
        participant API
        participant Approver
        participant Agent
        participant Vault

        Dev->>UI: Submit patch request<br/>prod/db/password = new-value
        UI->>API: POST /requests with key_values
        API->>API: KMS-wrap each value<br/>resolve policy → workflow
        API-->>UI: status: pending
        Approver->>UI: Approve
        UI->>API: POST /requests/:id/approve
        API->>API: Enqueue patch job
        Agent->>API: POST /jobs/claim
        API-->>Agent: patch job +<br/>list of wrap ids
        loop For each wrap
            Agent->>API: GET /agents/:id/wraps/:wrap_id
            API->>API: KMS-decrypt + single-shot consume
            API-->>Agent: value sealed to the agent's<br/>bound public key + recipient fingerprint
        end
        Agent->>Vault: GetValue(prod/db/password)
        Vault-->>Agent: existing bundle
        Agent->>Vault: PutValue (merged bundle)
        Agent->>API: POST /jobs/:id/complete (succeeded)
        API-->>UI: status: executed
    ```

=== "Discovery"

    ```mermaid
    sequenceDiagram
        participant Admin
        participant API
        participant Agent
        participant Vault

        Admin->>API: POST /jobs job_type=discover
        Agent->>API: POST /jobs/claim
        API-->>Agent: discover job payload
        Agent->>Vault: ListMetadata(scope)
        Vault-->>Agent: 47 secrets with<br/>custom_metadata tags
        Agent->>API: POST /agents/:id/secrets/bulk<br/>cluster + provider + items
        API->>API: Upsert on cluster+provider+ref<br/>preserve first_seen_at<br/>refresh labels jsonb
        Agent->>API: POST /jobs/:id/complete (succeeded)
        Admin->>API: GET /secrets?label=Environment:prod<br/>&label=Team:billing
        API-->>Admin: filtered list (GIN index)
    ```

=== "Gateway observation"

    The Control Plane never connects to Argo CD and holds no Argo CD
    credential. When a change reaches `executed` in an environment whose
    observation source is `gateway`, the api queues a task for each matching
    binding. A [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/) inside your boundary
    claims it, reads Argo CD with its own read-only token, and posts the
    result. In an environment set to `none`, the default, nothing observes
    the change. `Healthy` and `Synced` are Argo CD operational state, not
    proof that the workload picked up the new value, so the verdict is at
    most `unverified`.

    ```mermaid
    sequenceDiagram
        participant API
        participant Gateway
        participant ArgoCD

        Note over API: Patch request transitions to executed
        API->>API: Queue one task per binding<br/>that covers this secret
        Gateway->>API: POST /gateways/:id/tasks/claim
        API-->>Gateway: task, attempt_id, lease, deadline
        Gateway->>ArgoCD: GET /api/v1/applications/:name<br/>GET-only transport
        ArgoCD-->>Gateway: sync, health, operation phase, revision
        Gateway->>API: POST /tasks/:task_id/result
        API->>API: Check attempt and binding<br/>recompute stage outcome and verdict
    ```

## Defense-in-depth on the wire

Three layers of encryption protect every value-bearing flow:

```
TLS (mandatory)              - passive sniffers, compromised system CA
  ↓
Wire envelope (Piece 8b)     - TLS-terminating proxies, CP-side log leaks
  ↓
Storage envelope (Piece 8a)  - DB exfiltration, offline backup theft
```

| Direction | Wire envelope scheme |
|---|---|
| **CP → Agent** | X25519 ECDH + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM, sealed at retrieval to the public key bound at enrollment. The private key is generated by `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` in the customer's boundary and never reaches the CP. Even a TLS-terminating gateway sees only ciphertext. The X25519 key is a wire-encryption key, not a TLS client certificate. |
| **Agent → CP** | CP issues a KMS-wrapped data-encryption key; agent uses it for AES-256-GCM and zeroes the plaintext DEK immediately. The CP unwraps via the KMS backend. |
| **At rest** | KMS-envelope: per-row data key, wrapped by the configured `KeyManager` (LocalKMS for dev, Vault Transit or AWS KMS for production). |

## Why polyrepo

Nine repositories, one product. The `core` library is infra-free
(no Postgres driver, no Redis client, no Fiber import), so the
`agent` and `controller` can depend on it without pulling in
storage. The `api` and `worker` share Postgres/Redis but the worker
imports `api/pkg/*` only (never `internal/*`), so the dependency
direction is one-way and reviewable.

CI in every repo greps `go.sum` to enforce these boundaries. For
example, the agent's CI fails the build if it ever picks up
`jackc/pgx`, `lib/pq`, `redis/go-redis`, or similar drivers.

Read more: [REFACTOR_PLAN.md §4 polyrepo dependency graph](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/.github/blob/main/REFACTOR_PLAN.md).

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/teams-and-section-heads/

# Teams and section heads

Most organisations don't fit cleanly into a flat list of projects. A
real engineering org has sections, sub-teams, leads, and members, and
the people at each level need access to *their part of the world*, no
more and no less. The platform models this with a first-class **team
tree**: an N-level hierarchy where role grants scoped to a team
automatically fan out through that team's entire subtree.

## The model

Three entities, one rule.

### `teams`: the tree

Each team carries a name, optional description, status (`active` /
`archived`), and a nullable `parent_team_id`. Root teams have no
parent; everything else is a descendant. The depth is N. The schema
doesn't impose a limit.

```text
acme
├── platform
│   ├── platform-east
│   └── platform-west
└── security
    └── security-compliance
```

Sibling names must be unique under the same parent. `acme/platform/ops`
and `acme/security/ops` are both fine; two `ops` under `acme/platform`
are not. The constraint is per-parent, so renaming or re-parenting
never breaks cousins.

A team cannot be deleted while it has children; unparent or delete
those first. `team_members` rows cascade-delete with the team they
belong to (the user account stays; only the membership row goes).

### `team_members`: who belongs

A simple `(team_id, user_id)` join. **Structural only**: membership
does NOT grant any permission on its own. The platform deliberately
keeps "who you are" and "what you can do" in two tables so you can
reorganise teams without rewriting RBAC.

### Role grants scoped to a team

The connecting tissue. A row in `user_roles` carries a `scope` JSON
object; setting `scope.team_id = <team>` tells the access resolver
*"this grant applies to that team's entire subtree"*.

```json
{
  "user_id": "alice",
  "role_id": "<approver-role>",
  "scope": { "team_id": "acme/platform" }
}
```

Alice is now an approver for everything inside `platform` and every
descendant team. She can approve `platform-east` and `platform-west`
requests, and requests for a new sub-team created under `platform`
tomorrow, with no follow-up grant needed.

## The "section head" pattern

A common shape this model unlocks:

1. **Build the tree** under `/admin/teams`. Reflect your org chart:
   a top-level team per section, child teams per squad, grandchild
   teams if you have feature pods.
2. **Assign projects to teams** by setting `project.team_id` on
   create (or via `PUT /projects/:id/team` after). This is the wiring
   that lets the access resolver expand a team-scoped grant into a
   set of accessible projects.
3. **Grant the section head** on `/admin/assignments`: pick the user,
   pick the role (`secret.approve` for an approver, `secret.list +
   secret.request` for a developer-style lead), and pick the section
   team in the Team dropdown. Leave Project unset; the team scope
   makes it implicit.

That single grant produces this behaviour:

| The section head's view | How it works |
|---|---|
| `/secrets` shows every secret bound to every project under their section | `EffectiveProjectAccess` expands `team_id` → descendant teams (recursive CTE) → projects with `team_id` in that set |
| `/requests` lists requests from any project under their section | Same expansion, filtered server-side |
| Approve / Reject works for any of those requests | The approve gate runs `checkApproverScope` with the same resolver |
| Approve / Reject **refuses** on any request OUTSIDE their subtree | Returns 403 with the stable string `out_of_scope_project` |
| New sub-team added later under their section | Auto-covered, no follow-up grant |
| Project re-assigned to a different team | Auto-shifts in/out of scope, no manual cleanup |

## How requests respect the scope

The check fires at submit time AND at approve time, on top of the
normal `secret.list` / `secret.request` / `secret.approve` permission
check:

- **Submit gate**: `Requests.WithTenancyGate` validates the caller's
  `secret.request` grants cover the request's `project_id`, op is in
  the binding's `allowed_ops`, and every requested key is in
  `allowed_keys` (when non-null). Stable errors:
  `out_of_scope_project`, `out_of_scope_op`, `out_of_scope_key`.
- **Approve gate**: `checkApproverScope` validates the voter's
  `secret.approve` grants cover the request's `project_id`. Same
  team-subtree expansion as the submit gate.

Both gates have the same back-compat behaviour: legacy requests whose
`TargetScope["project_id"]` isn't a UUID bypass the team check (so
installs without scoped projects keep working byte-for-byte).

## How the UI uses this

The SPA hydrates a single `/users/me` call after login:

```json
{
  "id":           "<uuid>",
  "email":        "alice@example.com",
  "display_name": "Alice",
  "permissions":  ["secret.list", "secret.request", "secret.approve", "..."],
  "teams":        [{"id":"...","name":"platform","parent_team_id":null,"status":"active"}],
  "projects":     [{"id":"...","name":"Billing","status":"active"}]
}
```

- **Sidebar** items gate on the `permissions` array. The admin
  section hides entirely if no admin permission is held; individual
  nav items hide if their gating permission is missing.
- **`/secrets`** is filtered server-side to only the projects in
  `projects` (or every project if the caller holds a global grant).
- **Submit drawer** defaults to *"From my bindings"* mode for scoped
  users: pick a project from `projects`, pick one of its bound
  secrets, the form auto-fills provider type + ref + the allowed-ops
  / allowed-keys constraints. Admins (holders of `team.edit`) start
  on the free-form mode for onboarding new bindings.
- **`/me`** profile page renders the full payload: identity, the
  permission set, direct team memberships, and the accessible
  projects, all read from the same `AuthContext`.

Permission gating is strictly **fail-closed**: until `/users/me`
returns, `hasPermission(...)` is `false` for every key. A session
restored from `sessionStorage` shows the Dashboard + a *"Loading
permissions…"* line while the request is in flight; there is no
flash of admin nav for non-admins on rehydration.

## Practical advice

- **Keep teams shallow when you can.** Two or three levels covers
  most orgs. The recursive CTE handles depth N just fine, but a
  flatter tree is easier for admins to reason about.
- **Don't reuse `team_members` as a permission system.** Membership
  is structural metadata. Always grant capabilities via a role +
  scope.
- **Archive instead of delete** when a team is being wound down. The
  status flag preserves audit trails: requests filed against
  projects in an archived team subtree still resolve. Delete only
  when the team is truly empty and the historical references are no
  longer interesting.
- **A grant can target both `project_id` and `team_id`** in the same
  scope object. The resolver computes the union, so a user can be
  "the section head over `platform`" PLUS "co-owner of one specific
  project in `security`" via two separate grant rows or one combined
  scope.
- **Free-form mode in the submit drawer still works.** It's the
  default for admins, who are usually the ones submitting the first
  request against a brand-new binding. The api-side gate is the same
  in both modes; bound mode is a UX overlay that keeps scoped users
  from constructing requests that would 403.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/

# Threat model & hard rules

These are the rules the project never breaks. They're enforced
where possible by tests, schema constraints, and CI greps; where
that isn't possible, code review is the gate.

## Hard rules: never violated

### Value-bearing data

| Rule | How it's enforced |
|---|---|
| Secret values **never** appear in Postgres outside the KMS envelope | `TestWrap_PlaintextNotInDB` scans `encrypted_value` for the plaintext canary |
| Secret values **never** appear in Redis | The `pkg/runtime` package doesn't expose a generic `Set(key, value)`: only idempotency tokens, locks, rate-limit windows, pub/sub messages |
| Secret values **never** appear in audit metadata | Service layer audits `byte_length` + SHA-256 `content_hash` only; `TestWrap_AuditTrailHashesContentNotValue` scans the audit `metadata` column for the canary |
| Secret values **never** appear in API responses | Wire shapes in `internal/handlers/*` deliberately omit value fields; the request response carries `target_keys` (names) only |
| Secret values **never** persisted in the browser | The SPA writes nothing to `localStorage` / `sessionStorage` / IndexedDB. The only cookie is the HttpOnly `sb_session` cookie the api sets, which page scripts can't read |

### Provider credentials

| Rule | How it's enforced |
|---|---|
| Provider credentials **never** leave the agent's network boundary | The CP doesn't have any column or field that could hold one; the agent's resolvers refuse credential-shaped keys in the payload (e.g. seven banned `aws*Key*` names) |
| Provider credentials **never** in frontend code | The UI talks **only** to the Control Plane API; there's no provider SDK in the SPA's dependency tree |
| The Control Plane holds **no** Argo CD credentials | The api and worker have no Argo CD client: an `archguard` test in the api, worker and core repos fails the build if non-test code imports a package path containing `argocd`, `argoproj` or `argo-cd`, or builds an Argo CD API path, and it runs against seeded bad files so it can't pass vacuously. A router test fails if any route other than the read-only `GET /requests/:id/gitops` history mentions `gitops` or `argocd`. Migration 0049 dropped the table that held the old KMS-wrapped tokens; its test scans every text, bytea and jsonb column for canary token bytes. The Argo CD token lives only in the Gateway's own boundary |

### Append-only audit

| Rule | How it's enforced |
|---|---|
| `audit_events` rejects UPDATE and DELETE at the schema layer | `BEFORE UPDATE` / `BEFORE DELETE` triggers raise an exception; `TestAuditEvents_TableIsAppendOnly` runs `pool.Exec` against the triggers and asserts both fail |
| The repository interface for audit events has no `Update` / `Delete` methods | A typo in a SQL string can't surface through the interface; review would catch it |

### Network posture

| Rule | How it's enforced |
|---|---|
| The agent accepts no inbound connections for control-plane or user traffic | Its only listener serves `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/metrics` on `SB_LOCAL_ADDR`. The binary binds `127.0.0.1:8090` by default. The `agent` Helm chart binds `0.0.0.0:8090` because kubelet probes come from the node, creates no Service, and its default NetworkPolicy denies all ingress (`ingress: []`). Where the CNI doesn't enforce NetworkPolicy, that probe port is reachable on the pod IP from inside the cluster network. |
| The agent never imports any DB or Redis driver | The agent's CI greps `go.sum` for `pgx`, `lib/pq`, `redis/go-redis`, `mongo-driver`, etc., and fails the build if any appear |
| `core` stays infra-free | Same `go.sum` audit on the `core` repo; no `database/sql`, no `redis/go-redis` |
| Plain `http://` to the Control Plane is refused by default | Agent's `validateEndpoint` rejects non-https schemes unless `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true` is set; loud WARN log at startup if the flag is on |

### Gateway (Release 1, in progress)

The [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/) is optional. Release 1 is merged and
has not passed QA. These rules hold in the merged binary, chart and control
plane. The
full STRIDE analysis is the
[Gateway threat model](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/blob/main/docs/design/threat-model.md).

| Rule | How it's enforced |
|---|---|
| The Gateway changes nothing it observes | Argo CD is read through a transport pinned to the configured origin that allows GET to exact paths only: one Application by name, `session/userinfo` and the fixed can-i questions. The application list route is not admitted; it is reserved for discovery, which is not built. Every other method, path and query key is refused before the request leaves the process. The control-plane client refuses any route outside the Gateway endpoints |
| The Gateway refuses a token that can write | At boot and at every recheck (5 minutes by default) the Gateway asks Argo CD's can-i, project-wide and for each static target it has read, about application writes, `exec`, `logs`, ApplicationSet writes and AppProject changes. A `yes` refuses the start or stops the Gateway, and a question that cannot complete fails closed. The control plane dispatches no tasks for a connector that a replica reported `over_privileged` in the last 10 minutes. Limits are listed below |
| A recreated Application is not the same target | The Gateway treats `metadata.uid` as the identity and answers `target_identity_changed` when it changes. Pinning the uid in the values (`applications[].uid`) makes the check hold across restarts on every replica. Evidence and the catalog carry a scoped digest, never the uid. The control plane pins the first digest for each target. A different digest marks the target `identity_changed` and suspends every binding on it: no dispatch, evidence refused, no new binding. Only a platform admin with a global `gateway.bind` grant and a fresh second factor can re-confirm it, and both the change and the re-confirm are audited |
| The Gateway never reads Kubernetes Secrets | Release 1 has no Kubernetes access: the chart renders no Role and mounts no service-account token. The Release 2 Kubernetes connectors refuse to start if the service account can use any verb on `secrets` or a write verb on what they read, with no override |
| The control plane cannot redirect the Gateway | A task names a connector id and a target id only. Hosts, AppProjects and Applications come from the Gateway's local configuration |
| Gateway and agent credentials are separate | Own tables, `X-Gateway-Secret` header and `GatewayAuth` middleware. The secret is stored as a SHA-256 hash and compared in constant time |
| Argo CD health is never proof of propagation | The Argo CD connector reports at most `observed` with confidence `low` and attaches the caveat `argocd_health_not_proof`. The control plane recomputes every stage outcome from the reported facts, following [ADR 0001](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-gateway-observation-plane.md): a task that saw only Argo CD `Healthy` and `Synced` ends `unverified` with reason `context_only`, never `verified`. There is no `failed` verdict; missing or late evidence ends `pending` and then `timed_out` |

### Authentication & authorization

| Rule | How it's enforced |
|---|---|
| Single-shot wrap consumption is **atomic** | `MarkConsumed` is a single SQL UPDATE with `WHERE consumed_at IS NULL`; `TestRetrieve_ConcurrentAgents_ExactlyOneWins` proves 6 racers → exactly one wins |
| Agent secret comparisons are **constant-time** | `crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare` on every heartbeat path |
| User login is **constant-time-ish** even on unknown email | The auth service runs `bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword` against a dummy hash when the email isn't found, so an attacker can't enumerate users by latency |
| Generic 401 / 410 / 409 on every failure shape; the audit log carries the specifics | Login failures audit `actor=anonymous`, `error_kind=wrong_password` and `email_length` (never the email body; defends against audit-table spam) |
| Users authenticate with the session cookie **only** | Login returns no token and the api ignores `Authorization: Bearer` for users. The `sb_session` cookie is HttpOnly and `SameSite=Strict` (and `Secure` outside `SB_ENV=dev`), and logout, session revocation or disabling the user ends it server-side |

## Threat model: what we defend against

| Attacker | Attack | Defense |
|---|---|---|
| Passive network listener | Capture plaintext on the wire | TLS minimum; agent refuses `http://` by default |
| Compromised system CA bundle | Forge cert against your CP | Pin a private CA via `SB_CP_CA_FILE` (replaces system roots, doesn't add) |
| TLS-terminating proxy in a service mesh | Read plaintext between TLS termination and the api process | **Wire envelope**: X25519 sealing CP→Agent, KMS-DEK envelope Agent→CP; proxy sees only ciphertext |
| Database exfiltration / stolen backup | Read every secret wrap | **Storage envelope**: per-row KMS-wrapped data key; without the KMS the dump is noise |
| Misbehaving CP process logging payloads before encryption | Plaintext in app logs | Service-layer audits `content_hash` + `byte_length` only; handlers strip value fields from logs |
| Concurrent claim race on a wrap | Two readers see the same value | Atomic `MarkConsumed` with row lock; second caller gets 410 Gone |
| Replay of an already-consumed wrap | Re-fetch a leaked wrap | Schema CHECK enforces single-shot; storage-layer test asserts |
| Timing oracle on login | Enumerate emails by response time | Dummy bcrypt on unknown-email path |
| Forged or stolen user token | Sign a token, or replay one copied from a script or log, to act as a user | There is no user token to forge: the api reads no bearer token for users. A session is a server-side row behind the HttpOnly cookie, so revoking it or disabling the user stops it on the next request |
| Stale agent claiming after lease expired | Double-execution of a job | `WHERE claimed_by = $4 AND status = 'claimed'` on the complete UPDATE; owner mismatch returns 409 |
| Brute force / credential stuffing on `/auth/login` | Guess a local user's password | Per-account lockout after 5 consecutive wrong passwords (15 minutes, independent of source IP, kept in Postgres) plus a per-IP limit of 30 attempts per 60s as anti-scan. The per-IP limiter fails open when Redis is unavailable; the lockout does not. See [Authentication](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/). |
| Operator deploys with `SB_KMS_BACKEND=local` in production | Storage envelope uses a key that lives in the api's own env | The api refuses to boot with `local` unless `SB_ENV=dev`, and `SB_ENV` defaults to `production`. The `secrets-bridge` chart refuses `kms.backend=local` with `env=production` at render time. |
| Weak or shared local-admin credentials | Local password login as the only way in | OIDC sign-in (PKCE, group-claim to role mapping, back-channel logout). Local login stays as break-glass, and every successful local sign-in emits a `BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN` audit event with `severity=CRITICAL`. |
| Long-lived agent credentials passing through people | Copy an `agent_secret` from a browser, a chat message or a ticket | Direct mint (`POST /api/v1/agents`), which returns the long-lived secret to the admin, answers `403` unless the dev-only `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true` is set. Agents enroll with one-time, hash-only, short-TTL tokens bound to one provider connection. `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` receives the long-lived credential once and pipes it into the customer's secret store, so it is never shown in the console or the browser. |
| Swap an agent's wire key | Register an attacker key so the CP seals values to it | The key is bound at enrollment after a proof-of-possession challenge, and there is no route that replaces it. Rotation needs `agent.mint`, a fresh second factor, a one-time rotation token and the agent secret, runs the same challenge and is audited with old and new fingerprints. Every agent request carries `X-Agent-Key-Fingerprint`; a mismatch gets `409 agent_key_mismatch` |
| Read the agent key from the control plane | Get the private key from the CP, the console, logs or Helm state | The private key is generated by `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` in the customer boundary and only its public key reaches the CP. The agent chart takes only a Secret name (`identity.existingSecret`), so no key is in Helm values or release state |

## Threat model: what we don't yet defend against (open P0 work)

| Attacker | Attack | Mitigation status |
|---|---|---|
| Compromised host running the agent | Steal the agent credential and wire key (the files in the read-only identity Secret) | **Open**: `agent_secret` is a long-lived bearer secret, and the X25519 key opens values sealed to it. Revoke the agent and enroll a new one; the wire key can be rotated on its own. The CP holds neither in plaintext. Workload identity (SPIFFE / IRSA) and rotation are [agent#12](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/agent/issues/12) + [api#28](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api/issues/28) |
| KMS master key rotation breaks the platform | Operator can't rotate without downtime | **Open**: tested runbook is [api#31](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api/issues/31) |
| Customer admin who controls a Gateway | Report false Argo CD state for their own requests | **Accepted for Release 1**: evidence is customer-side attestation, and the design labels it with the Gateway that observed it. Signed evidence is [gateway#7](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/issues/7) and must ship before Gateway evidence is presented as compliance evidence |
| Integrator who grants the Gateway's Argo CD account a resource action | Restart or change workloads through `action/...` with the Gateway's token | **Residual, integrator review**: can-i cannot see a grant on `action/*` or `action/<group>/<kind>/<name>`, only a wildcard `*` action. The [minimal policy](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#the-minimal-policy) is one `applications, get` line per allowed AppProject, and any other line is the integrator's review |
| Integrator who grants the Gateway's Argo CD account `applications, get` on another AppProject | Read Application state outside the allowlist with the Gateway's token | **Residual, integrator review**: the local allowlist bounds what the Gateway itself reads. The read probe (`applications get` on `*/*`) reports the connector `degraded` only for a `*/*` or `*` grant, so a grant on one other AppProject, such as `tenant-b/*`, is not visible. The policy review must check it |
| Argo CD 2.4 to 2.14 with logs RBAC off | Read pod logs through `applications, get` | **Residual, integrator setting**: on 2.4 to 2.14 logs follow `applications, get` unless `server.rbac.log.enforce.enable: "true"` is set in `argocd-cm`, and the `logs get` probe answers `no` for the minimal policy while the logs stay readable. The setting is required for a Gateway on those versions. Argo CD 3.0 and later always enforce logs RBAC. Before 2.4, `applications, get` always grants logs and cannot be restricted, so those versions are not supported |
| DBA with direct Postgres access | Drop the audit triggers | **Acknowledged**: the schema is a defense; database-level RBAC and audit-log shipping to a separate system are deployment-side responsibilities |

Remaining findings from the 2026-09 security assessment are tracked in
[api#192](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api/issues/192).

## What we don't do: by design

- **We don't store secret values long-term.** Wraps have a TTL
  measured in minutes / hours. The platform is not a secrets
  *store*; it's a governance + access plane on top of one.
- **We don't broker provider credentials.** The agent reads its own
  Vault token / IRSA role from its own environment. The CP never
  sees them.
- **We don't terminate TLS for the user.** The Helm chart wires
  ingress; the api itself is a plain HTTP server behind that
  terminator. TLS is mandatory in production but enforced at the
  network boundary, not inside the api process.
- **We don't sync K8s secrets from the CP.** The `controller`
  reconciles a CRD via GitOps semantics; the CP itself has no
  inbound connectivity into any workload cluster.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/glossary/

# Glossary

Terms used across the docs, the code, and the BRD.

#### `access_request`
The first-class object the workflow flows around. A request to view
(`type=read`) or update (`type=patch`) one or more keys at a
specific provider reference. Carries a status (`pending`,
`approved`, `rejected`, `cancelled`, `executed`, `failed`,
`expired`).

#### Agent
The outbound-only worker process that runs inside the
target account / cluster. Holds provider credentials *for its own
boundary only*; never accepts inbound connections except health
probes and metrics on `SB_LOCAL_ADDR`; never imports a database or Redis
driver. One agent per
cluster identity (`SB_CLUSTER_NAME`).

#### `audit_event`
An append-only row in the `audit_events` table. Carries `actor`,
`action`, `resource`, `status`, `correlation_id`, `metadata` (jsonb,
never carries plaintext), `occurred_at`. Schema-level triggers
reject UPDATE and DELETE.

#### `correlation_id`
The chain identifier propagated through every audit event for one
request lifecycle. Click any `corr` chip in the UI's Audit page to
filter the whole table to that chain.

#### Control Plane (CP)
The collection of `api` + `worker` + `Postgres` + `Redis` + a `KMS`
backend. Makes decisions, holds metadata, never holds plaintext
values.

#### Gateway
An optional, outbound-only, read-only process that runs inside your
boundary and reports Argo CD rollout state to the control plane as
metadata. It never writes, never reads Kubernetes Secrets and has no
path to the agent. Argo CD `Healthy` and `Synced` are operational
state, not proof that a secret reached a workload. Release 1 is in
progress; see [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/).

#### KMS backend
The pluggable envelope-encryption layer. Three implementations ship:
`local` (dev only, master key in `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY`),
`vault-transit` (production with HashiCorp Vault), `aws-kms`
(production on AWS with IRSA / instance role). Selected by
`SB_KMS_BACKEND`.

#### Provider
A third-party secrets store: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager,
GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secret. Secrets
Bridge augments providers; it doesn't replace them.

#### `policy_rule`
Selector-based mapping from `(project, environment, secret_ref,
provider)` to a workflow. Walked in priority order; first match
wins. The seed `match-all` rule at priority 0 is the fallback.

#### `secret_wrap`
A KMS-encrypted envelope holding one key's plaintext for the
duration of one request. TTL'd, single-shot, atomic-consume.
Auditing tracks `content_hash` + `byte_length` but never the
value.

#### Single-shot
A consume-once semantic for wraps. The `consumed_at` column flips
atomically under a row-level lock; a second caller gets `410 Gone`.
The platform uses this for both the agent path (patch flow) and
the user path (read flow).

#### Wire envelope
The defense-in-depth layer above TLS. CP→Agent uses X25519 sealing
to the agent's registered public key; Agent→CP uses a KMS-issued
data-encryption key the agent zeroes after one AES-GCM operation.
Even a TLS-terminating proxy sees only ciphertext.

#### Workflow
A reusable approval template: minimum approver count, justification
required, TTLs for the various wrap lifecycle phases. There is no
self-approval setting: a requester can never approve their own
request. The policy match picks the workflow at submit; approval
reads the workflow's current approver count when the vote is cast.

#### Wrap summary
The value-free metadata projection of a wrap (id, key_name,
consumed flag, expires_at). Lets the UI render the Wraps card on
the request detail page without ever fetching plaintext until the
user clicks Reveal.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/faq/

# Frequently asked questions

Short answers to common questions about Secrets Bridge. Each answer links to
the page with the full detail.

## What is Secrets Bridge?

Secrets Bridge is a secrets control plane. It governs who may use the secrets
your team already keeps in AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault, and adds
access requests, approval workflows, RBAC, audit and agent execution around
them. The control plane makes decisions and keeps metadata, an agent inside
your boundary executes, and the provider holds the values. See the
[Overview](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/) and the [Architecture](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/architecture/).

## Does Secrets Bridge store secret values?

No. The control plane keeps requests, approvals and audit metadata, and the
values stay in your provider. A value in flight exists only as a
KMS-encrypted wrap that is consumed once and has a short TTL. Values never
appear in Redis, audit metadata, control-plane logs or browser storage, and
request responses carry key names only. The one response that returns a
value is the reveal itself, once, to the person who asked. See the
[Threat model & hard rules](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/) and
[Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/).

## Does it replace HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager?

No. Your provider stays the source of truth for secret values, and Secrets
Bridge governs access, approvals, audit and agent execution around it. The
agent uses only the credentials configured inside its own network boundary,
and the control plane never holds provider master credentials. See
[What's intentionally out of scope](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/#whats-intentionally-out-of-scope).

## Which secret providers does it support?

HashiCorp Vault (KV v2, with token or Kubernetes auth) and AWS Secrets Manager
(the standard AWS SDK credential chain, such as IRSA or an instance role) work
today through the agent. Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager are on the
roadmap: their agent resolvers are placeholders, as is the Kubernetes Secret
resolver. See [Providers supported](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/providers/) and
[Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/).

## Does the agent need an inbound port?

No. The agent only opens outbound connections, to the control plane and to
its local provider, and has no Postgres, Redis or Kubernetes API access to
Secrets. Its only listener serves `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/metrics`; the
`agent` Helm chart binds it on the pod IP for kubelet probes, creates no
Service for it and denies all ingress with its default NetworkPolicy. See the
[Agent](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/agent/) page and
[Network posture](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/#network-posture).

## How does an agent get its credentials?

An admin creates a one-time enrollment token bound to one provider
connection. The token is short-lived, stored only as a hash and returned
once. An operator runs `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` inside their boundary:
it generates the agent's X25519 key locally, exchanges the token for
`agent_id` and `agent_secret`, and the operator stores all three in AWS
Secrets Manager, Vault or a Kubernetes Secret. The agent reads them from a
read-only Secret and keeps no state of its own. The control plane stores
only the public key and a hash of the secret. An admin can revoke the agent
at any time, and its heartbeats and job polls stop being accepted
immediately. See [Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/).

## How do approvals work?

When you submit a request, the policy rules are matched in priority order and
the first match picks a workflow. The workflow sets the approval ceremony:
the minimum number of approvers, whether a justification is required, and the
TTLs. Approvers with `secret.approve` approve or reject from the Requests
page, which needs a fresh second factor, and a requester can never approve
their own request (the api answers `403 separation_of_duties_violated` and
audits the attempt). See [Policy templates](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/policy-templates/),
the [Glossary](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/glossary/#workflow) and
[Bootstrap & first sign-in](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/#submitting-your-first-read-request).

## Can a secret be revealed directly in production?

No. Direct reveal needs the caller to hold `secret.reveal.direct`, a matched
policy rule with `direct_reveal_allowed=true`, and an environment whose `kind`
is `non_prod`. The PolicyEngine zeroes `direct_reveal_allowed` for `prod`
environments whatever the policy says, and the refusal is audited. See
[Project environments](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/project-environments/) and
[Direct reveal permission](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#direct-reveal-permission-slice-l4).

## How is a secret value delivered to the person who asked for it?

After approval, the agent claims the read job, fetches the value from the
provider and posts it to the control plane as an encrypted wrap, one per key.
When you click Reveal, the api consumes the wrap atomically and decrypts it
with the KMS backend, so a second fetch of the same wrap gets `410 Gone`. The console shows the
value once and clears it when the reveal closes; a
[reveal session](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/reveal-sessions/) also ends after a TTL of 10
to 300 seconds set by the matched policy rule. See the read flow in the
[Architecture](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/architecture/).

## What is a cross-team request?

It is a value handoff between two teams that don't share access to each
other's secrets. Team A submits the request, a Team B member with
`secret.value.provide` fills in the values, a Team A approver (and a security
approver when the workflow requires one) verifies, and the agent writes the
value into Team A's provider. No user can play more than one of these roles on
the same request. See [Cross-team requests](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/cross-team-requests/).

## What is audited?

Audit events record actions, IDs, statuses, reasons and timestamps, and a
correlation ID links every event in one request's lifecycle. They never carry
plaintext values, tokens or wrap bodies. The `audit_events` table is
append-only: Postgres triggers reject UPDATE and DELETE. See the
[Glossary](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/glossary/#audit_event) and
[Append-only audit](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/#append-only-audit).

## Does it support SSO, OIDC and MFA?

Yes. You can sign in through an OIDC provider set with the `SB_OIDC_*`
variables (PKCE, group-claim to role mapping, back-channel logout), through
Google configured from the console (merged, not yet through QA), or with a
local password kept as break-glass. MFA uses TOTP authenticator apps or
WebAuthn security keys: approve, reject and reveal need a fresh second
factor, and login-time MFA is on by default outside `SB_ENV=dev`. See
[Authentication](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/) and
[OIDC with Authentik](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/oidc-authentik/).

## How do I try it locally?

Clone the `api` repo, start Postgres and Redis with
`docker compose up -d postgres redis`, and run the api with `SB_ENV=dev` and
the `local` KMS backend; the UI runs from the `ui` repo with `npm run dev`. On first boot
against an empty database the api seeds three dev users and logs their
passwords once, and the guide then enrolls an agent against a HashiCorp Vault
dev server. The setup uses dev-only switches, so keep it on your machine and
never load real secrets into it. See
[Running locally with docker compose](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/docker-compose/).

## How do I deploy it in production?

Install the Helm charts published on GHCR: `secrets-bridge` for the api, ui,
worker and controller, and `secrets-bridge-agent` for one agent per workload
cluster or account. You provide Postgres and Redis on a private network, a
real KMS backend (`vault-transit` or `aws-kms`) and an ingress with TLS. The
chart refuses `kms.backend=local` with `env=production`, and
[Operations](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/) has the hardening checklist to work
through before you expose the install.

## How mature is it?

Secrets Bridge is open source and pre-1.0, and the first release has not been
tagged yet. [Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/) keeps what is implemented,
what is QA-certified (such as project access, direct reveal with TTL, prod
reveal refusal and the cross-team flow), what is in progress and what is on
the roadmap apart. Features listed as in progress, such as the Gateway and
Google sign-in, have not passed QA.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/

# Components

The project is split into nine repositories under the
[`secrets-bridge`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge) GitHub
organisation. Each one has a single responsibility; the dependency
direction is one-way and reviewable.

| Repo | Language | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| [`core`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/core/) | Go | Provider interface + connectors, shared types. **Infra-free: no Postgres, no Redis.** |
| [`api`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/api/) | Go (Fiber v3) | Control Plane API. Owns Postgres + Redis + the workflow/RBAC domain. |
| [`worker`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/worker/) | Go | Background sweepers (including the Gateway observation sweepers), periodic discovery scheduler. No Argo CD client. |
| [`agent`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/agent/) | Go | Outbound-only execution agent. **No Postgres / Redis dependency.** |
| [`controller`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/controller/) | Go (kubebuilder) | Kubernetes CRD reconciler. Receives the v0.1.0 operator. |
| [`gateway`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/) | Go | Optional, outbound-only, read-only observation of Argo CD rollout state. **No Postgres / Redis, no Kubernetes client in Release 1.** Release 1 in progress. |
| [`ui`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/ui/) | React + TS + Vite | SPA dashboard. No SSR. |
| [`charts`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts) | Helm / YAML | Helm charts for the control plane, the agent and the Gateway ([production deployment](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/#production-deployment)). |
| `docs` | mkdocs-material | This site. |

## Dependency graph

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    core["core<br/>provider interface +<br/>shared types"]
    api["api<br/>Postgres + Redis<br/>workflow + audit"]
    worker["worker<br/>sweepers"]
    agent["agent<br/>outbound only"]
    controller["controller<br/>K8s reconciler"]
    gateway["gateway<br/>outbound only,<br/>read-only"]
    ui["ui<br/>React SPA"]
    charts["charts<br/>Helm bundle"]

    api -->|"imports"| core
    worker -->|"imports"| api
    worker -->|"imports via pkg"| core
    agent -->|"imports"| core
    agent -.->|"HTTPS only"| api
    controller -->|"imports"| core
    ui -.->|"HTTPS only"| api
    gateway -.->|"HTTPS only"| api
    charts -.->|"deploys"| api
    charts -.->|"deploys"| worker
    charts -.->|"deploys"| agent
    charts -.->|"deploys"| controller
    charts -.->|"deploys"| ui
    charts -.->|"deploys"| gateway
```

The forbidden edges:

- `agent` → `api/internal/storage` (would pull Postgres into the
  workload network)
- `agent` → `api/internal/runtime` (would pull Redis)
- `controller` → `api/pkg/storage` (same reasoning)
- `core` → anything that imports `database/sql` / `redis/*`
- `gateway` → `api`, `worker`, `agent`, `controller`, any database,
  Redis or KV driver, or `k8s.io/client-go`

CI in each repo greps `go.sum` to enforce these directions; the
build fails if a forbidden module path appears.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/api/

# Control Plane API (`api`)

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/api`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api)
· Stack: Go 1.25 + [Fiber v3](https://docs.gofiber.io) +
[pgx v5](https://github.com/jackc/pgx) +
[go-redis v9](https://github.com/redis/go-redis)
· Container: `golang:1.25-alpine` build → `distroless/static:nonroot`

The decision-making tier. Holds metadata, owns the workflow + RBAC
domain, mediates between users (via the SPA) and agents (via
outbound HTTPS).

## Layout

```
api/
├── cmd/api/                # main, config, server bootstrap
├── internal/
│   ├── auth/               # permission catalog, scope resolvers, auth.Require
│   ├── handlers/           # HTTP layer (one file per aggregate)
│   ├── middleware/         # Auth (session cookie), default-deny gate, RequestID, Logger, Recover
│   ├── observability/      # slog JSON logger
│   └── services/           # business logic (one file per aggregate)
└── pkg/
    ├── storage/            # Postgres repositories + migrations (embed.FS)
    ├── runtime/            # Redis primitives (locks, idempotency, rate limit, pub/sub)
    ├── keymgmt/            # KMS backends (local / vault-transit / aws-kms)
    └── sealing/            # X25519 + HKDF + AES-GCM for wire envelope
```

The `internal/` boundary is closed; the `pkg/` boundary is
deliberately open because `worker` imports `pkg/storage` and
`pkg/runtime`.

The api has no Argo CD client. `internal/archguard` fails the build if
non-test code imports a package path containing `argocd`, `argoproj` or
`argo-cd`, or contains `/api/v1/applications` or
`/api/v1/stream/applications`. A router test fails if any route path
contains `gitops`, `argocd` or `argo-cd`, except the read-only history route
`GET /api/v1/requests/:id/gitops`. Argo CD state reaches the api only as
[Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/) evidence.

## How a request gets its identity

`middleware.AuthWith` resolves the caller once per request, in this order:

1. **Session cookie** (`sb_session`, HttpOnly), issued by `/auth/login`
   and the sign-in callbacks. It is the only user credential: logout,
   session revocation and disabling the user end it.
2. Otherwise the caller is anonymous, and the default-deny gate on
   `/api/v1` answers `401` for every route that isn't explicitly public.
   Per-route `auth.Require(perm)` checks then run on top for authenticated
   callers.

`Authorization: Bearer` is not read for users. Login returns no token, so
scripts keep the session cookie in a cookie jar (`curl -c jar` to sign in,
`-b jar` after).

Agent routes under `/api/v1/agents/:id/` authenticate separately, with the
agent's `X-Agent-Secret`. `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll/challenge` and `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll`
authenticate with the one-time enrollment token in the body; every agent
request also carries `X-Agent-Key-Fingerprint`, checked against the key bound
at enrollment.

The legacy `X-User-Id` header is **ignored** unless the api runs with
`SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_HEADER_AUTH=true`, a dev-only switch that lets anyone
claim any identity. It is checked only after the session cookie,
and it must never be set on a deployment anyone else can reach. See
[Insecure switches](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#insecure-switches-dev-only).

## Runtime endpoints

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | Always 200. Liveness. |
| `GET /readyz` | Aggregated readiness across `postgres` + `redis` checks (+ KMS at boot). 503 with per-check failure map on failure. |
| `GET /metrics` | Prometheus exposition. |
| `POST /api/v1/auth/login` | Email + password. Sets the `sb_session` cookie and returns `{expires_at, user}`. |

See [HTTP API endpoints](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/api-endpoints/) for the
full surface.

## Configuration

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `API_ADDR` | no | `:8080` | Listen address |
| `DATABASE_URL` | yes | - | `postgres://...` |
| `REDIS_URL` | yes | - | `redis://...` |
| `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY` | yes when `SB_KMS_BACKEND=local` | - | base64 32 bytes |
| `SB_KMS_BACKEND` | no | `local` | `local` / `vault-transit` / `aws-kms` |
| `SB_KMS_VAULT_ADDR` / `SB_KMS_VAULT_TOKEN` / `SB_KMS_VAULT_KEY` | yes for `vault-transit` | - | |
| `SB_KMS_AWS_REGION` / `SB_KMS_AWS_KEY_ID` | yes for `aws-kms` | - | Alias OK; ARN stored in audit |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | recommended on first boot | - | Seeds local-admin user; idempotent |

See [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/) for the
exhaustive list, including the
[dev-only insecure switches](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#insecure-switches-dev-only)
and the [retired settings](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#retired-settings) such as
`SB_GITOPS_ENABLED`, which are logged by name and switch nothing on.

## What's stable, what isn't

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| The four request lifecycles (submit / approve / reject / cancel) | Stable |
| Patch + read flows end-to-end against Vault + AWS SM | Stable |
| Single-shot wrap consumption | Stable, race-tested (6 concurrent racers) |
| Session-cookie login + `auth.Require(perm)` gating on write endpoints | Stable |
| OIDC sign-in (PKCE, group-to-role mapping, back-channel logout) | Shipped; see [Authentication](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/) |
| Per-tenant KMS scoping | **Not shipped**, tracked as Piece 8c |
| Login brute-force defence | Shipped: per-account lockout (5 wrong passwords, 15 minutes) plus per-IP rate limits on the auth routes and a per-agent heartbeat limit; see [Authentication](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/) |
| Tested key-rotation runbook | **Not shipped**, tracked at [api#31](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api/issues/31) |

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/agent/

# Agent

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/agent`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/agent)
· Stack: Go 1.25 stdlib `net/http` (no Fiber) +
[hashicorp/vault/api](https://github.com/hashicorp/vault) +
[aws-sdk-go-v2/service/secretsmanager](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2)
· Container: `golang:1.25-alpine` → `distroless/static:nonroot`

The execution tier. Runs inside the target account / cluster.
Holds provider credentials for its own boundary only; the Control
Plane never sees them.

## Hard rules enforced by CI

| Rule | How |
|---|---|
| No database driver | CI greps `go.sum` for `pgx`, `lib/pq`, `mysql`, `mongo-driver`; fails on hit |
| No Redis client | CI greps `go.sum` for `redis/go-redis`, `gomodule/redigo`; fails on hit |
| No inbound listener except probes | The only listener serves `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/metrics` on `SB_LOCAL_ADDR`. The binary defaults to `127.0.0.1:8090`. The `agent` Helm chart binds `0.0.0.0:8090` because kubelet probes come from the node, creates no Service for it, and its default NetworkPolicy denies all ingress to the pod. |
| Read-only credentials, no durable state | The agent reads `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` from `SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR`, refuses a file with group write or any bit for others (`mode & 0o037 != 0`), and writes no file, PVC or Kubernetes Secret |
| TLS required to the CP | `validateEndpoint` refuses `http://` unless `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true` |
| Plaintext zeroed after one use | `client.Zero([]byte)` is called via `defer` on every value-bearing slice |

## Boot sequence

The agent is stateless. Its credential and its X25519 wire-encryption key are
created before it runs, by `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` on an operator
workstation, and reach the pod through a read-only Secret. See
[Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dir as Credentials dir (read-only)
    participant Agent
    participant CP
    Agent->>Agent: validateEndpoint (https or fail)
    Dir->>Agent: agent_id, agent_secret, private_key
    Note over Agent: refuse missing, malformed or too-open files<br/>(mode & 0o037 != 0)
    Agent->>Agent: derive public key and fingerprint
    par Heartbeat loop
        loop every SB_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL
            Agent->>CP: POST /agents/:id/heartbeat<br/>X-Agent-Secret + X-Agent-Key-Fingerprint
        end
    and Claim loop
        loop every SB_CLAIM_INTERVAL
            Agent->>CP: POST /agents/:id/jobs/claim
            CP-->>Agent: job or 204
        end
    end
```

The agent never generates a key at runtime, never enrolls at start and never
registers a public key: the key is bound at enrollment. When the control plane
answers `409 agent_key_mismatch`, the loaded key is not the bound one, usually
after a rotation the pod hasn't picked up yet. A wrap whose
`recipient_key_fingerprint` is not the agent's own is refused before it is
opened.

!!! note "Heartbeat response shape"
    A **bodyless** heartbeat returns an empty **204**, the shape existing
    agents rely on. A heartbeat with an optional JSON body
    (`status` / `agent_version` / `capabilities`) returns **200**
    `{status, server_time, next_heartbeat_seconds}` and records the reported
    fields; the first heartbeat also transitions an `enrolled` agent to
    `active`. See the [HTTP API reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/api-endpoints/#agents).

## Configuration

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SB_CP_ENDPOINT` | yes | - | `https://api.secrets-bridge.example` |
| `SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR` | no | `/etc/secrets-bridge/agent` | Read-only directory with the files `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` (base64 of 32 bytes). Every file is required. The `agent` chart mounts `identity.existingSecret` here |
| `SB_CLUSTER_NAME` | yes for discovery jobs | - | Stamped on every discovered secret |
| `SB_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | Bounded by api's stale-after window |
| `SB_CLAIM_INTERVAL` | no | `5s` | Claim cadence |
| `SB_CLAIM_CONCURRENCY` | no | `4` | Worker pool size; non-blocking semaphore |
| `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT` | no | `false` | Dev only: allows `http://` to the CP ([insecure switches](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#insecure-switches-dev-only)) |
| `SB_CP_CA_FILE` | no | - | Pin a private CA (replaces system roots) |
| **Provider creds** (per resolver) | yes | - | See [Providers supported](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/providers/) |

There is no environment variable for the credential or the key. The full list,
including the provider settings, is in the
[configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#agent).

!!! warning "Direct mint is a dev-only break-glass"
    The direct mint (`POST /api/v1/agents`) is refused with
    `403 direct_agent_mint_disabled` unless the api runs with
    `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true`, and it requires a public key like
    enrollment does. Use it for dev and tests only. Onboard agents with an
    enrollment token; see [Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/).

## Executors that ship today

| Job type | Executor | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `patch` | `PatchExecutor` | Fetches wraps → `GetValue` (existing bundle) → merge → `PutValue` → mark consumed. Idempotent re-runs (untouched keys survive). |
| `read` | `ReadExecutor` | Fetches one bundle → selective `target_keys` split → `POST /agents/:id/wraps` per key → zero plaintext after each post |
| `discover` | `DiscoverExecutor` | `ListMetadata(scope)` → preserve native tags verbatim into the CP's `labels` jsonb (Vault `custom_metadata`, AWS Tags, etc.) |

## Provider resolvers

The agent dispatches by `payload.target_provider_type` via
`ResolverByType`. Today:

| Type | Status | Auth |
|---|---|---|
| `vault` | ✅ ships | Token (`SB_VAULT_TOKEN`) or Kubernetes (`SB_VAULT_KUBERNETES_ROLE`) |
| `aws-sm` | ✅ ships | Standard AWS SDK chain (IRSA / instance role / `AWS_*` env) |
| `gcp-sm` | placeholder | Stub returns `NotConfiguredResolver` |
| `azure-kv` | placeholder | Stub returns `NotConfiguredResolver` |

Every resolver refuses credential-shaped keys in the
`target_provider_config` (e.g. `awsSecretAccessKey`, `token`,
`sessionToken`) so a future api bug can't accidentally ship a
credential to the agent over the wire.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/worker/

# Worker

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/worker`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/worker)
· Stack: Go 1.25 + `api/pkg/storage` + `api/pkg/runtime` (via local
`replace` directive) + Prometheus client
· Container: `golang:1.25-alpine` → `distroless/static:nonroot`

Background workhorse for the platform's lifecycle hygiene and the Gateway
observation sweepers. The worker never talks to Argo CD and holds no KMS
access; Argo CD state comes only from a [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/).

## Sweepers shipped today

| Name | Cadence | Job |
|---|---|---|
| `wraps-expired` | 60s | Delete `secret_wraps` past `expires_at` |
| `secrets-stale` | 5m | Flip discovered `secrets` rows whose `last_seen_at < cutoff` to `status='missing'` |
| `agents-stale` | 60s | Flip agents whose `last_seen_at < cutoff` to `status='stale'` |
| `jobs-recovery` | 30s | Mark `sync_jobs` rows whose claim lease expired without a complete as `status='expired'` |
| `discover-scheduler` | 5m | Enqueue one discover job per configured target (env var today; admin API tracked) |
| `observation-leases` | 30s | Put Gateway observation tasks whose lease ran out back to `queued`. Opt-in with `SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED` |
| `observation-deadlines` | 30s | Close open observation tasks past their deadline as `timed_out` (`deadline_reached` or `gateway_unavailable`), never failed. Opt-in |
| `gateways-stale` | 1m | Flip Gateways with no heartbeat for `SB_WORKER_GATEWAYS_STALE_AFTER` (2m) from `active` to `stale`. Opt-in |
| `gateway-replicas-prune` | 1h | Delete Gateway replica rows not seen for 24h. Opt-in |
| `users-pending` | 1m | Post one webhook message about accounts newly [waiting for approval](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/#notify-admins-from-the-worker), by email only. Registered only when `SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL` is set |

## Multi-replica safety

Every sweeper acquires a Redis lock before running:

```go
lock := scheduler.AcquireLock("worker:sweeper:" + name)
if errors.Is(err, runtime.ErrLockHeld) { /* metric, return */ }
// run + StartRenewal + Release on tick end
```

So you can scale the worker deployment to N replicas; exactly one
runs each sweeper per tick, the others record `worker_scheduler_lock_skipped_total`
(a metric, not a warn-level log, because N-1 of N replicas always skip).

## Notification sinks

| Sink | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `NoOp` | default | Logs at the event's severity |
| `Webhook` | ships | JSON POST; `FormatSlack=true` switches to `{text: ...}` envelope. 4xx is permanent (no retry); 5xx is transient (with backoff). |
| `Fanout` | ships | `errors.Join` across N sinks; one bad sink doesn't block siblings |
| Native Slack | placeholder | Tracked as a follow-up |
| Email / SMTP | placeholder | |
| PagerDuty | placeholder | |

## Hard rules

- Stateless (NFR-08): all state in Postgres + Redis
- No secret values logged or notified. Sweeper errors carry
  counts + cutoffs + sweeper names, never row contents. The one
  exception is `users-pending`, whose message lists the emails of
  waiting accounts. It goes to the webhook only, and the worker logs
  counts only
- No provider SDKs imported (worker doesn't fetch values; the
  agent does)
- No Argo CD client and no KMS backend. The `internal/archguard` test fails
  the build if non-test code imports a package path containing `argocd`,
  `argoproj` or `argo-cd`, or builds an Argo CD API path
- Multi-replica safe by construction
- Fails loud on misconfig at boot (e.g. `SB_DISCOVER_TARGETS_JSON`
  parse error → exit 1)

## Configuration

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | yes | - | Same Postgres as the api |
| `REDIS_URL` | yes | - | Same Redis as the api |
| `SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED` | no | `false` | Turns on the four Gateway observation sweepers. Their intervals are in the [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#worker) |
| `SB_DISCOVER_TARGETS_JSON` | no | - | Array of `{agent_id, provider, config, scope}`; admin API replaces this |
| Sweeper interval overrides | no | per-sweeper defaults | `SB_WORKER_WRAPS_EXPIRED_INTERVAL`, etc. See [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#worker) |

The `SB_WORKER_GITOPS_*` settings are retired: if set, the worker logs their
names once at startup and ignores them. See
[Retired settings](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#retired-settings).
