Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/controller/

# Controller

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/controller`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/controller)
· Stack: Go 1.26 + [controller-runtime](https://sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime)
· Container: `golang:1.26-alpine` → `distroless/static:nonroot`

The Kubernetes operator. Receives the v0.1.0 CRD reconciler and is
the GitOps consumer for cluster-internal sync.

## What ships

- `api/v1alpha1` group with the `SecretsSync` CRD (ported verbatim
  from v0.1.0; only the module-path import changed)
- The reconciler validates the CR by calling
  `Providers.Build()` for both refs and reports `Ready=Validated`
  / `Ready=ProviderError`. It does **not** run the sync loop
  itself
- Provider registry injected on the Reconciler struct (matches the
  `Register(r)` pattern in `core/providers/*`)

## Key behavioural change from v0.1.0

The v0.1.0 reconciler embedded the sync engine. The new
architecture moves execution to the **agent** (BRD §12.4):

| What the new reconciler does | What it deliberately doesn't |
|---|---|
| Loads the CR | Run a `for name in source` loop |
| Validates refs via `Providers.Build()` | Skip-if-unchanged content-hash comparison |
| Sets `Ready=Validated` on success | Read `GetValue` from any provider |
| Sets `Ready=ProviderError` with the factory's text | Write `PutValue` to any provider |
| Re-queues every `spec.refreshInterval` | Delete orphans |

The sync work is dispatched to the agent via the CP's job queue.
The controller is a **GitOps gate** for the cluster, not the
executor.

## Configuration

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KUBECONFIG` | for out-of-cluster runs | - | In-cluster uses the projected SA token |
| `LEADER_ELECTION_NAMESPACE` | no | the controller's own namespace | |
| `METRICS_ADDR` | no | `:8080` | Prometheus exposition |

See the controller's `config/` kustomize tree for the CRD + RBAC +
sample CR.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/

# Gateway

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/gateway`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway)
· Stack: Go 1.26, stdlib `net/http`, `log/slog`, Prometheus client
· Container: `golang:1.26-alpine` → `distroless/static:nonroot`, published as
`ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/gateway`, signed with cosign and shipped with an SBOM and
build provenance ([verifying releases](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/verifying-releases/))
· Chart: `oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-gateway`

The control plane decides, the agent executes, and the Gateway observes. A
Gateway runs inside your security boundary, reads the state of the Argo CD
Applications you list in its local configuration, and reports that state to the
control plane as metadata. It never changes anything, and it is optional.

!!! warning "Release 1 is in progress"
    The Gateway binary, its Helm chart, the control-plane registry and the
    observation path (tasks, leases, results, evidence, verdicts, the worker
    sweepers and the console pages) are merged. Release 1 has not passed QA.

    The Gateway is the only Secrets Bridge component that talks to Argo CD.
    The control plane holds no Argo CD credentials and has no Argo CD client.
    Installs that used the old control-plane poller follow the
    [Gateway cutover](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway-cutover/) runbook.

## Where it sits

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph cp ["Control plane: decides"]
        API["api<br/>policy, approvals,<br/>Gateway registry, audit"]
        PG[("Postgres")]
        API <--> PG
    end

    subgraph boundary ["Your boundary"]
        Agent["Agent: executes<br/>provider reads and writes"]
        GW["Gateway: observes<br/>optional, read-only"]
        Provider[("Secret provider")]
        Argo["Argo CD"]
    end

    Agent -->|"outbound HTTPS<br/>X-Agent-Secret"| API
    GW -->|"outbound HTTPS<br/>X-Gateway-Secret"| API
    Agent -->|"read and write values"| Provider
    GW -->|"GET only<br/>applications, get"| Argo
```

The agent and the Gateway each open their own outbound HTTPS connection to the
control plane. There is no connection between them in either direction, and the
agent does not depend on the Gateway. The control plane never connects into
your network on the Gateway path.

## What it is

| Property | What it means in the code |
|---|---|
| Optional | Governance and execution work without a Gateway. By design, a request with no Gateway observing it shows as unverified, never as failed. |
| Outbound only | The only listener is `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/metrics` on a loopback address (`127.0.0.1:8091` by default). A non-loopback address, including `localhost`, is refused at boot. |
| Read-only | Argo CD is read through a GET-only transport. The control-plane client can reach only the Gateway endpoints. No sync, rollback, refresh or patch is possible. |
| Metadata only | It reports sync status and revision, health, the last operation phase and the reconcile time. It never decodes Helm values, condition messages or health messages, and it reads no Kubernetes Secrets. |
| Bound connectors only | Connectors and targets come from a local file. The control plane names only a connector id and a target id. It cannot point the Gateway at a new host, project or Application. |
| Stateless | No database, no Redis, no volume. Several replicas share one Gateway identity. |

## What it is not

Argo CD `Healthy` and `Synced`, or a finished sync, are operational state. They
are not proof that a new secret value reached a running workload: a secret
change does not change Git, so an Application can be healthy and synced while
its pods still hold the old value. The Argo CD connector reports at most
`observed` with confidence `low`, attaches the caveat `argocd_health_not_proof`
to every observation that is not an error. The control plane never turns it
into a `verified` verdict: a task that saw only Argo CD `Healthy` and `Synced`
ends `unverified` with the reason `context_only`.

A Gateway that is offline, not deployed or not yet bound means the observation
is `pending`, and `timed_out` once the deadline passes. It never means the
deployment is healthy, and it never fails the request. There is no `failed`
verdict. Execution and approvals do not wait for it.

The Gateway is not an execution path. It does not call the agent, receive
values or wraps, or hold provider credentials.

## Release 1 scope

Release 1 is Argo CD rollout-state observation only
([gateway#12](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/issues/12)).

- The supported connector kind is `argocd`. It reads one Application by name
  with `GET /api/v1/applications/{name}` (with `?appNamespace=` when the
  target sets one), checks its token at boot with
  `GET /api/v1/session/userinfo`, and asks Argo CD's can-i API
  (`GET /api/v1/account/can-i/...`) that its token holds no write or other
  dangerous right. See
  [Argo CD privilege checks](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#argo-cd-privilege-checks).
- An Application's `metadata.uid` is its identity. A deleted and recreated
  Application under the same name gets an `error` observation with code
  `target_identity_changed`, never the new object's state. Evidence and the
  catalog carry a scoped digest of the uid, never the uid. The control plane
  pins the first digest for each target and suspends the target's bindings
  when it changes, until a platform admin re-confirms it. See
  [Application identity](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#application-identity).
- With only `argocd` connectors, the Gateway reads no Kubernetes API. It builds
  no Kubernetes client, needs no service-account token and no RBAC, and runs
  no Kubernetes self-check.
- The `eso` (External Secrets Operator) and `rollout` (Deployment rollout)
  connectors are Release 2. Their code is in the repo, but the Gateway refuses
  a connectors file that names them unless `SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS=true`
  is set. That switch is not supported for production, and the Gateway logs a
  WARN at boot while it is on. The Helm chart does not render these kinds and
  never sets the switch.

What the Argo CD connector proposes for the stage `argocd_context` (the
control plane recomputes every outcome from the reported facts):

| Outcome | When |
|---|---|
| `observed`, confidence `low` | The Application is `Healthy` and `Synced`, with no operation or a `Succeeded` one, and was reconciled after the change |
| `not_observed` | Anything else, including `Progressing`, `Degraded`, `OutOfSync`, a failed operation, or state reconciled at or before the change. `Degraded` is context, not a failure of the secret change |
| `unverifiable` | The Application is outside the AppProjects allowed in the local configuration. No status is reported |
| `error` | Argo CD cannot be read. A fixed error code, never a message |

## Observation flow

Each environment has an observation source: `gateway` or `none` (the
default). When a change reaches `executed`, the control plane reads that source
once. For `gateway` it creates Gateway tasks; for `none` nothing observes the
change. There is no fallback to any other observer.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Agent
    participant CP as Control plane
    participant GW as Gateway
    participant Argo as Argo CD
    participant UI as Request page
    Agent->>CP: job complete, request reaches executed
    CP->>CP: environment source is gateway
    CP->>CP: one task per matching binding, queued
    Note over CP: first claim allowed 10s later (not_before)
    GW->>CP: POST /gateways/:id/tasks/claim
    CP-->>GW: task with attempt_id, lease 60s, deadline
    GW->>Argo: GET /api/v1/applications/{name}
    Argo-->>GW: sync, health, operation, reconcile time
    opt work takes longer than the lease
        GW->>CP: POST /tasks/:task_id/lease
    end
    GW->>CP: POST /tasks/:task_id/result
    CP->>CP: check attempt, lease, schema, binding, time window
    CP->>CP: recompute stage outcome, compute verdict
    CP-->>GW: accepted, task_state, verdict, next
    UI->>CP: GET /requests/:id/observations
    CP-->>UI: rollup and stages, observed operational state
```

1. **Task.** A patch or cross-team request that reaches `executed` in an
   environment whose source is `gateway` gets one task for each enabled
   binding that covers its secret scope, where the Gateway is not revoked or
   disabled, the Argo CD connector is approved and the bound target is still
   advertised. Release 1 tasks carry one stage, `argocd_context`. The first
   claim is allowed 10 seconds after `executed`. The deadline is the binding's
   `observation_timeout_seconds` (default 1800), raised to cover the target's
   advertised refresh interval and progress deadline plus 5 minutes, and never
   more than 24 hours. With no matching binding, no task is created and the
   request shows "No observation configured".
2. **Claim.** The Gateway claims for itself only. The task is chosen by the
   authenticated Gateway id, never by anything in the body. A claim leases one
   task to one replica with a new `attempt_id` and a 60-second lease (capped
   at the deadline). Each replica holds at most one task, and the Gateway at
   most `max_inflight_tasks` (default 20). Nothing to claim answers `204`
   with `Retry-After: 5`.
3. **Lease.** The Gateway renews the lease while it works, or releases the
   task early with a reason (`shutdown`, `over_capacity`,
   `connector_unavailable`). A release is never a failure. A lease that runs
   out puts the task back in the queue, and the old `attempt_id` can no longer
   renew, release or post a result.
4. **Result.** The result is accepted only for the attempt the control plane
   dispatched to that Gateway, while its lease is live and before the
   deadline. The evidence must name the connector and target in the task, that
   connector must be approved and belong to the Gateway, the binding must still
   be live in the request's own environment and project, and the reported
   Application must be the object the target advertises. The schema is closed:
   unknown or duplicate keys are refused. Timestamps must fall inside the
   attempt, allowing for clock skew. A repeated result with the same body
   returns the stored answer (`duplicate`); a different body for the same
   attempt is a conflict.
5. **Verdict.** The control plane recomputes the stage outcome from the
   reported facts and does not take the Gateway's word for it. Evidence, the
   task state, the verdict and the audit events are written in one
   transaction. A stage that is not yet `observed` puts the task back in the
   queue with a backoff of 15, 30, 60 and then 120 seconds until the deadline.

What the verdicts mean in Release 1:

| Verdict | Reason | When |
|---|---|---|
| `pending` | | The task is open (`queued` or `leased`) |
| `unverified` | `context_only` | Argo CD was `Healthy` and `Synced`, idle or `Succeeded`, and reconciled after the change. This is observed operational state, so the verdict stays unverified |
| `unverified` | `no_stage_observed` | The stage ended `unverifiable`, for example an Application outside the allowed AppProjects |
| `unverified` | `gateway_errors` | Five Gateway-reported errors or refused attempts. The task is `dead` |
| `unverified` | `superseded_by_later_write`, `source_changed`, `binding_removed` | A later change to the same secret, a change of the environment's source away from `gateway`, or a deleted binding cancelled the open task |
| `timed_out` | `gateway_unavailable` | The deadline passed and the Gateway was not seen since the task was created, or is not `active` |
| `timed_out` | `deadline_reached` | The deadline passed while the Gateway was up, for example while Argo CD stayed `Progressing` or `OutOfSync` |

`verified` and `partially_observed` exist in the schema for the Release 2
stages (`eso_sync`, `workload_rollout`). A Release 1 task never reaches them.
There is no `failed` verdict, so a Gateway that is offline or late leaves the
request `pending` and then `timed_out`, never failed.

Revoking or disabling a Gateway moves its leased tasks back to `queued` and
refuses the old attempts. A disabled Gateway can be enabled again; a revoked
one cannot. Tasks it can no longer claim end `timed_out` at their deadline.

## Security model

The Gateway fails closed. Where it cannot prove a rule holds, it refuses to
start, stops claiming, or stays not ready.

| Rule | How it holds |
|---|---|
| GET only to Argo CD | Each Argo CD client is pinned to the scheme and host of its `base_url` and allows GET only to exact paths: one Application by name, `session/userinfo` and the can-i question for each probe it asks. The application list route is not admitted; it is reserved for discovery, which is not built. Every other method, path and query key is refused before the request leaves the process. `resource-tree`, `managed-resources`, `manifests` and the `exec`, `logs` and other stream paths are blocked even though Argo CD's `applications, get` permission allows some of them, and so is `?refresh=`, which would make Argo CD patch the Application. Redirects are refused, proxy variables are ignored, and an Application response is capped at 2 MiB. |
| Least-privilege Argo CD account | The token needs `applications, get` on each allowed `<project>/*` and nothing else. It is mounted as a file and re-read when it rotates. At boot and at every recheck (5 minutes by default) the Gateway asks can-i, for each allowed AppProject and each static target it has read, whether the token may sync, change or delete Applications, exec, read logs, write ApplicationSets or change the AppProject. A `yes` refuses the start, or stops a running Gateway, with no override. A read probe (`applications get` on `*/*`) that answers `yes` reports the connector `degraded` and leaves it running, since every read stays bounded by the local allowlist. Grants on resource actions (`action/...`) and `applications, get` on one other AppProject are not visible to can-i and are left to the integrator's policy review. On Argo CD 2.4 to 2.14, `server.rbac.log.enforce.enable: "true"` is required, and Argo CD before 2.4 is not supported. See [the minimal policy](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#the-minimal-policy). |
| No Secrets access, ever | Release 1 has no Kubernetes access at all. For the Release 2 Kubernetes connectors, a boot self-check refuses to start if the service account can use any verb on `secrets`, or any write verb on a resource a connector reads. A failed review call also refuses the boot. There is no override. The check repeats at every recheck (5 minutes by default) and stops the Gateway if a grant appears. |
| Writes only to the control plane | The control-plane client refuses any method or path other than the Gateway endpoints, uses no proxy and never follows redirects. Enrollment refuses any URL that is not `https`. |
| Credential at rest | The control plane stores a SHA-256 hash of the Gateway secret and compares it in constant time. On the Gateway side the identity is a read-only file. A file that other users can read, or that its group can write, is refused at boot. |
| Revocation | After a revoke, the next heartbeat or catalog upload gets `401`. The Gateway stops claiming and stays up and not ready, with the reason in its log, so the pod does not restart-loop. |
| Separate identity | Gateways have their own tables, header and middleware. An agent credential cannot authenticate as a Gateway, and a Gateway credential cannot reach agent routes. |

Gateway evidence is customer-side attestation: whoever controls a Gateway can
report false state for their own requests. The design accepts that for Release 1
by labelling evidence "observed by Gateway X". Signed evidence
([gateway#7](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/issues/7)) must ship
before Gateway evidence is presented as compliance evidence.

## Runtime behaviour

- A replica is ready when the control plane has accepted a recent heartbeat
  and the catalog, and every connector self-check passes. A connector that is
  `degraded` only because of the read probe has passed its self-check.
- Claiming pauses while no heartbeat has been accepted within
  `SB_GATEWAY_CP_UNREACHABLE_AFTER` (default `2m`), the catalog is not
  accepted, or a connector is unverified. It resumes once all three hold again.
- A `401` or an unsupported contract version stops claiming and leaves the
  process up and not ready.
- `gateway healthcheck` is the client for the exec probes, since the image has
  no shell or curl and the local server listens on loopback only. It sends one
  GET to `/readyz` (or `/healthz` with `--live`) and exits 0 on a 200.

## Further reading

- [Install and enroll a Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/)
- [Gateway configuration](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#gateway)
- [ADR 0001: Gateway as an outbound-only observation plane](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-gateway-observation-plane.md)
- [Gateway threat model](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway/blob/main/docs/design/threat-model.md)
- [Chart README](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/blob/main/gateway/README.md)

# UI (SPA)

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/ui`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/ui)
· Stack: Vite 6 + React 18 + TypeScript 5 + Tailwind 3 +
TanStack Query 5 + React Hook Form 7 + Zod 3 +
react-router-dom v6
· Container: multi-stage Node build → `nginx:1.27-alpine`,
unprivileged user 101

The operator-facing surface. A single-page application served as
static assets behind the same hostname as the api (path-based
routing: `/` → ui, `/api/v1/*` → api).

## Pages shipped today

| Route | Page | What |
|---|---|---|
| `/` | Dashboard | KPI cards, pending approvals (preview), recent audit activity (preview), providers health (preview), **agents** card (real), requests-this-week chart (preview) |
| `/requests` | Requests | My-requests filter pills (All / Pending / Approved / Rejected / Executed × patch / read) + Approver queue with inline Approve / Reject (with-reason) |
| `/requests/:id` | Request detail | Timeline, Approvals, **Wraps** (single-shot Reveal modal, read flow), the **Argo CD (observed by Gateway …)** panel with Gateway evidence, a muted **Argo CD history (before the Gateway)** card with the rows the retired control-plane poller wrote before the [cutover](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway-cutover/), read from `GET /requests/:id/gitops` and shown by `history_status` with the label *context only* (requester only, hidden when there are none), Details, Approver actions, Cancel-own |
| `/agents` | Agents | Revoke confirm, and a Mint drawer with a **reveal-once panel** for the agent secret. The drawer calls the legacy direct mint, which the api refuses (`403`) unless the dev-only `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT` is on; onboard agents by [enrollment](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/#enrolling-your-first-agent) |
| `/secrets` | Discovered secrets | Filter strip (cluster / provider / ref prefix / status / label chips), two-pane (table + sticky details with provider_config JSON) |
| `/audit` | Audit log | Filter strip + correlation drill-in chip on every row, sticky details with metadata JSON |
| `/admin/projects` | Projects | Master-detail (340px project rail + envs panel); soft-delete via archive/restore. The **Observation** column shows each environment's source (**Gateway** or **None**) to `gateway.list` holders; **Change…** appears only with `gateway.bind` |
| `/admin/roles` | Roles | Permission chip picker hydrated from `GET /permissions` (canonical catalog) |
| `/admin/assignments` | Assignments | User × role × scope table; scope chips with `=` separator |
| `/admin/workflows` | Workflows | TTL knobs, min approvers, justification required |
| `/admin/policies` | Policies | Selector → workflow priority-ordered list |
| `/admin/gateways` | Gateways | Create, enroll, approve connectors, bind targets, disable, enable and revoke [Gateways](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/) |
| `/login` | Login | Real email + password against `POST /auth/login`, which sets the HttpOnly session cookie |

## Hard rules baked into the SPA

| Rule | Where |
|---|---|
| No credential in page scripts, nothing in localStorage / sessionStorage / IndexedDB | The api sets an HttpOnly, `SameSite=Strict` session cookie and the api client sends it with `credentials: 'include'`. `src/auth/AuthContext.tsx` holds identity from `GET /users/me`, with no token field. A reload keeps the session |
| HTTPS required on non-localhost | `src/api/client.ts` throws at module-load if `VITE_API_BASE_URL` is `http://` for non-loopback |
| No SSR | Vite SPA build; nginx serves static assets only |
| Strict CSP | `default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| Initial bundle ≤ 500 KB gzipped (FR-13) | CI bundle-size budget; currently ~125 KB |
| Typed shapes carry no secret values | `src/api/types.ts` has no `value` / `plaintext` / `token` fields by design |
| Container unprivileged + RO-FS friendly | nginx `USER 101`, tmp paths under `/tmp` |
| **Reveal-once modals** clear plaintext on close | `useEffect(() => () => setDecoded(null), [])` on both the wrap-reveal and agent-secret modals |

## Design system

The SPA matches the Figma file `Secrets Bridge - Brand` byte-for-byte
on the brand pages: fonts (Inter + JetBrains Mono), colors (Navy
900 / Dark Navy / Cyan accent), brand-gradient primary CTAs,
`StatusPill` variants, and the reveal-once UX pattern.

See [Design system](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/) for the brand voice,
tokens, and Figma file reference.

## Configuration

The SPA is configured at **build time**, not runtime:

| Env var | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `VITE_API_BASE_URL` | empty (same-origin) | Set to `https://api.example.com` only when serving the UI on a different origin |

Production deployments serve the UI and the api behind the same
ingress with path-based routing so cookies + CORS aren't in play.

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/core/

# Core (shared library)

Repo: [`secrets-bridge/core`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/core)
· Stack: Go 1.24, **infra-free**

Shared types + the provider interface every other Go service
depends on. Deliberately small: adding anything Postgres-shaped or
Redis-shaped here is a CI failure on the dependent repos.

## What lives in `core`

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `providers/` | The `Provider` interface, `SecretRef` / `SecretMetadata` / `SecretValue` / `SecretVersion` / `PutOptions` / `ProviderScope`, concurrent `Registry`, plus the Vault + AWS Secrets Manager connector packages |
| `sync/` | Doc-only placeholder (the sync engine lives in the agent + worker; this package is reserved) |
| `types/` | Doc-only placeholder |

## The metadata / value split

```go
type Provider interface {
    GetMetadata(ctx, ref) (SecretMetadata, error)        // CP, discovery, controller
    ListMetadata(ctx, scope) ([]SecretMetadata, error)
    GetValue(ctx, ref) (SecretValue, error)              // agent only
    PutValue(ctx, ref, value, opts) (SecretVersion, error) // agent only
}
```

The interface is the load-bearing architectural decision in the
whole project. The CP only ever needs metadata; the agent only
ever needs values. Different processes hold different trust.

`SecretValue.String()` and `.GoString()` both return `"<redacted>"`,
verified across every default formatting verb in `core#3`, so a
casual `log.Printf("%+v", value)` can't leak.

## What `core` deliberately doesn't have

- No `database/sql` import
- No `github.com/redis/...` import
- No HTTP framework dependency
- No knowledge of workflow / RBAC / audit (those live in the api)

If you find yourself wanting to add any of these, your code
belongs in `api` or `agent` instead.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/

# Design system

One system covers the console, this site and the brand marks. It aims for an operations tool written by the engineers who answer for it: plain, exact and quiet, with one ultramarine accent and nothing decorative.

Read these before you write copy, build a page or make an image:

1. **[Brand voice](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/brand-voice/)**: how we describe the product and its maturity, and the words we avoid.
2. **[Tokens and theme](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/tokens/)**: colours for light and dark, the type scale, spacing, radii, and where each repo reads them.
3. **[Logos and assets](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/assets/)**: the Checkpoint mark, its approved colourings, the product icons and the architecture illustration.

## The short version

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Name | **Secrets Bridge**, two words, everywhere. In logos it comes from the lockup files; never retype it. |
| Fonts | IBM Plex Sans for what people read, IBM Plex Mono for what machines read (refs, key names, paths, times, code). Weights 400, 500 and 600. |
| Accent | Ultramarine `#3141C8` on light, periwinkle `#9AA3FF` on dark. A signal only: links, one primary button per view, the current tab, the focus ring. |
| Surfaces | Paper `bg`, white `surface`, `ink` text. Panels separate with a border, not a shadow. |
| Corners | Square. 4 px is the largest radius. Only avatars are round. |
| Status | A small square and the exact status word. Colour never carries a status alone. |
| Secret values | Never shown outside the reveal panel: no values, lengths, hashes or previews. |

## Where it lives

- The console reads the tokens from `src/index.css` in the [`ui`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/ui) repo (Tailwind `@theme`), with light and dark themes.
- This site maps the same tokens onto mkdocs-material in `docs/stylesheets/brand.css`.
- Logos, icons and the illustration are served from this site's `assets/` folder, listed on [Logos and assets](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/assets/).

If something here doesn't cover your case, open an issue in [`secrets-bridge/docs`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/docs/issues) and we'll either extend the system or write down the exception.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/brand-voice/

# Brand voice

Write the way the engineer who has to defend the claim in a review would.

## Rules

- **Say what we keep.** "We don't keep your secret values. We keep requests, approvals and audit metadata." Never "zero-knowledge" or "bank-grade".
- **Describe the mechanism.** "The agent connects out, so you open no inbound ports." Not "seamless connectivity".
- **Label maturity exactly.** Use the words on [Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/): implemented, QA-certified, in progress, roadmap. Not "production-ready".
- **Short sentences, plain verbs, sentence case.** "Ask for access. Someone approves. The agent reads it." No exclamation marks, no emoji.
- **No proof we don't have.** No invented customers, certifications, percentages or uptime.
- **Address the reader as "you".** Name people and teams: "Waiting for Sam Noor", not "Pending approval".
- **Errors say what happened and what to do.** "That code wasn't accepted. Nothing was retrieved."

## Describing the product

| Where | Wording |
|---|---|
| One line | Secrets Bridge governs who may use the secrets a team already keeps in AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault. |
| A little more | It adds access requests, approvals, audit and agent execution around those secrets. It keeps requests, approvals and audit metadata; the values stay in your provider. |
| Providers | Name the ones that work today. Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager are on the roadmap; say so when you mention them. |
| Maturity | Open source and pre-1.0. Link to [Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/) rather than restating it. |

## Words we avoid

seamless, effortless, military-grade, bank-grade, unbreakable, guaranteed, revolutionary, zero-knowledge, production-ready, SOC 2-ready (or any certification we don't hold).

## Examples

=== "README intro"

    ```markdown
    # Secrets Bridge

    Secrets Bridge governs who may use the secrets your team already keeps
    in AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault. It adds access requests,
    approvals, audit and agent execution around them. The values stay in
    your provider.
    ```

=== "Error message"

    ```text
    That key is outside the binding's allowed keys for this environment.
    Ask a project admin to check the binding.
    ```

=== "Pull request summary"

    ```markdown
    ## Summary

    The agent now refuses a job that names a different KV mount from the
    one it was configured with. Before, it read from the job's mount.
    ```

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/tokens/

# Tokens and theme

The console, this site and the brand assets use one set of tokens with light and dark values. Take every colour, size, radius and font from here; never copy a hex value out of a screenshot.

- **Console:** `src/index.css` in the [`ui`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/ui) repo declares them as CSS variables and maps them into Tailwind with `@theme`. `data-theme` on `<html>` switches light and dark, and the system setting is the default.
- **This site:** `docs/stylesheets/brand.css` maps them onto mkdocs-material's variables for its light and dark schemes.

## Colour

Build every screen from `bg`, `surface`, `ink`, `muted`, `border` and `rule`: roughly 70% `bg`, 13% `surface`, 10% `ink`, 5% `muted` and `rule`, and about 2% `accent`.

| Token | Light | Dark | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bg` | `#F6F5F1` | `#0F1013` | Paper. Page background behind everything; about 70% of a screen. |
| `surface` | `#FFFFFF` | `#17191E` | Panels, tables, dialogs, drawers and inputs sitting on bg. |
| `sunken` | `#EFEEE9` | `#1D1F25` | Row hover, current nav item, read-only boxes, key chips. |
| `ink` | `#15171C` | `#ECECEE` | Primary text and the production environment tag. 16.4:1 on bg (light), 16.1:1 (dark). |
| `muted` | `#5B606B` | `#A2A6AF` | Secondary text: subtitles, table headers, times, hints. 5.8:1 on bg (light), 7.8:1 (dark); passes 4.5:1 on surface and sunken too. |
| `border` | `#DDDBD4` | `#2B2E36` | Outer edges of panels, tables and dividers between sections. Decorative only: never the only edge of a control. |
| `rule` | `#E8E6E0` | `#22252B` | Hairlines between rows inside a table, list or log. |
| `edge` | `#7E838D` | `#686D7A` | Control borders (inputs, secondary buttons), dashed empty states, hollow status squares. At least 3.3:1 on bg, surface and sunken in light; 3.2:1 in dark. |
| `accent` | `#3141C8` | `#9AA3FF` | Ultramarine. The brand mark, links, the one primary button per view, current-tab underline, focus ring, reveal progress. About 2% of a screen. 7.1:1 on bg (light), 8.2:1 (dark). |
| `on-accent` | `#FFFFFF` | `#0F1013` | Text and icons on accent fills (primary button, nav count). 7.7:1 (light), 8.2:1 (dark). |
| `accent-soft` | `#E9EBFB` | `#1D2140` | Control-plane zone in diagrams and the avatar background. Never a status. |
| `accent-line` | `#BFC5F3` | `#3A4285` | Border for accent-soft areas. |
| `ok` | `#1E7A46` | `#6FCF97` | Success: approved, executed, reveal ready, copied. Text on ok-bg, bg and surface (4.7:1 or more); always with a word. ok and bad differ by hue more than lightness, so never rely on the colour of a status square alone. |
| `ok-bg` | `#E6F4EC` | `#132219` | Success fill behind ok text. |
| `ok-line` | `#A7D7BA` | `#24432F` | Border around ok-bg. |
| `warn` | `#7A5200` | `#F2C14E` | Waiting: pending, pending_values, pending_verification. Text on warn-bg, bg and surface. |
| `warn-bg` | `#FFF3D6` | `#2A2210` | Waiting fill behind warn text. |
| `warn-line` | `#EACB86` | `#4E4024` | Border around warn-bg. |
| `bad` | `#B3261E` | `#FF8A80` | Failure: rejected, refused, failed, validation errors. Text on bad-bg, bg and surface; always with a word. |
| `bad-bg` | `#FDECEA` | `#2C1513` | Failure fill behind bad text; hover on danger buttons. |
| `bad-line` | `#F1B8B3` | `#4E2522` | Border of danger buttons and error banners. |
| `info` | `#3E4A5C` | `#B7C0CF` | Neutral information labels. Text on info-bg. |
| `info-bg` | `#EEF0F3` | `#1B1F27` | Neutral information fill. |
| `info-line` | `#C9CED8` | `#323846` | Border around info-bg. |
| `scrim` | `rgba(21,23,28,0.36)` | `rgba(0,0,0,0.6)` | Overlay behind dialogs and drawers. |

`accent` is a signal: the mark, links, one primary button per view, the current tab, the focus ring, reveal progress. It is never a large fill, a status, or emphasis in running text. `edge` is for what you operate (input and secondary-button borders); `border` and `rule` only separate.

## Status

Show the exact API status as a word after a small square:

| Status | Square | Token |
|---|---|---|
| pending, pending_values, pending_verification | hollow | `warn` |
| approved, executed | solid | `ok` |
| rejected, refused, failed | solid | `bad` |
| cancelled, expired | hollow | `edge` |

A reveal condition (ready, consumed, expired) shows separately from the status, in `ok` or `muted` text. `executed` alone never means a reveal is available.

## Type

IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono (SIL Open Font License 1.1), weights 400, 500 and 600, self-hosted. Emphasis is weight, never italics or colour. Sentence case everywhere, including buttons and navigation.

| Group | Style | Size / line | Weight | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Website | `display` | 64 / 66 | 600 | The home page hero only |
| Website | `page-title` | 42 / 47 | 600 | Page h1 |
| Website | `section` | 38 / 43 | 600 | Home page sections |
| Website | `heading` | 23 / 30 | 600 | Headings in docs pages |
| Website | `lede` | 18 / 29 | 400 | The paragraph under a title |
| Website | `body-docs` | 16 / 27 | 400 | Docs body text |
| Console | `console-title` | 20 / 24 | 600 | Page h1 in the console |
| Console | `dialog-title` | 17 / 22 | 600 | Dialog and drawer titles |
| Console | `block-heading` | 13.5 / 20 | 600 | Above tables and panels |
| Console | `body` | 13.5 / 20 | 400 | Prose in the console |
| Console | `ui` | 13 / 18 | 500 | Controls |
| Console | `caption` | 12.5 / 18 | 400 | Hints |
| Console | `label` | 12 / 16 | 500 | Table headers |
| Mono | `mono`, `mono-small` | 13, 12 | 400 | Refs, key names, paths, times, IDs |

## Space, shape and size

| Token | Value |
|---|---|
| `space-1` to `space-8` | 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32 px |
| `radius-sm` | 3 px (tags) |
| `radius-md` | 4 px, the largest radius |
| `radius-round` | 50%, avatars only |
| `control-md` / `control-sm` / `control-touch` | 32 px default, 28 px in tables, 44 px on phones |
| `sidebar` / `rail` | 216 px console sidebar, 260 px overview side column |

Panels separate with a `border` line, never a shadow. The `overlay` shadow is only for dialogs, drawers and toasts.

## Accessibility

- Text at least 4.5:1, and controls, focus rings and status squares at least 3:1, against their background in both themes. The usage notes above give the ratios.
- Focus ring: 2 px solid `accent`, 2 px offset, on every interactive element.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Nothing in the product needs animation.

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/design/assets/

# Logos and assets

## The Checkpoint mark

Two squares joined by a route that turns once at a ring. Use the files below; never redraw the mark or retype the wordmark.

- Use the **horizontal lockup** (mark and wordmark) by default, the **mark alone** in square spaces, and the **favicon** form below 20 px.
- **Approved colourings:** ultramarine on `bg` or `surface`; periwinkle (`accent` dark) with light ink on dark; white on ultramarine; black; white.
- **Clear space** is 3/8 of the mark height on every side.
- Trademark clearance has not been checked.

| File | Use |
|---|---|
| [`logo-horizontal-color.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/logo-horizontal-color.svg) | Lockup on light backgrounds (this site's header) |
| [`logo-horizontal-dark.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/logo-horizontal-dark.svg) | Lockup on dark backgrounds |
| [`logo-mark.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/logo-mark.svg) | Mark alone, light backgrounds |
| [`logo-mark-dark.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/logo-mark-dark.svg) | Mark alone, dark backgrounds |
| [`favicon.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/favicon.svg) | Browser tabs and anything under 20 px |
| [`apple-touch-icon.png`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/apple-touch-icon.png) | iOS home screen (180 px) |
| [`og-banner.png`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/og-banner.png) | Social cards (1200 × 630) |

## Product icons

Four icons on a 24 px grid, 1.75 stroke, mitred joins, butt ends, one colour: request, approval, agent and audit. Inline them as SVG so they take `currentColor`.

| File | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [`icon-request.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/icons/icon-request.svg) | A request |
| [`icon-approval.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/icons/icon-approval.svg) | An approval |
| [`icon-agent.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/icons/icon-agent.svg) | The agent |
| [`icon-audit.svg`](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/icons/icon-audit.svg) | The audit log |

Right angles and 45° only; no curves except the checkpoint ring. No padlocks, shields, keys, clouds or circuit traces. No emoji.

## Diagrams

The architecture illustration ([light](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/architecture-light.svg), [dark](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/assets/architecture-dark.svg)) follows the diagram rules:

- Arrows point away from the side that opens the connection; solid opens, dashed returns.
- The control plane has an `accent-soft` fill with an `accent` edge. Customer infrastructure has a dashed `edge` outline.
- Providers connect only to the agent. Never draw a line from a provider to a browser or the console. Name providers in text; don't draw their logos.

Documentation diagrams use Mermaid, not screenshots.

# Operations

Everything you need to run Secrets Bridge.

| Page | When you'd read it |
|---|---|
| [Running locally with docker compose](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/docker-compose/) | First time trying it locally; smoke tests in CI |
| [Bootstrap & first sign-in](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/) | After the stack is up, how to sign in, enroll your first agent, run your first request |
| [Sign in with Google](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/) | Connecting a Google Workspace from the console and approving new accounts (in progress) |
| [Object storage](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/object-storage/) | Setting up an S3 or S3-compatible bucket for media such as logos (in progress) |
| [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/) | Installing and enrolling an optional Gateway for Argo CD observation (Release 1, in progress) |
| [Gateway cutover](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway-cutover/) | Upgrading an install that used the control-plane Argo CD poller: bind Gateways first, rotate the Argo CD token afterwards |
| [Verifying images and charts](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/verifying-releases/) | Checking the cosign signature, SBOM and provenance of images and charts before you deploy them |
| [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/) | Exhaustive env-var table for `api` / `agent` / `worker` / `controller` / `gateway`, plus the dev-only insecure switches |
| [Troubleshooting](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/troubleshooting/) | When things go wrong, common pitfalls + how to read the audit log |

## Production deployment

Install with the Helm charts from the
[`charts`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts) repo. Both publish as
OCI artifacts on GHCR:

| Chart | OCI reference | What it installs |
|---|---|---|
| `secrets-bridge` | `oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge` | api, ui, worker and controller behind one Ingress, in the control-plane cluster |
| `secrets-bridge-agent` | `oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-agent` | One outbound-only agent per workload cluster or account |
| `secrets-bridge-gateway` | `oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-gateway` | Optional. One read-only Gateway per boundary for Argo CD observation ([Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/), Release 1 in progress) |

Images publish to `ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/` as well. Until the first
`v0.1.0` release, chart versions look like `0.0.1-dev.<sha>`; pin an exact
version from the [package list](https://github.com/orgs/secrets-bridge/packages).

The chart defaults are the hardened baseline, so keep them rather than
writing your own Deployments: non-root pods with read-only root
filesystems, NetworkPolicies on by default, minimal RBAC, and render-time
guards. `helm install` fails before anything starts when `kms.backend=local`
is combined with `env=production`, when `env` or `kms.backend` is unknown,
when a production image resolves to a mutable `:dev` or `:latest` tag
without a digest, or when the agent's control-plane endpoint is plain
`http://`.

```bash
# 1. Pre-create the env Secret the chart reads (secrets.existingSecret,
#    default name secrets-bridge-env): DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL and the
#    SB_KMS_* settings for your backend. Deliver it with
#    External Secrets, sealed-secrets or similar; never commit it.

# 2. Install the control plane. Production needs every image pinned.
helm install secrets-bridge oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace secrets-bridge --create-namespace \
  --set ingress.host=secrets-bridge.example.com \
  --set kms.backend=aws-kms \
  --set kms.awsKms.region=us-east-1 \
  --set kms.awsKms.keyId=alias/sb-wrap \
  --set api.image.digest=sha256:<digest> \
  --set ui.image.digest=sha256:<digest> \
  --set worker.image.digest=sha256:<digest> \
  --set controller.image.digest=sha256:<digest>
```

Then onboard agents with the `secrets-bridge-agent` chart in enrollment
mode; see [Enrolling your first agent](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/#enrolling-your-first-agent).
Each chart's README in the `charts` repo documents every value.

Around the charts you provide:

- A managed Postgres + Redis on a private network (we test against
  Postgres 17 + Redis 7)
- A real KMS backend (`vault-transit` or `aws-kms`, **never** `local`
  outside dev)
- An ingress controller with TLS and a real certificate

## Hardening checklist (before exposing to anyone)

- [ ] `SB_ENV` is `production` (the default), never `dev`
- [ ] `SB_KMS_BACKEND` is `vault-transit` or `aws-kms`
  (**never** `local`)
- [ ] None of the api's
  [insecure switches](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#insecure-switches-dev-only) are set:
  `SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_HEADER_AUTH`, `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT`,
  `SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR`, `SB_MFA_DEV_ALLOW_PWD` are unset or
  `false`, and `SB_PROVIDER_CONN_REJECT_SECRETS` is unset or `true`
- [ ] `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT` on the agent is **unset** (default
  is to refuse `http://`), and the chart's `cp.insecureTransport` is
  `false`
- [ ] Agents are onboarded with one-time enrollment tokens and
  `secrets-bridge-agent enroll`; each agent's identity Secret
  (`agent_id`, `agent_secret`, `private_key`) lives in your secret store or a
  Kubernetes Secret that only the agent and its operators can read, and is
  in no Helm values, Git repository or CI log
- [ ] TLS terminator (ingress) configured with HSTS + a real
  certificate
- [ ] `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` is **rotated** immediately
  after first login
- [ ] The admin user has a real OIDC identity assigned and the local
  admin is disabled (see [Authentication](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/))
- [ ] Postgres is on a private network: the api + worker are the
  only clients
- [ ] Redis is on a private network: the api + worker are the
  only clients
- [ ] Audit-event shipping is configured (the schema-level
  append-only triggers are a defense, not a substitute for
  off-host log shipping)
- [ ] Backup the KMS master key / Vault Transit key / AWS CMK:
  it's the only thing that can unwrap your envelopes

See the [Threat model](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/) for the
attacker postures these defend against.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/docker-compose/

# Running locally with docker compose

A local loop for trying Secrets Bridge on one machine. The compose file
lives in the [`api`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api) repo. It starts
Postgres 17 and Redis 7, and can also build and run the api. The UI and the
agent run from their own repos.

!!! danger "Local development only"
    This setup uses dev-only switches: `SB_ENV=dev`, the `local` KMS backend,
    and for the agent walkthrough `SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR` and
    `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT`. They are listed under
    [Insecure switches](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#insecure-switches-dev-only). Never expose
    this stack beyond your machine and never load real secrets into it.

## Quick start

### 1. Start Postgres and Redis

```bash
git clone https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api.git
cd api
docker compose up -d postgres redis
```

### 2. Generate dev keys

Generate fresh keys for every new environment. Never reuse a value from
these docs, an old compose file or another environment.

```bash
export SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"   # master key for the local KMS backend
```

The `local` KMS backend refuses to start without `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY`.

### 3. Run the api

From the `api` checkout (Go 1.25 or newer):

```bash
export SB_ENV=dev   # allows the local KMS backend and seeds three dev users
export DATABASE_URL="postgres://secrets_bridge:devpass@localhost:5432/secrets_bridge?sslmode=disable"
export REDIS_URL="redis://localhost:6379/0"
go run ./cmd/api
```

In another terminal:

```bash
curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/readyz
# → {"status":"ready"}
```

On its first boot against an empty database the api seeds three dev users
(an admin, an approver and a requester) and logs each user's email and
password **once**. Copy them from that log output. Set `SB_DEV_SEED_PASSWORD`
before the first boot if you want one shared password instead of a random
one per user.

!!! note "Running the api in a container instead"
    `docker compose up -d --build` also builds the `api` service from the
    repo's Dockerfile and runs it on port 8080. Export the keys from step 2
    in the same shell first: the api container reads `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY`
    from your environment and exits with an error when it is unset. Older
    copies of the compose file shipped a fixed dev master key instead; pull
    the latest `main` rather than reusing it.

### 4. Run the UI

From a checkout of the [`ui`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/ui) repo
(Node 22 or newer):

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open **http://localhost:5173/**. The Vite dev server proxies `/api` to
`http://localhost:8080`. Sign in with the admin user from the api's boot
log. `SB_ENV=dev` is what lets the session cookie work over plain
`http://localhost`.

## Wiring an agent end to end (Vault example)

An admin creates a one-time token for a provider connection,
`secrets-bridge-agent enroll` exchanges it for the agent credential and
generates the X25519 key locally, and the agent reads both from a read-only
directory. The steps below run everything locally. See
[Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/) for the model.

```bash
# 1. A throwaway Vault dev server on localhost, with a fake value in it.
export VAULT_DEV_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
docker run -d --name sb-vault-dev -p 127.0.0.1:8200:8200 \
  -e VAULT_DEV_ROOT_TOKEN_ID="$VAULT_DEV_TOKEN" hashicorp/vault:2.2
docker exec -e VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 -e VAULT_TOKEN="$VAULT_DEV_TOKEN" \
  sb-vault-dev vault kv put secret/team-alpha/dev/db DB_PASSWORD=not-a-real-password

# 2. Restart the api with SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR=true (dev only):
#    the dev Vault listens on http://, which provider connections refuse
#    by default.

# 3. Sign in as the seeded admin. The password goes to jq on stdin, so
#    it never shows in the process list. The session cookie goes into a
#    private cookie jar; every call below sends it with -b.
CP=http://localhost:8080
JAR=$(mktemp) && chmod 600 "$JAR"
read -rp 'Admin email: ' SB_ADMIN_EMAIL
IFS= read -rsp 'Admin password: ' SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n' "$SB_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | jq -Rn '{email: input, password: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/login" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-

# 4. Register the Vault provider connection.
CONN_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"local-vault","type":"vault","auth_method":"token","cluster_name":"local",
       "scope":{"address":"http://127.0.0.1:8200","mount":"secret"},
       "discover_interval_seconds":3600}' \
  | jq -r .id)

# 5. From a checkout of the agent repo: create a one-time enrollment token
#    for that connection (15 minutes by default) and hand it to enroll on
#    stdin. The bundle lands in a shell variable, then in three owner-only
#    files. Dev only: in a real install it goes to your secret store.
#    SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true lets enroll and the agent use the local
#    http:// endpoint, the same dev-only switch as the runtime.
cd ../agent   # wherever you cloned github.com/secrets-bridge/agent
mkdir -p -m 700 .local/credentials
SB_BUNDLE=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections/$CONN_ID/agent-enrollment-token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"local-agent","expected_cluster_name":"local","expected_provider_type":"vault"}' \
  | jq -j .enrollment_token \
  | SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true go run ./cmd/agent enroll --cp-endpoint "$CP" --token-file - \
      --name local-agent --cluster-name local --provider-type vault \
      --format json --output -)
for k in agent_id agent_secret private_key; do
  (umask 077 && jq -j ".$k" <<<"$SB_BUNDLE" > ".local/credentials/$k")
done
unset SB_BUNDLE

# 6. Run the agent against that directory. It runs in the background;
#    `kill %1` stops it. SB_VAULT_KV_MOUNT has to be the connection's mount
#    from step 4. The agent defaults to `kv`; with a mismatch it refuses
#    discovery and points reads and patches at the wrong mount.
SB_CP_ENDPOINT="$CP" SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true \
SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR="$PWD/.local/credentials" SB_CLUSTER_NAME=local \
SB_VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 SB_VAULT_TOKEN="$VAULT_DEV_TOKEN" \
SB_VAULT_KV_MOUNT=secret \
  go run ./cmd/agent > .local/agent.log 2>&1 &

# 7. After a few seconds the agent is listed, `active`, against the connection.
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections/$CONN_ID/agents" | jq
```

The token is spent by step 5. The agent only reads `.local/credentials` and
writes nothing, so a restart reuses the same files. The files must stay
owner-only: the agent refuses a file with group write or any bit for others.
To start over, revoke the agent, delete `.local/credentials` and create a new
token.

## Ports

| Host port | Service | What |
|---|---|---|
| `8080` | api | Control Plane API: `/api/v1/*`, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics`. Change it with `API_HOST_PORT` when the api runs in compose. |
| `5432` | postgres | Postgres 17 (`secrets_bridge` / `devpass`) |
| `6379` | redis | Redis 7 |
| `4566` | localstack (`--profile awskms`) | LocalStack KMS, for trying the `aws-kms` backend |
| `5173` | Vite dev server | The UI, from the `ui` repo |
| `8200` | Vault dev server | Only if you started it for the agent walkthrough |

The compose file publishes its ports on `127.0.0.1` only, so nothing is
reachable from other machines. Older copies of the compose file published
Postgres and Redis on every interface with fixed dev credentials; if yours
still does, pull the latest `main` before you start it on a shared network.

## Resetting state

```bash
# Stop everything and drop the Postgres volume (wipes all data,
# including the seeded users)
docker compose down -v
docker rm -f sb-vault-dev   # if you started it
rm -rf .local/credentials  # in the agent checkout
```

## What docker compose is good for, what it's not

| Use it for | Don't use it for |
|---|---|
| Local development | Production |
| Smoke tests and e2e in CI | Multi-replica deployments |
| Following along with this docs site | Anything internet-exposed |
| Demoing to a colleague | Storing real secrets |

For production, install the hardened Helm charts on a real Kubernetes
cluster with managed Postgres and Redis and a real KMS backend. See
[Production deployment](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/#production-deployment).

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/

# Bootstrap & first sign-in

After the api starts for the first time, the platform has to be
**bootstrapped** with a usable admin identity. Otherwise nothing
can be done: every write endpoint is gated by
`auth.Require(perm)` and there are no role assignments yet.

## What "bootstrapped" means

Two things happen on first boot when `local_users` is empty and
the bootstrap env vars are set:

1. **A local admin user is created**, bcrypt-hashed password
   stored in `local_users` (idempotent: a second boot with the
   same env vars is a no-op once any user exists).
2. **The new user is bound to the seed `admin` role** with global
   scope, via the existing user_roles flow.

The api logs both actions at INFO in its JSON log output:

```
{"msg":"bootstrap local admin created","user_id":"<uuid>","email":"admin@example.com"}
{"msg":"bootstrap admin assignment created","user_id":"<uuid>","role":"admin","scope":"global"}
```

## Configuration

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` | recommended on first boot |  | Becomes the local-admin email |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | recommended on first boot |  | **Rotate immediately after first sign-in** |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USER_ID` | optional |  | Pre-OIDC escape hatch: assigns the admin role to a specific opaque `user_id` (matches the future OIDC `sub` claim). Use this alongside `_EMAIL`/`_PASSWORD` if you want both the local-admin login and a pre-arranged OIDC identity to hold admin. |

## First sign-in

1. Open the UI (`http://localhost:5173/` for the
   [local docker compose setup](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/docker-compose/)).
2. You'll be redirected to `/login`.
3. Enter the email + password from the env vars (or a dev user from
   the api's first-boot log when it runs with `SB_ENV=dev`).
4. With `SB_ENV=dev` you land on the Dashboard with the `Agents Online`
   KPI showing `0 / 0`. On a production install, where login-time MFA
   is on by default, you land on **Second factor** first: add an
   authenticator app or a security key, then **Continue** asks for it
   once and opens the Dashboard
   ([Step-up vs login-time MFA](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#step-up-vs-login-time-mfa)).

The api keeps you signed in with an HttpOnly session cookie, which
the SPA's scripts can't read. Sign out from the console to end the
session.

## Rotating the admin password

There's no UI surface for this in the current slice. For now, use
`psql` directly against the api's Postgres:

```bash
# Generate a bcrypt hash for the new password
NEW_HASH=$(htpasswd -bnBC 12 "" "your-new-password" | tr -d ':\n' | sed 's/^.\$2y/$2y/')

# Update the row (local docker compose setup; use your own psql
# connection elsewhere)
docker compose exec -T postgres \
  psql -U secrets_bridge -d secrets_bridge \
  -c "UPDATE local_users SET password_hash = decode('$(echo "$NEW_HASH" | xxd -p)', 'hex') WHERE email = 'admin@example.com';"
```

A real password-change endpoint + UI page lands as a follow-up.

## Disabling the local admin (after OIDC ships)

Once you've added a real OIDC identity with the admin role, you
can disable the local-admin row so brute-force attempts against
its bcrypt hash are pointless:

```sql
UPDATE local_users SET disabled = TRUE WHERE email = 'admin@example.com';
```

A disabled user's login attempts return the same generic
`401 invalid credentials`; the audit log records
`error_kind=user_disabled`.

## Enrolling your first agent

An admin creates a one-time token bound to a provider connection. An operator
then runs `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` on a trusted workstation: it generates
the agent's X25519 key locally, exchanges the token for `agent_id` and
`agent_secret`, and prints the bundle once, to be stored in your secret store or
a Kubernetes Secret. The agent pod only reads that Secret. See
[Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/) for the model, the AWS Secrets Manager
and Vault variants, and key custody.

Create the token in the console or through the API, as below. You need
`agent.mint` (the seed `admin` role has it), an active
[provider connection](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/provider-connections/) and, on a production install,
a second factor on your account: login-time MFA is on by default outside
`SB_ENV=dev`, so add an authenticator app under **Second factor** in the
console first ([Step-up vs login-time MFA](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#step-up-vs-login-time-mfa)).

```bash
CP=https://secrets-bridge.example.com   # http://localhost:8080 for the local setup

# Sign in. The password is read from the terminal and handed to jq on
# stdin (printf is a shell builtin), so it is never in a command line,
# the shell history or the process list. The session cookie goes into a
# private cookie jar.
JAR=$(mktemp) && chmod 600 "$JAR"
read -rp 'Admin email: ' SB_ADMIN_EMAIL
IFS= read -rsp 'Admin password: ' SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n' "$SB_ADMIN_EMAIL" "$SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | jq -Rn '{email: input, password: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -c "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/login" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-
unset SB_ADMIN_PASSWORD

# Step up with your TOTP factor (production: login-time MFA is on; skip
# this block on the local SB_ENV=dev setup). Fresh for 15 minutes.
FACTOR_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/users/me/mfa/factors" \
  | jq -r 'map(select(.kind == "totp"))[0].id')
CHALLENGE_ID=$(curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/mfa/challenge" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"kind":"totp"}' | jq -r .challenge_id)
IFS= read -rsp 'TOTP code: ' SB_TOTP_CODE; echo
printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n' "$CHALLENGE_ID" "$FACTOR_ID" "$SB_TOTP_CODE" \
  | jq -Rn '{challenge_id: input, factor_id: input, code: input}' \
  | curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -o /dev/null -X POST "$CP/api/v1/auth/mfa/verify" \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @-
unset SB_TOTP_CODE

# Pick the provider connection the agent will serve.
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections" \
  | jq '.[] | {id, name, type, cluster_name, status}'
CONN_ID=<provider-connection-id>

# Create the one-time token and hand it straight to enroll on stdin, then
# write the bundle into a Kubernetes Secret in the workload cluster. The
# token, agent_secret and private_key are never printed, never in argv and
# never on disk.
kubectl create namespace secrets-bridge   # skip if it already exists
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" -X POST "$CP/api/v1/provider-connections/$CONN_ID/agent-enrollment-token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"cluster-a-agent","expected_cluster_name":"cluster-a","expected_provider_type":"vault"}' \
  | jq -j .enrollment_token \
  | secrets-bridge-agent enroll --cp-endpoint "$CP" --token-file - \
      --name cluster-a-agent --cluster-name cluster-a --provider-type vault \
      --format env --output - \
  | kubectl -n secrets-bridge create secret generic secrets-bridge-agent-identity \
      --from-env-file=/dev/stdin
rm -f "$JAR"
```

All body fields are optional. `expires_in_seconds` defaults to 900 (15
minutes) and is clamped to 60 to 86400. When `expected_cluster_name` or
`expected_provider_type` is set, an enrollment that reports anything else is
refused. The response carries the token exactly once, so don't log or paste
the whole response.

Then install the `agent` chart with the Secret's name (see
[Production deployment](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/#production-deployment) for the chart
source):

```bash
helm install secrets-bridge-agent oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-agent \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace secrets-bridge \
  --set clusterName=cluster-a \
  --set cp.endpoint=https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
  --set image.digest=sha256:<agent-digest> \
  --set identity.existingSecret=secrets-bridge-agent-identity \
  --set providers.vault.enabled=true \
  --set providers.vault.addr=https://vault.example.com \
  --set providers.vault.kubernetesRole=secrets-bridge-agent
```

The agent reads `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` from the Secret,
mounted read-only at `/etc/secrets-bridge/agent`, and starts heartbeating.
Restarts read the same Secret. The agent shows up under
`GET /api/v1/provider-connections/<id>/agents` and turns `active` on its
first heartbeat.

If enrollment is refused (expired token, wrong cluster name or provider
type), fix the cause and create a new token. An unused token stops working
when it expires, so keep `expires_in_seconds` short. See
[Troubleshooting: agent](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/troubleshooting/#agent).

!!! warning "Direct agent mint is a dev-only break-glass"
    `POST /api/v1/agents` is the legacy direct mint, which hands back a
    long-lived `agent_secret` and also requires a public key. The api refuses it with
    `403 direct_agent_mint_disabled` unless it runs with
    `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true`. Leave that switch off outside a
    local dev loop; see [Insecure switches](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#insecure-switches-dev-only).

## Submitting your first read request

Once you have an agent running and `provider creds`
configured for it:

1. **Sidebar → Requests → + New request**
2. **Read** type
3. **Provider**: Vault (or AWS Secrets Manager)
4. **Project** and **Environment**: the project and environment the
   secret is bound to. Environment is required when the binding is
   scoped to one
5. **Secret reference**: e.g. `prod/db/password`
6. **Keys**: e.g. `DB_PASSWORD` (or leave one empty row for "all
   keys in the bundle")
7. **Justification**: required, typically an incident or ticket
   number
8. **Submit** → you're navigated to the request detail page

Then sign in as a second user with the `secret.approve` permission
and approve from the Requests page's Approver queue. The requester
can never approve or reject their own request, whatever their role
(admin included) or the workflow says: the api answers
`403 separation_of_duties_violated` and audits the attempt.

Once approved → agent claims → fetches → posts wrap → request →
`executed`. Refresh the detail page; the Wraps card now shows
`DB_PASSWORD` with the **Reveal (one-time)** button. Click it,
confirm, see the value, copy it, close.

That's the whole read flow.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/

# Agent onboarding

An agent runs inside your boundary (a Kubernetes cluster, a VPC, an account)
and talks outbound only, to the control plane and to its local provider. It is
stateless: it reads its identity from a read-only Secret and never writes a
file, a PVC or a Kubernetes Secret.

Onboarding has four steps:

1. An admin creates a one-time enrollment token in the console.
2. An operator runs `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` on a trusted workstation
   inside your boundary. The command generates the agent's X25519 key pair
   locally and exchanges the token for the agent credential.
3. The operator stores the result in AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or a
   Kubernetes Secret.
4. The agent is deployed with the `agent` Helm chart and
   `identity.existingSecret` pointing at that Secret.

!!! note "First-release requirement"
    This flow is a requirement for the first release
    ([skills#116](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/skills/issues/116)). It
    replaces the earlier enrollment at pod start with a PVC, which is removed.
    It is in progress, not live: see [Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/).

## The flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Admin
    participant CP as Control plane
    participant Op as Operator workstation
    participant Store as Your secret store
    participant Agent
    Admin->>CP: Create one-time enrollment token (agent.mint)
    CP-->>Admin: enrollment_token (shown once, stored as a hash)
    Admin->>Op: hand over the token out of band
    Note over Op: enroll generates the X25519 key pair locally
    Op->>CP: POST /agents/enroll/challenge {token, public_key}
    CP-->>Op: challenge sealed to the public key
    Note over Op: opens the challenge with the private key
    Op->>CP: POST /agents/enroll {token, challenge_id, challenge_response}
    CP-->>Op: agent_id, agent_secret (returned once), public_key_fingerprint
    Op->>Store: agent_id, agent_secret, private_key (stdin, never argv)
    Store-->>Agent: read-only Secret at /etc/secrets-bridge/agent
    loop heartbeat and claim
        Agent->>CP: X-Agent-Secret + X-Agent-Key-Fingerprint
        CP-->>Agent: 200 / job
    end
```

The control plane checks the enrollment token without spending it, seals a
random challenge to the submitted public key, and only creates the agent when
the operator returns the decrypted challenge. That proves the enrolling client
holds the private key. The token is consumed in the same transaction that
creates the agent, and the agent is bound to the token's provider connection.

## Key custody

| Material | Generated by | Held by | The control plane keeps |
|---|---|---|---|
| X25519 private key (`private_key`) | `secrets-bridge-agent enroll`, on your workstation | Your secret store and the agent pod | Nothing |
| X25519 public key | Derived from the private key | Sent at enrollment | The public key and its fingerprint (`sha256:` plus hex) |
| Agent credential (`agent_id`, `agent_secret`) | The control plane, returned once | Your secret store and the agent pod | `agent_id` and the SHA-256 of `agent_secret` |
| Enrollment token | The control plane | The admin, briefly | A hash, until it is spent or expires |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph boundary ["Your boundary"]
        CLI["secrets-bridge-agent enroll<br/>(operator workstation)"]
        Store["AWS Secrets Manager / Vault /<br/>Kubernetes Secret"]
        Pod["Agent pod<br/>read-only /etc/secrets-bridge/agent"]
        CLI -->|"agent_id, agent_secret, private_key<br/>(stdin pipe)"| Store
        Store -->|"ESO or kubectl, mounted 0400 read-only"| Pod
    end
    subgraph cp ["Control plane"]
        DB["public key + fingerprint<br/>SHA-256 of agent_secret"]
    end
    CLI -->|"public key + challenge response"| DB
    Pod -->|"X-Agent-Secret + X-Agent-Key-Fingerprint<br/>(outbound HTTPS)"| DB
```

The X25519 key is a wire-encryption key. The control plane seals the values it
sends to the agent (for example, a patch value) to this key, so only the agent
can open them. It is not a TLS client certificate and plays no part in TLS: the
agent still verifies the control plane's certificate, and it authenticates with
`agent_secret`. The private key never leaves your boundary, and nothing in the
console or the API can show it.

Every request the agent makes carries `X-Agent-Key-Fingerprint`. The control
plane compares it with the key bound at enrollment, and the agent refuses a
sealed value whose recipient fingerprint is not its own. There is no API call
that replaces an agent's public key in normal operation; a key changes only
through the audited [rotation](#rotate-the-wire-key) below.

### Where secrets must never go

Keep the enrollment token, `agent_secret` and `private_key` out of:

- Helm values, `--set` flags and Argo CD or Flux application specs;
- shell arguments and shell history (read the token at a silent prompt and pass
  it on stdin, as shown below);
- Git, including a generated Secret manifest (`enroll --format k8s-secret` is
  for piping into
  `kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=secrets-bridge-agent -f -`,
  never for committing);
- the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation (see the
  warning below);
- CI logs and job output;
- the browser, chat messages and tickets.

!!! warning "Apply the agent Secret server-side"
    Client-side `kubectl apply -f -` stores the whole object it applies,
    including the plaintext `agent_secret` and `private_key` from
    `stringData`, in the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration`
    annotation. That copy sits outside `.data`, where tools that treat
    metadata as non-sensitive can expose it. The same happens with
    `kubectl create secret ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`.
    Use `kubectl apply --server-side`, which keeps no such copy, or
    `kubectl create secret generic --from-env-file=/dev/stdin`. To check a
    Secret, run
    `kubectl -n secrets-bridge get secret secrets-bridge-agent-identity -o jsonpath=''`:
    it must not list `last-applied-configuration`.

`enroll` writes nothing secret to stderr or to logs. It may print the
`agent_id` and the key fingerprint to stderr.

## Step 1: create an enrollment token

In the console, an admin with `agent.mint` creates a one-time enrollment token
for the provider connection the agent will serve. The token is tied to that
connection, and optionally to an expected cluster name and provider type. It
expires after 15 minutes by default and works once. Scripts can call
`POST /api/v1/provider-connections/:id/agent-enrollment-token` instead; see
[Enrolling your first agent](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/#enrolling-your-first-agent).

## Step 2: enroll from your workstation

Run `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` (the agent binary, as a subcommand) on a
trusted machine inside your boundary. It needs HTTPS access to the control
plane.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--cp-endpoint` | The control plane URL. `https://` only, with the same TLS options as the agent runtime |
| `--token-file ` | The enrollment token, from a file or from stdin (`-`). There is no `--token` flag |
| `--name`, `--provider-type` | Required. The agent's name and provider type (`aws-sm`, `vault`). The provider type must match the token's expected value when it has one |
| `--cluster-name`, `--region` | Reported at enrollment. The cluster name must match the token's expected value when it has one |
| `--output ` | Where the bundle goes. A file is created with mode `0600` and refused if it exists. `-` is stdout |
| `--format json\|env\|k8s-secret` | Bundle format, `json` by default. `env` is `key=value` lines for `kubectl create secret generic --from-env-file`; `k8s-secret` is a Secret manifest for `kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=secrets-bridge-agent -f -` (never client-side apply) |
| `--secret-name` | Name of the Secret in the `k8s-secret` format. Default `secrets-bridge-agent-identity` |

The bundle has `agent_id`, `agent_secret`, `private_key` and
`public_key_fingerprint`. The agent ignores `public_key_fingerprint`, and the
chart mounts only the other three keys, so a Secret with all four is fine. Pipe it straight into your secret store, as in step 3,
so it never lands on disk or in the terminal. Each example reads the token at a
silent prompt first:

```bash
read -rsp 'Enrollment token: ' SB_ENROLL_TOKEN; echo
```

and runs `unset SB_ENROLL_TOKEN` at the end. `printf` is a shell builtin, so the
token does not show up in the process list.

## Step 3: store the credential

Pick one store. The agent only reads the Kubernetes Secret, so External Secrets
Operator (ESO) is one way to fill that Secret, not a runtime dependency.

=== "AWS Secrets Manager"

    Create the secret first with your infrastructure code (empty, with the tags
    and KMS key you want). Then write the bundle to it:

    ```bash
    printf '%s' "$SB_ENROLL_TOKEN" \
      | secrets-bridge-agent enroll --cp-endpoint https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
          --token-file - --name prod-eu-agent --cluster-name prod-eu --provider-type aws-sm \
          --region us-east-1 --format json --output - \
      | aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
          --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:secrets-bridge/agents/prod-eu \
          --secret-string file:///dev/stdin
    unset SB_ENROLL_TOKEN
    ```

    Then sync it into the cluster with an ESO `ExternalSecret` that copies the
    `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` properties. The chart repo has
    a tested example in
    [`agent/examples/eso-aws-secrets-manager`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/tree/main/agent/examples/eso-aws-secrets-manager).

=== "Vault"

    ```bash
    printf '%s' "$SB_ENROLL_TOKEN" \
      | secrets-bridge-agent enroll --cp-endpoint https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
          --token-file - --name prod-eu-agent --cluster-name prod-eu --provider-type vault \
          --format json --output - \
      | vault kv put -mount=kv secrets-bridge/agents/prod-eu -
    unset SB_ENROLL_TOKEN
    ```

    `vault kv put  -` reads the JSON object from stdin. Sync it with an
    ESO `ExternalSecret`; see
    [`agent/examples/eso-vault`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/tree/main/agent/examples/eso-vault).

=== "Kubernetes Secret"

    ```bash
    kubectl create namespace secrets-bridge
    printf '%s' "$SB_ENROLL_TOKEN" \
      | secrets-bridge-agent enroll --cp-endpoint https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
          --token-file - --name prod-eu-agent --cluster-name prod-eu --provider-type vault \
          --format env --output - \
      | kubectl -n secrets-bridge create secret generic secrets-bridge-agent-identity \
          --from-env-file=/dev/stdin
    unset SB_ENROLL_TOKEN
    ```

    The same script is in
    [`agent/examples/kubectl-secret`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/tree/main/agent/examples/kubectl-secret).
    `secrets-bridge-agent-identity` is the documented name and the default of
    `--secret-name`. Restrict `get` on Secrets in that namespace to the people
    who run the agent.

If the pipe fails after the control plane answered (for example, the secret
store refused the write), the bundle is lost and the token is spent. Revoke the
half-created agent and start again with a new token.

### Least-privilege write access for whoever runs enroll

The person or pipeline that runs `enroll` needs to write one entry, and nothing
else.

AWS Secrets Manager, for an existing secret (the `-??????` matches the random
suffix AWS adds to the ARN):

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "WriteOneAgentCredential",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "secretsmanager:PutSecretValue",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:secrets-bridge/agents/prod-eu-??????"
    }
  ]
}
```

When the secret uses a customer managed KMS key, also allow
`kms:GenerateDataKey` and `kms:Encrypt` on that key, with the condition
`kms:ViaService = secretsmanager.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`. The writer needs no
`GetSecretValue`. ESO reads with its own role, which needs
`secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on the same ARN (and `kms:Decrypt` through
Secrets Manager), and nothing else.

Vault, KV version 2 mounted at `kv`:

```hcl
# Writer: the operator who runs enroll.
path "kv/data/secrets-bridge/agents/prod-eu" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}
```

```hcl
# Reader: the ESO role that syncs the Secret.
path "kv/data/secrets-bridge/agents/prod-eu" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
```

## Step 4: deploy the agent

```bash
helm install secrets-bridge-agent oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge-agent \
  --version <chart-version> \
  --namespace secrets-bridge \
  --set clusterName=prod-eu \
  --set cp.endpoint=https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
  --set image.digest=sha256:<agent-digest> \
  --set identity.existingSecret=secrets-bridge-agent-identity \
  --set providers.vault.enabled=true \
  --set providers.vault.addr=https://vault.example.com \
  --set providers.vault.kubernetesRole=secrets-bridge-agent
```

`identity.existingSecret` names the Secret, never its contents, so these values
are safe to commit. The chart:

- mounts the Secret read-only at `/etc/secrets-bridge/agent` with
  `defaultMode: 0400`, and sets `SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR` to that path;
- maps the keys `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` to files of the
  same name (`identity.keys.*` maps other key names);
- renders no PVC, no writable volume and no Role or RoleBinding;
- refuses the removed settings (`identity.mode`, `identity.persistence`,
  `enrollment.*` and others) at render time, naming the key.

Secret volume files are owned by root. The chart requires
`podSecurityContext.fsGroup` (default `65532`), which gives them the agent's
group, and kubelet then adds the group read bit, so the files show up in the pod
