as `0440 root:65532`. Without `fsGroup` they stay `0400 root:root` and the
non-root agent can't read them. The agent accepts owner and group read, and
refuses a file with group write or any permission for others
(`mode & 0o037 != 0`).

At start the agent loads the three files, derives the public key and its
fingerprint, and sends the fingerprint with every request. It fails closed: a
missing, empty or malformed file, or a file that is too open, stops it before it
contacts the control plane. It never generates a key and never falls back to an
ephemeral one.

To check the result, compare the fingerprint `enroll` printed with the one the
console shows for the agent. The agent turns `active` on its first heartbeat.

## Restarts and reschedules

A restart or a move to another node reads the same Secret. The agent keeps no
local state, so nothing is lost and no token is needed. Because two pods can run
briefly during a rolling update with the same identity, set
`strategy.type: Recreate` in the chart if you want no overlap.

## Rotate the wire key

Rotation replaces the X25519 key and keeps `agent_id` and `agent_secret`.

1. An admin requests the rotation in the console, or with
   `POST /api/v1/admin/agents/:id/key-rotation`. This needs `agent.mint` and a
   fresh second factor. The answer is a one-time rotation token that expires
   after 15 minutes. The request is audited as `agent.key_rotation.requested`.
2. On the workstation, with the current credential available as a read-only
   directory, run:

    ```bash
    printf '%s' "$SB_ROTATION_TOKEN" \
      | secrets-bridge-agent rotate-key --cp-endpoint https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
          --credentials-dir /path/to/current/credentials \
          --rotation-token-file - --format json --output - \
      | aws secretsmanager put-secret-value \
          --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:secrets-bridge/agents/prod-eu \
          --secret-string file:///dev/stdin
    unset SB_ROTATION_TOKEN
    ```

    `rotate-key` generates the new key locally and runs the same challenge as
    enrollment, sealed to the new key. The control plane then binds the new key,
    increments `public_key_version` and audits `agent.key.rotated` with the old
    and new fingerprints. Write to Vault the same way as in step 3.

    `kubectl create secret` refuses a Secret that exists, so update a
    Kubernetes Secret in place with a server-side apply:

    ```bash
    printf '%s' "$SB_ROTATION_TOKEN" \
      | secrets-bridge-agent rotate-key --cp-endpoint https://secrets-bridge.example.com \
          --credentials-dir /path/to/current/credentials \
          --rotation-token-file - --format k8s-secret --output - \
      | kubectl -n secrets-bridge apply --server-side \
          --field-manager=secrets-bridge-agent --force-conflicts -f -
    unset SB_ROTATION_TOKEN
    ```

    `--force-conflicts` takes over the fields that `kubectl create secret` (or
    another field manager) set at enrollment; without it the apply stops with
    a conflict. A server-side apply over a Secret that an earlier client-side
    apply wrote also drops the old `last-applied-configuration` annotation.
3. Restart the agent once the Kubernetes Secret has the new key: wait for ESO
   to sync it (or force a sync), then `kubectl rollout restart` the Deployment.
   With `reloader.enabled=true` (the chart default) and
   [stakater/reloader](https://github.com/stakater/Reloader) installed, the
   restart happens on its own.

Between step 2 and the restart, the running agent still holds the old key and
gets `409 agent_key_mismatch`. Nothing is lost: wraps are sealed when the agent
fetches them, so queued work is sealed to the new key once the restarted agent
picks it up.

## Revoke an agent

1. Revoke the agent in the console (or `POST /api/v1/admin/agents/:id/revoke`
   with a reason, needs `agent.revoke`). Its next heartbeat or claim is refused,
   and any open rotation tokens and challenges for it stop working.
2. Uninstall the chart or scale the Deployment to zero.
3. Delete the Kubernetes Secret and the entry in AWS Secrets Manager or Vault.
4. For a replacement, start again at step 1 with a new enrollment token.

An unused enrollment token can be revoked on its own with
`POST /api/v1/agent-enrollment-tokens/:id/revoke`.

## Gateway parity

The [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/) runs the same way at the storage level: it is
stateless, and it reads `gateway_id`, `gateway_secret` and, when a connector has
discovery on, the optional `snapshot_key` from read-only Kubernetes Secrets. It
has no X25519 key and no PVC, and it keeps its own enrollment token and scopes,
separate from agents.

## Safety properties

- One-time enrollment tokens: hashed at rest, short TTL, single use, bound to
  one provider connection.
- Proof of possession: an agent is created only when the enrolling client opens
  a challenge sealed to the key it submitted.
- The control plane stores the public key and a hash of `agent_secret`, never
  the private key or the plaintext secret.
- No key substitution: a key changes only through the audited rotation flow.
- Outbound only: no inbound ports, and no Postgres, Redis or Kubernetes API
  dependency.
- Metadata-only audit: `agent.enroll.challenge`, `agent.enroll` (success or
  denied, with the fingerprint and provider connection), `agent.key.mismatch`,
  `agent.key_rotation.requested`, `agent.key.rotated` and `agent.revoked` record
  IDs, fingerprints and reasons, never a token, secret, key or challenge.
- Direct mint (`POST /api/v1/agents`) is a dev and test switch, off unless
  `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true`, and it also requires a public key.

When something fails, see [Troubleshooting: agent](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/troubleshooting/#agent).
For the API contract, see [HTTP API endpoints](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/api-endpoints/#agents);
for the agent's settings, the [agent component reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/agent/).

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/

# Authentication

Secrets Bridge has **three ways to sign in**: an OIDC provider set with `SB_OIDC_*` environment variables, [Google configured from the console](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/), and the local password, which stays available as break-glass. It gates Tier 2 operations (approve, reject, reveal) behind **fresh MFA**. This page explains the model end-to-end so an operator knows what's enforced where.

## The session model (Slices A2 + C)

Sessions are **server-side**, not stateless tokens.

| Concept | Where it lives |
|---|---|
| Identity proof | `sb_session` cookie, HttpOnly, Secure (prod), SameSite=Strict |
| Source of truth | `sessions` table in Postgres, `revoked_at`, `expires_at`, `idle_expires_at`, `last_mfa_at`, `ip`, `user_agent` |
| Cookie content | 32 random bytes, base64url; **SHA-256 stored**, plaintext returned ONCE in Set-Cookie |
| Revocation | Immediate, `UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at = NOW()`; next request fails validation |

**The SPA never holds a token.** Closing the tab + reopening it re-uses the same cookie. Reload, navigate, refresh, all hit the server. There is no `localStorage` / `sessionStorage` keypair to steal.

### TTLs (architect Q3)

| TTL | Default | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute | 8 hours | Hard ceiling from session create; the browser drops the cookie at this point |
| Idle | 30 minutes | Slides forward on every authenticated request; clamped to the absolute TTL |
| Step-up | 15 minutes | `last_mfa_at` must be within this window for Tier 2 ops |

A user who hasn't acted in 30 minutes is logged out idle-side; a user who's been active for 8 straight hours is logged out absolute-side. Both require a fresh login.

## Account lockout (Slice A1)

Five consecutive wrong-password attempts pin the account out for 15 minutes. State lives in Postgres (`local_users.failed_login_count` + `locked_until`), not Redis, a cache flush must **not** silently re-enable a locked account.

Even a *correct* password is rejected during the lock window. The 6th attempt with the right password fails just like the wrong ones, operators must wait out the timer or have a sibling admin clear the lock via psql.

The audit trail captures every state change:

- `auth.login` with `status=denied` + `error_kind=wrong_password` + `failed_login_count=N`, every wrong attempt
- `auth.lockout.applied`, written exactly once, when the threshold is crossed
- `auth.login` with `status=denied` + `error_kind=account_locked`, every attempt against a locked account
- `auth.login` with `status=success` + `BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN` (severity=CRITICAL), successful sign-in, see below

### Rate limit (per-IP, anti-scan)

| Endpoint | Limit | Window |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /auth/login` | 30 | 60s |
| `GET /auth/oidc/callback` | 60 | 60s |
| `GET /auth/providers` | 120 | 60s |
| `GET /auth/sso/google/start` | 30 | 60s |
| `GET /auth/sso/google/callback` | 60 | 60s |
| `POST /auth/oidc/{logout,backchannel}` | 60 | 60s |
| `POST /agents/:id/heartbeat` | 6 per-agent | 60s |
| `GET /requests/:id/wraps/:wrap_id` | 20 per-user | 60s |

The login / callback caps are **deliberately permissive** so users behind shared CGNAT (an entire ISP or VPC behind one egress IP) aren't locked out by their neighbours. **Brute-force defence lives in the per-account lockout above**, not the per-IP rate limit, the lockout is IP-independent so rotating source IPs doesn't dodge it. Tuned for carrier-grade NAT and other shared-egress networks.

## OIDC sign-in (Slices B + C + E)

One env-var Identity Provider (architect Q4). The api refuses to mount the `/auth/oidc/*` routes unless `SB_OIDC_ISSUER` is set; until then, only `/auth/login` (local password) and, when it is turned on, [Google from the console](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/) accept sign-ins.

The flow:

```
SPA → GET /api/v1/auth/oidc/start
api → 302 to IdP with PKCE state/nonce/code_challenge
IdP → user authenticates + consents
IdP → 302 back to /api/v1/auth/oidc/callback?code=...&state=...
api → verify state, exchange code, verify ID token (signature + audience + nonce)
api → JIT upsert local_users row keyed on email-or-sub
api → reconcile user_roles against the configured group claim (see below)
api → stamp last_mfa_at if amr ⊇ {strong-factor}
api → Set-Cookie + 302 to return_to
SPA → /users/me → render
```

### Group-claim → role mapping (Slice E)

`SB_OIDC_GROUP_MAP` is a JSON object mapping IdP group names to Secrets Bridge role names:

```json
{
  "sb-admins":    "admin",
  "sb-approvers": "approver",
  "sb-devs":      "developer"
}
```

The reconciler runs on **every** OIDC sign-in:

- User has a mapped group → grant added (if absent), `granted_by='system:oidc'`
- User no longer has a mapped group → grant revoked
- Mapped role doesn't exist in the catalog → silent skip + audit (typo doesn't 5xx the login)
- Reconcile failure → audited as `auth.oidc.reconcile_failed`; user still signs in

### The reconciler invariant (don't break this)

> The reconciler **only** touches `user_roles` rows with `granted_by = 'system:oidc'`.

Admin-assigned grants, the `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USER_ID` grant, every manually-curated team-scoped grant, every grant created via `POST /api/v1/user-roles`, carry a different `granted_by` value and are **invisible** to the reconciler. They survive every reconcile pass, including the "user belongs to no mapped groups" case.

This protects:

1. The break-glass admin from getting locked out when the IdP returns no groups during an outage.
2. Manually-curated team-scoped grants (which OIDC has no way to express in v1).
3. Operator overrides during incident response.

If you ever find yourself "cleaning up" this filter, **stop**. It is the security boundary, not an accident.

## Google sign-in from the console

Separate from the env-var provider above, an admin with `auth.sso.edit` can connect a Google Workspace under **Admin → Sign-in**, with no restart. Its accounts are bound by Google's issuer and subject rather than by email, the ID token's `hd` claim must be in the allowed Workspace domains, and new accounts wait for an admin's approval by default. Existing accounts connect Google from their profile after a fresh second factor. Both providers can be configured at once; the login page shows a button for each.

See [Sign in with Google](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/) for setup, approvals and the audit events.

## MFA + step-up (Slices H + I, current model)

Tier 2 operations (approve / reject / reveal-wrap; future: rotate, role-edit, provider-edit) require a session whose `last_mfa_at` is within the step-up TTL.

**The Control Plane owns MFA enrollment + step-up directly.** Identity stays with the IdP; MFA is an app-level concern. This is an architectural inversion of the original Slice D design (described as the legacy path further down). Every user enrolls one or more factors in the SPA at `/me/mfa`; step-up runs through the api's `/auth/mfa/{challenge,verify}` endpoints. Local-admin and OIDC users follow the same enrollment surface and the same step-up flow.

### Factor types

| Kind | Library on the api side | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `totp` | stdlib (RFC 6238, HMAC-SHA1, 6 digits, 30 s step, ±1 step skew) | Compatible with every authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden, YubiKey Authenticator). |
| `webauthn` | `github.com/go-webauthn/webauthn` (FIDO2 / WebAuthn) | Hardware-backed: YubiKey, Solo, Titan, platform authenticators (Touch ID / Face ID / Windows Hello). Phishing-resistant by design. |

WebAuthn requires the chart's `api.config.mfa.webauthn.rpId` + `api.config.mfa.webauthn.rpOrigins` to be set. When either is empty the api mounts only the TOTP routes (and the SPA's `/me/mfa` page hides the "Add security key" button). See [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/) for the values.

### Enrollment ceremony

Both kinds follow the same two-step shape (Stripe / GitHub / AWS Console model):

1. **`POST /users/me/mfa/<kind>/.../start`** mints the challenge + envelope-encrypts the factor secret + parks the encrypted blob in Redis under a 10-minute challenge id. Nothing lands in Postgres yet.
2. **`POST /users/me/mfa/<kind>/.../confirm` (or `…/finish`)** consumes the Redis blob (GETDEL, single-shot), verifies the user's response, and only then persists the factor row.

A wrong TOTP code or a failed WebAuthn attestation **burns the challenge**, the user restarts from step 1. This blocks an attacker from brute-forcing the 6-digit space against a single secret.

The SPA exposes the enrollment surfaces at `/me/mfa`. A user with zero factors sees an accent-coloured "Add MFA factor →" nudge in the sidebar; an enrolled user sees a quieter "Security" link.

### Step-up ceremony

When a Tier 2 op hits the api's `RequireFreshMFA` gate on a stale session:

```
401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: step-up max_age=900 acr_values=mfa
```

The SPA's global onError interceptor opens the step-up modal:

1. Modal asks the user to pick a factor, filtered by what they have enrolled.
2. SPA calls `POST /auth/mfa/challenge { kind }` for the chosen kind.
3. **TOTP path**, user types the 6-digit code; SPA calls `POST /auth/mfa/verify { challenge_id, factor_id, code }`.
4. **WebAuthn path**, SPA calls `navigator.credentials.get(...)` with the api-issued options; ships the assertion back via `POST /auth/mfa/verify { challenge_id, response }`.
5. On `204 No Content` the session is MFA-fresh, the api stamped `last_mfa_at` on the **same session row** (no new cookie). The user re-clicks the original button.

### Two related responses the interceptor routes

| Response | What it means | SPA action |
|---|---|---|
| `412 mfa_enrollment_required` | User has zero factors enrolled. | Navigate to `/me/mfa`. The step-up modal would be a dead-end. |
| `401 factor_compromised` | WebAuthn sign-count regression, the api detected a possible cloned authenticator and revoked every session for the user. | Hard-navigate to `/login`. |

### Recommended factor priority

When you onboard users, encourage this enrollment order:

1. **WebAuthn (hardware key, YubiKey, Solo, Titan)**, phishing-resistant, no shared secret on the device, no battery.
2. **WebAuthn (platform, Touch ID / Face ID / Windows Hello)**, phishing-resistant, no extra device to carry, but tied to one machine.
3. **TOTP via authenticator app (Aegis, 1Password, Authy)**, universal fallback; vulnerable to phishing kits that proxy the code.
4. **SMS / email OTP**, Secrets Bridge does NOT support this. SIM swap and email-account takeover are well-documented bypasses.

Operators should enrol **at least two factors** per privileged user, one hardware key plus one TOTP backup, so a lost YubiKey doesn't lock them out of Tier 2 ops.

### Step-up vs login-time MFA

There are two postures, and the default depends on `SB_ENV`:

- **Login-time MFA** is the default for `SB_ENV=production`: every authenticated route needs a session that was verified with a second factor at least once.
- **Step-up only** is the default for `SB_ENV=dev`: only Tier-2 operations (approve, reject, reveal) ask for a fresh second factor, and browsing needs only the session cookie.

Production defaults to login-time MFA because step-up alone does not protect an account that has no second factor yet. Such an account can add its first factor using only its session (the enrollment routes have to stay open for that), and then pass step-up with it. With login-time MFA, a user with no factor adds one right after primary sign-in, before any other route answers.

`SB_REQUIRE_MFA_AT_LOGIN` overrides the default either way, set in the env Secret or as `api.config.mfa.requireMFAAtLogin: true` or `false` in the chart. The chart renders the variable only for an explicit `true` or `false`, and then it wins over the env Secret. Left unset, the chart renders nothing and the env Secret's value, or else the default for `SB_ENV`, applies. A chart value that isn't a boolean (a quoted `"false"`, a `0`) fails the render; in the env Secret it falls back to the default with a warning at boot. Turning it off outside dev also logs a warning at boot.

!!! warning "Upgrading a production install"
    Before this default, login-time MFA was off unless you set it. After the upgrade:

    - A user with no second factor is sent to **Second factor** once on the first page load, with a banner saying why. After adding an authenticator app or a security key, **Continue** asks for it and the console opens. An action that needs a second factor (approve, reject, reveal) offers to add one in place instead of leaving the page.
    - A user who already has a factor is asked for it on the first page load of each new session, not only on approve, reject or reveal.
    - Scripts that sign in with `curl` need a second factor and a step-up; see [Gateway, step 2](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#2-sign-in-and-step-up).
    - **Check your values file.** One copied from an older chart may still say `requireMFAAtLogin: false`, the default it used to write out. That line keeps the gate off after the upgrade, and the api says so at boot (`login-time MFA is OFF ... outside dev`). Delete it.

    You can opt out with `requireMFAAtLogin: false` (or `SB_REQUIRE_MFA_AT_LOGIN=false` in the env Secret), but don't outside dev: an account with no second factor is then protected by its session alone.

When login-time MFA is on:

- A fresh session with no MFA stamp gets `401 step_up_required` from every route outside the carve-outs below when the user has a factor, and `412 mfa_enrollment_required` when they have none.
- In the console, a `401` opens the step-up dialog right after sign-in. A `412` on a page load sends the user to **Second factor** once, with a banner; a `412` on an action (approve, reject, reveal, save) offers to add a factor in place, asks for it, then retries the action.
- Tier-2 routes still enforce the 15-min freshness window via the per-route `RequireFreshMFA`.

Carve-outs the gate ALWAYS allows through (so it isn't self-locking):

```
GET    /api/v1/users/me                 SPA identity hydration
GET    /api/v1/users/me/projects        identity-adjacent
GET    /api/v1/users/me/mfa/factors     SPA factor-kind picker
POST   /api/v1/users/me/mfa/totp/*      enrollment must reach
POST   /api/v1/users/me/mfa/webauthn/*  the user pre-stamp
DELETE /api/v1/users/me/mfa/factors/:id factor removal
POST   /api/v1/auth/logout              always allow sign-out
POST   /api/v1/auth/mfa/challenge       the gate's own ceremony
POST   /api/v1/auth/mfa/verify          ditto
```

Pick the posture by environment, not by user:

| Posture | When it fits |
|---|---|
| **Login-time MFA** (default for `env=production`) | Every production deployment. It is the only posture in which an account with no second factor is protected. |
| **Step-up only** (default for `env=dev`, or `requireMFAAtLogin: false`) | Laptop and dev clusters. Outside dev, only if every user already has a second factor and you accept the browsing-only exposure of a stolen session. |

The two postures share the same factor enrollment surface (`/me/mfa`) and the same verify endpoint (`/auth/mfa/verify`), the gate position is the only difference. Switching between them is a single env-var change + pod roll; users keep their enrolled factors.

## OIDC-trust MFA (Slice D, legacy, opt-in)

The api retains the original Slice D path for deployments whose IdP genuinely owns MFA (Microsoft Entra / Okta with strong-factor policy bound), so an operator can keep that posture during a transition window.

Set `api.config.oidc.trustAmrForMFA: true` (renders `SB_OIDC_TRUSTED_AMR_MFA=true`) to opt in. When enabled, the OIDC callback stamps `last_mfa_at` on the session whenever the ID-token `amr` claim includes one of the RFC 8176 strong-factor identifiers:

| Factor | Code |
|---|---|
| Multi-factor (explicit) | `mfa` |
| One-time password | `otp` |
| Hardware key | `hwk` |
| FIDO2 / WebAuthn | `fido` |
| Software-secured key | `swk` |
| Smart card | `sc` |
| Proof-of-possession | `pop` |
| Biometric, iris | `eye` |
| Biometric, fingerprint | `fpt` |
| Biometric, retina | `retina` |

`pwd` and `kba` are not strong. **The app-MFA path (above) runs in parallel**, a user can still satisfy step-up via `/auth/mfa/verify` even when the OIDC-trust knob is on. Operators flip this knob OFF (the default) once every user has enrolled an app-MFA factor; `amr` continues to be recorded in audit either way.

**Hard rule:** `SessionService.MarkMFA` only fires from `MFAVerifyService.Verify` (the app path) OR from the OIDC callback when `TrustAMRForMFA=true`. The architectural invariant is that exactly one path writes `last_mfa_at`. New callers in the api codebase need explicit justification or the step-up gate's contract collapses.

## Break-glass (local-admin) policy (architect Q1)

Local-admin sign-in via `/auth/login` is the **break-glass surface**, the way operators sign in when the IdP is down, the OIDC client is misconfigured, or the network is partitioned. It is **not** the day-to-day sign-in path once OIDC is configured.

Every successful local-admin sign-in emits a high-severity audit event:

```
action:   BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN
status:   success
severity: CRITICAL    (in metadata)
actor:    user:<uuid>
```

**Route this audit action into your alert pipeline.** Splunk / Datadog / Grafana Alertmanager, whichever you use, page the on-call when a `BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN` shows up outside of an open incident bridge. The Slack notification recipe:

```yaml
# Example: worker notification sink (when configured) or external SIEM rule
when:
  action: BREAK_GLASS_LOGIN
  severity: CRITICAL
then:
  notify:
    channel: "#security-incidents"
    message: |
      Break-glass local-admin login by ${actor}.
      Expected? If not, open an incident.
      Session ID: ${metadata.session_id}
      IP: ${metadata.ip}
      User-agent: ${metadata.user_agent}
```

### Local-admin sessions + step-up

Local-admin users go through the **same app-MFA enrollment + step-up surfaces as OIDC users**. The local-admin sign-in path does not stamp `last_mfa_at` directly, every Tier 2 op the operator runs is gated by a fresh `/auth/mfa/verify` against an enrolled factor.

Operationally this means:

- A local-admin user with no factor enrolled hits `412 mfa_enrollment_required` on the first Tier 2 op and is routed to `/me/mfa` to enrol.
- After enrolling, every Tier 2 op runs through the step-up modal, same flow as OIDC users.
- If the operator is in the middle of an IdP outage and *also* hasn't enrolled an MFA factor, they should enrol one immediately, the IdP outage doesn't block factor enrollment, and once enrolled they can satisfy step-up without the IdP.

This is a tighter posture than the pre-H4 architecture, where local-admin users were forced through `/auth/oidc/start?step_up=mfa` for every Tier 2 op and effectively couldn't approve anything during an IdP outage. App-MFA closes that gap.

If you're routinely approving as the break-glass user, your operating model is still wrong, that account should be reserved for "the IdP is broken and I need to fix it." But during a real IdP outage the break-glass user can now approve cleanly without an additional dependency.

### Disabling break-glass entirely

For deployments that want to refuse local-admin sign-in once OIDC is configured, the chart will gain a `SB_LOCAL_ADMIN_ENABLED=false` flag in a follow-up. Today the flag is implicit, leave `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` unset and no local-admin account exists, so `/auth/login` always fails with `invalid credentials`.

## Direct reveal permission (Slice L4)

Slice L4 added `secret.reveal.direct` to the permission catalog and seeded it onto the bootstrap `developer` role.

The permission is a NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT gate. Three conditions must all hold for a direct-reveal request to auto-execute:

1. The caller holds `secret.reveal.direct` (route-level `auth.Require`).
2. The matched `policy_rules` row has `direct_reveal_allowed=true`.
3. The matched environment's `kind` is `non_prod`.

If any one of these fails, the API returns 403 and the SPA shows an inline error. The dev endpoint never bypasses approval against a `prod`-classified env, the PolicyEngine zeroes `direct_reveal_allowed=true` server-side regardless of operator misconfig. See [Project environments](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/project-environments/#kind-vs-type-why-both) for the `kind` model and [Policy templates](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/policy-templates/#template-1-non-prod-direct-reveal) for ready-to-paste rules.

Operators who want a stricter baseline can strip `secret.reveal.direct` from the developer role via the existing Roles admin endpoint, the rest of the developer surface (`secret.request`, `audit.read`) is unaffected.

## What this page does NOT cover

- **RBAC enforcement** at the route level. Sidebar nav already hides admin pages without `team.edit` / `role.edit`; route-level enforcement on the api lands in a follow-up.
- **Audit log forwarding** to SIEM. The api emits structured slog JSON; pick that up with Fluent Bit / Vector and route to wherever.
- **mTLS for agent ↔ api**. Slice B of the workload-identity track replaces the static agent secret with a SPIFFE / IRSA-backed identity. Tracked separately from the user-auth series.

For the chart-side knobs (`api.config.oidc.*`, `api.config.bootstrap.userId`), see [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/). For the underlying threat model + hard rules, see [Threat model](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/threat-model/).

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/

# Sign in with Google

An admin can connect the company's Google Workspace from the console, with
no environment variables and no redeploy. People in the allowed Workspace
domains then sign in with Google. By default, the first sign-in creates an
account that waits until an admin approves it and gives it a role.

!!! warning "Merged, not yet through QA"
    Google sign-in is in the api, console and worker on `main`, but it has
    not passed a QA cycle. See [Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/).

This page covers:

- [setting it up](#set-up-google-sign-in): the public address, the Google
  OAuth client, the console settings, Test and Turn on;
- [who can sign in](#who-can-sign-in) and how accounts are matched;
- [approving new accounts](#approve-new-accounts), and the
  [option to skip approval](#letting-people-in-without-approval);
- [connecting Google to an existing account](#connect-google-to-an-existing-account);
- [the worker message](#notify-admins-from-the-worker) for new accounts;
- [how it sits next to the env-var OIDC provider](#next-to-the-env-var-oidc-provider)
  and the break-glass admin.

The examples use `https://secrets.example.com` as the install's address and
`example.com` as the Workspace domain.

## How it works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor P as New user
    participant UI as Console
    participant API as api
    participant G as Google
    actor A as Admin
    P->>UI: Sign in with Google
    UI->>API: GET /api/v1/auth/sso/google/start
    API->>G: redirect with PKCE, nonce and state
    G->>API: GET /api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback?code=...
    API->>API: check email_verified, hd and email domain
    API->>API: create account, waiting for approval
    API->>UI: session cookie, redirect
    UI->>P: Waiting for approval page
    A->>UI: Admin → Users, Approve with a role and scope
    UI->>API: POST /api/v1/users/:id/approve
    P->>UI: Check again
    UI->>P: console with the granted access
```

## Before you start

You need:

- an account with a global `auth.sso.edit` grant and an enrolled second
  factor. The seeded `admin` role holds `auth.sso.edit`, so the bootstrap
  admin can do this right after the [first sign-in](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/);
- a public `https` address for the install, the one people type in the
  browser;
- a Google Workspace and a Google Cloud project in it where you can create
  OAuth clients.

**Every change asks for a fresh second factor.** Saving the public address
or the waiting limit, creating, editing or removing Google, replacing the
client secret, Test, Turn on and Turn off all go through the step-up dialog
(`RequireFreshMFA`). Whoever holds `auth.sso.edit` decides who can sign in,
and the step-up means a stolen session cookie alone can't change these
settings.

## Set up Google sign-in

### 1. Set the public address

Redirect URIs are built from the install's configured public address, never
from the request's `Host` or `X-Forwarded-*` headers. A forged header can't
send the authorization code somewhere else. The address comes from one of
two places:

| Source | How | In the console |
|---|---|---|
| `SB_PUBLIC_URL` | Set it in the api's environment, for example in the chart's `secrets.existingSecret`. The worker reads the same Secret. | Shown read-only, with "Set by SB_PUBLIC_URL on this install" |
| The console | **Admin → Sign-in → Public address**. The field is prefilled from the address you are using. | Editable |

When `SB_PUBLIC_URL` is set it always wins, and `PUT /sso/settings` refuses
to change the address (`409 public_url_from_env`).

The address must be an absolute `https` URL with no user info, query or
fragment. A trailing slash is dropped. Plain `http` is accepted only for
`localhost` or a loopback address, and only when `SB_ENV=dev`. The api
refuses to start with an invalid `SB_PUBLIC_URL`. The console warns, without
blocking, when a saved address isn't `https` or looks internal.

Google can't be turned on until an address is set, and while none is set
the login page doesn't offer Google.

The **Public address** card also holds the **waiting limit**, the most
accounts that can wait for approval at once. It defaults to 50 and accepts
1 to 10,000. See [The waiting limit](#the-waiting-limit).

### 2. Create the OAuth client in Google Cloud Console

With the address saved, **Admin → Sign-in → Google → Set up Google** shows
the redirect URL to copy. It is always the public address plus
`/api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback`:

```text
https://secrets.example.com/api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback
```

In the Google Cloud project:

1. Set the OAuth consent screen's user type to **Internal**, so only
   accounts in your Workspace can use the client.
2. Create an **OAuth client ID** of application type **Web application**.
3. Add the redirect URL above under **Authorized redirect URIs**, exactly
   as the console shows it.
4. Copy the client ID and the client secret.

Secrets Bridge uses Google's fixed issuer (`https://accounts.google.com`)
and its discovery document, so you don't enter an issuer. It asks for the
`openid`, `email` and `profile` scopes.

### 3. Enter the client in the console

In the **Set up Google** drawer:

| Field | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Client ID | From the OAuth client. Required, at most 255 characters, no spaces. |
| Client secret | From the OAuth client. Saved encrypted and never shown again. |
| Workspace domains | One per line, for example `example.com`. At least one, at most 20. They are lowercased and de-duplicated. |
| New people | **Wait for approval** (the default) or **Let them in right away**. |
| Role for new people | Only with **Let them in right away**. Optional. See [Letting people in without approval](#letting-people-in-without-approval). |

The provider is saved **turned off**.

**The client secret is write-only.** It is envelope-encrypted with the
configured KMS (a fresh data key, AES-256-GCM), the same way TOTP secrets
are stored. No response returns it, only `client_secret_set: true`, and it
is never logged or put in audit metadata. The console shows it as "Saved",
with **Replace…** to set a new one. Replacing it is its own call,
`PUT /sso/providers/:id/secret`, audited as `sso_provider.secret_rotate`.
`PUT /sso/providers/:id` refuses a `client_secret` field with `400`.

### 4. Test, then turn it on

**Test** sends you through Google with your own account and back to
**Admin → Sign-in**. It runs every check a real sign-in runs, creates
nothing, issues no session, and works while Google is still off. The result
shows as "Google sign-in works." or as the reason it didn't pass, and only
the admin who ran it sees that reason.

**Turn on** needs a public address, a client secret and at least one
domain. If any is missing the api answers `409 provider_not_ready` with a
`missing` list, and the console names what to set. Once on, the login page
shows **Sign in with Google** above the password form.

Changes take effect on the next sign-in, without a restart: the OAuth client
is built from the saved settings on every round trip.

## Who can sign in

On every Google sign-in, including returning users, the api checks:

- the email is verified by Google (`email_verified`);
- the ID token's `hd` claim (the Workspace domain) is present and in the
  allowed domains;
- the email's domain is in the allowed domains as well.

`hd` is only present for Workspace accounts. A personal Google account with
an address in an allowed domain has no `hd`, so it is refused. Removing a
domain from the list refuses people in it from their next sign-in. When
exactly one domain is allowed, the api also passes it to Google as the `hd`
hint, so the account chooser offers only accounts in that Workspace.

**Accounts are matched by Google's issuer and subject, never by email.**
The binding lives in the `user_identities` table, unique on (issuer,
subject). The first sign-in of a Google identity:

- creates a new account when its email isn't used by any account here;
- is **refused** when the email already belongs to an account. That
  person signs in with their password and
  [connects Google](#connect-google-to-an-existing-account) instead. This
  stops a Google account with, say, the bootstrap admin's address from
  reaching the bootstrap admin's account.

The round trip itself uses PKCE (S256), a nonce and a single-use state
that lives 5 minutes and is bound to the browser by the `sb_sso_state`
cookie. Return paths must be on the same origin, as for the
[env-var OIDC provider](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#oidc-sign-in-slices-b-c-e).

**Every refused sign-in gets the same answer.** The browser goes to
`/login?error=sso`, and the login page says "You couldn't be signed in with
that account." whatever the reason. The page never tells an outsider which
emails have accounts. The reason goes to the audit log; see
[Troubleshooting](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/troubleshooting/#google-sign-in-refused).

## Approve new accounts

With **Wait for approval** on, a new account starts waiting. Until it is
approved it can only read `GET /users/me` and sign out. Every other route
answers `403 account_pending_approval`, and the console sends the person to
a **Waiting for approval** page with **Check again** and **Sign out**. This
is enforced at session validation and at sign-in. If a waiting account signs in through the env-var OIDC provider,
its group mapping is skipped, so it gets no role from IdP groups either.

Admins who can approve see:

- a count on **Users** in the sidebar;
- a banner on **Overview** with a link while anyone is waiting;
- the **Waiting for approval** list on **Admin → Users**, longest wait
  first;
- optionally, a [webhook message from the worker](#notify-admins-from-the-worker).

Approving and declining need a **global** `user_role.edit`. A team-scoped
grant, or `team.edit`, is not enough.

**Approve…** picks a role and, optionally, limits it to a team or a project.
The api grants the role and clears the waiting flag in one transaction, so
a failed grant leaves the account waiting. The scope is checked with the
same rules as `POST /user-roles`: only `project_id`, `team_id`,
`environment`, `secret_ref_prefix` and `provider_type` are accepted, each a
non-empty string, IDs as UUIDs. A malformed scope is refused with `400`
instead of being widened. The person gets the access on their next
request, or after **Check again**.

**Decline…** disables a waiting account after a confirmation, and its
sessions end on their next use. Decline only works on waiting accounts
(`409 user_not_pending` otherwise), so it can't disable an active account
or the break-glass admin. A declined account keeps its waiting flag, so it
can't be approved or re-enabled from the console, and that Google account
can't sign in again.

### The waiting limit

At most 50 accounts can wait at once by default; change the limit on
**Admin → Sign-in → Public address**. Past it, new Google sign-ins are
refused with the same generic page until you approve or decline some.
Declined accounts don't count. Refusals at the limit are audited as
`user.pending_refused`, aggregated per 10-minute window: the first refusal
in a window writes one event, and the next window writes a summary with the
count and the first and last times. A burst of sign-ins can't fill the
append-only audit log.

### Letting people in without approval

With **Let them in right away**, a new account starts active. You can pick
a **Role for new people**, granted globally when the account is created.
Without one, the account starts with no role, and an admin grants one on
the Users page.

The default role must be non-privileged: every permission it holds must be
in `secret.list`, `secret.request` and `audit.read` (`audit.read` only
shows a user their own events). The api refuses anything else with
`400 default_role_privileged`, and a default role with approval on with
`400 default_role_needs_approval_off`. The seeded `developer` role doesn't
qualify, because it holds `secret.reveal.direct`. Create a role with only
those permissions if you want approval off.

The rule holds after the provider is saved too:

- widening a role that a provider uses as its default
  (`PUT /roles/:id/permissions`) is refused with `409 role_is_sso_default`,
  and deleting it with `409` until you choose another default;
- the role is checked again at every sign-in. If it no longer qualifies,
  the new account waits for approval like any other, and the api audits
  `sso_provider.default_role_refused`.

## Connect Google to an existing account

Existing accounts, including the bootstrap admin, are never linked by
email. The owner connects Google from their profile:

1. Sign in with the password.
2. Open the profile page and click **Connect Google**. It asks for a fresh
   second factor.
3. Choose the Google account. It must pass the [same checks](#who-can-sign-in)
   as a sign-in.
4. Back in the console, the profile shows the connected account.

Google must be turned on. The round trip is bound to the session that
started it: the callback parks the result in a one-time ticket that lives 2
minutes, and the console redeems it with `POST /auth/sso/google/finish`,
which only succeeds on that same session (otherwise `403
sso_ticket_refused`). A Google identity already connected to another
account is refused (`409 link_refused`, reason `identity_taken`), and the
profile says so. A link is audited as `user.identity_link`.

**Disconnect…** also needs a fresh second factor and is audited as
`user.identity_unlink`. After it, the owner signs in with their password
again.

**An account created by a Google sign-in can't disconnect Google.** It was
given a random password nobody knows, so Google is its only way in.
`DELETE /users/me/identities/google` answers `409 identity_required`, and
the profile explains why instead of offering **Disconnect…**.

## Notify admins from the worker

The worker's `users-pending` sweeper posts a message when accounts start
waiting. It needs `SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL`, and isn't registered without it;
the console's count and banner still work.

| Variable | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL` | (unset) | Where to post. Required for this message. |
| `SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_SLACK_FORMAT` | `false` | `true` posts `{"text": ...}` for a Slack incoming webhook. |
| `SB_WORKER_USERS_PENDING_INTERVAL` | `1m` | How often it runs, and so the most often admins hear about new accounts. At least `30s`, or the worker refuses to start. |
| `SB_PUBLIC_URL` | (unset) | Used for the link to Admin → Users. Unset, the address saved in the console is used. |

Each run posts **at most one message**. It covers the accounts that started
waiting since the last message: up to 10 by email, oldest first, then "and
N more", the total still waiting when older ones are left, and a link to
`<public address>/admin/users`:

```text
[info] 2 new accounts are waiting for approval
• sara@example.com
• omar@example.com
Approve or decline them in Admin → Users: https://secrets.example.com/admin/users
```

The message carries **emails only**, never display names, because a display
name comes from the person's Google account and can contain anything. It
goes to the webhook only. The worker logs counts, never who is waiting.
Each account is announced once. A failed post is retried on the next run,
together with anyone who arrived since. Declined accounts are left out.

## Next to the env-var OIDC provider

The [env-var OIDC provider](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#oidc-sign-in-slices-b-c-e)
(`SB_OIDC_ISSUER` and the other `SB_OIDC_*` variables) keeps working as
before. When both are configured, the login page shows two buttons, **Sign
in with Google** and **Sign in with single sign-on**, and each provider
handles its own sign-ins. The env-var provider still matches accounts by
verified email and doesn't create waiting accounts.

When `SB_OIDC_ISSUER` is already Google (`https://accounts.google.com`),
the console refuses to add Google (`409 env_provider_is_google`), the login
page doesn't offer the console provider, and a provider saved earlier can't
be turned on.

**Password sign-in and the break-glass admin are never turned off by these
settings.** No sign-in setting disables `POST /auth/login`, and decline
only touches waiting accounts. If Google is misconfigured or down, sign in
with the bootstrap admin's password and fix it under Admin → Sign-in.

## Audit events

| Action | When |
|---|---|
| `sso_provider.create`, `.update`, `.delete`, `.enable`, `.disable` | Google changed in the console. Old and new values of the domains, the approval setting and the default role. Never the secret, only whether one is set. |
| `sso_provider.secret_rotate` | The client secret replaced |
| `sso_settings.update` | The public address or the waiting limit changed, with old and new values |
| `sso_provider.test` | A Test round trip, `success` or `denied` with `error_kind` |
| `auth.sso.callback` | A Google sign-in or Connect Google round trip, `success` or `denied` with `error_kind` |
| `user.pending` | An account created waiting for approval |
| `user.sso_provision` | An account created active, with approval off |
| `user.approve`, `user_role.grant` | An admin approved an account, with the role and scope |
| `user.decline` | An admin declined an account |
| `user.pending_refused` | Sign-ins refused at the waiting limit, aggregated per 10 minutes |
| `sso_provider.default_role_refused` | A default role no longer qualified at sign-in, so the account waits |
| `user.identity_link`, `user.identity_unlink` | Google connected to or disconnected from an account |

None of them carries a token, code, ticket or secret.

## API

The routes are listed in the [HTTP API reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/api-endpoints/#sign-in-with-google),
and the permissions in the [permissions catalog](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/permissions/#authentication).

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/oidc-authentik/

# OIDC with Authentik

This guide configures [Authentik](https://goauthentik.io/) as the IdP for Secrets Bridge. Authentik is the **worked example**, Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, and Entra ID work the same way; the screens are different but the contract (issuer URL, client id / secret, redirect URL, scopes, group claim) is identical.

Prerequisites:

- A running Authentik instance with admin access.
- A running Secrets Bridge installation. See [Bootstrap & first sign-in](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/).
- A public hostname for the SPA + api, e.g. `https://secrets-bridge.example.com`.

## 1. Create the application in Authentik

In the Authentik admin:

1. **Applications → Applications → Create**
   - Name: `Secrets Bridge`
   - Slug: `secrets-bridge`
   - Group: (your choice, controls who can see it in the user library)
2. **Applications → Providers → Create → OAuth2/OpenID Provider**
   - Name: `secrets-bridge`
   - Authorization flow: `default-provider-authorization-explicit-consent` (or implicit, your call)
   - Client type: **Confidential**
   - Client ID: `secrets-bridge` (or whatever, note it down)
   - Client Secret: Authentik generates one, note it down, store it in the env Secret
   - Redirect URIs: `https://secrets-bridge.example.com/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback`
   - Signing key: the same key your other apps use, or `authentik Self-signed Certificate`
   - Scopes: leave the default OpenID + profile + email scopes selected; **also enable the `groups` scope** (Authentik exposes group memberships via this scope)
3. Back in the Application, bind the provider you just created.

The **issuer URL** you'll need for Secrets Bridge is:

```
https://authentik.example.com/application/o/secrets-bridge/
```

(Note the **trailing slash**, Authentik's discovery endpoint is `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration` and that resolves only with the slash present.)

## 2. Configure the group claim

Group-claim → role mapping is the architect Q5 deferral that Slice E delivered. The reconciler reads the `groups` claim by default and maps each IdP group to a Secrets Bridge role.

Authentik emits the `groups` claim automatically when the `groups` scope is granted on the provider, no scope mapper to configure.

If your Authentik install has groups named differently from your Secrets Bridge roles, set the map in `values.yaml`:

```yaml
api:
  config:
    oidc:
      groupClaim: groups   # the default; matches Authentik
      groupMap:
        sb-admins:    admin
        sb-approvers: approver
        sb-devs:      developer
```

The chart serializes this map to JSON and exposes it as `SB_OIDC_GROUP_MAP`. The api binary's `ValidateOIDCGroupMap` fails the boot if the JSON is malformed or has empty keys/values, operators get the signal up front, not as a 401 in production.

### The reconciler invariant (you cannot disable this)

The reconciler **only** touches `user_roles` rows with `granted_by = 'system:oidc'`. Admin-assigned grants are invisible to it. See [Authentication → The reconciler invariant](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#the-reconciler-invariant-dont-break-this) for what this protects. Repeat in your runbook so the next on-call doesn't relax the filter as "cleanup."

## 3. Configure Secrets Bridge

In your chart values:

```yaml
api:
  config:
    oidc:
      issuer:             "https://authentik.example.com/application/o/secrets-bridge/"
      clientId:           "secrets-bridge"
      redirectUrl:        "https://secrets-bridge.example.com/api/v1/auth/oidc/callback"
      scopes:             "openid profile email groups"
      postLogoutRedirect: "https://secrets-bridge.example.com/"
      groupClaim:         groups
      groupMap:
        sb-admins:    admin
        sb-approvers: approver
        sb-devs:      developer
```

And in the env Secret (`secrets.existingSecret`, typically `secrets-bridge-env`):

```
SB_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<the secret Authentik generated above>
```

Apply the chart upgrade:

```bash
helm upgrade secrets-bridge ./charts/secrets-bridge \
  -n secrets-bridge \
  -f my-values.yaml
```

The api pod rolls automatically, the chart's `checksum/config` annotation includes the OIDC issuer + groupMap, so a Helm upgrade that flips OIDC on/off or rewrites the mapping triggers a fresh pod.

## 4. Sign in

Browse to `https://secrets-bridge.example.com/login`. The SPA probes the api for OIDC availability via `/api/v1/auth/oidc/start` and renders the **"Sign in with SSO"** button above the local-admin form when OIDC is mounted.

Click it. The redirect chain runs:

1. SPA → api `/auth/oidc/start` → Authentik authorize endpoint
2. Authentik prompts for credentials (and MFA, see below)
3. Authentik → api `/auth/oidc/callback?code=...&state=...`
4. api verifies + JIT-creates the user + reconciles roles + Set-Cookie
5. api → 302 to the SPA's original page

If your user's `groups` claim contained `sb-admins`, the reconciler grants the `admin` role on the way through. Your first sign-in lands you on the Dashboard with full permissions.

If your `groups` claim contained none of the mapped groups, the user is provisioned with **no role grants**. An admin must assign one from `/admin/assignments` before the user can do anything beyond `/users/me`.

## 5. MFA, Authentik vs the Control Plane

**The current model has the Control Plane own MFA enrollment + step-up directly.** Identity stays with Authentik; users enrol a TOTP factor or a WebAuthn credential in the Secrets Bridge SPA at `/me/mfa`; step-up runs through the api's `/auth/mfa/{challenge,verify}` endpoints. See [Authentication → MFA + step-up](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#mfa-step-up-slices-h-i-current-model) for the full model. You do **not** need to configure MFA inside Authentik for Secrets Bridge to enforce it.

If you want Authentik to handle MFA on the IdP side instead (so the same MFA stage protects every app behind Authentik, not just Secrets Bridge), set `api.config.oidc.trustAmrForMFA: true` in the chart. The api will then stamp `last_mfa_at` when the ID-token `amr` claim carries an RFC 8176 strong factor, see [Authentication → OIDC-trust MFA (Slice D, legacy)](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#oidc-trust-mfa-slice-d-legacy-opt-in). The two paths run in parallel; users on a `trustAmrForMFA: true` deployment can still satisfy step-up via the app-MFA path if they prefer.

The IdP-trust path remains useful when you have a uniform MFA policy across many apps (Entra / Okta with org-wide WebAuthn enforcement). Most Secrets Bridge deployments are simpler with the app-MFA default.

### Enabling MFA in Authentik (only if you flip `trustAmrForMFA: true`)

1. **Flows & Stages → Stages → Create → WebAuthn Authenticator Setup**
2. Add the stage to your default authentication flow (or a user-self-enrolment flow).
3. Mark the stage as **required** for users with any of your `sb-admins` / `sb-approvers` groups, those are the people who'll need step-up MFA on every approve.

### Verifying `amr` is correct (IdP-trust path only)

After a user signs in with WebAuthn through Authentik, check the audit row on the Secrets Bridge side:

```sql
SELECT metadata->>'amr', metadata->>'session_id', occurred_at
FROM audit_events
WHERE action = 'auth.oidc.callback'
ORDER BY occurred_at DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

You should see `amr` as `["mfa"]` (or `["pwd","mfa"]` for a password-then-WebAuthn flow). If you only see `["pwd"]`, the IdP did not assert MFA, Tier 2 ops will demand step-up via the app-MFA path (a fine outcome if you've enrolled the factor there) OR fail closed (if you haven't). That's a sign your Authentik flow isn't enforcing the WebAuthn stage; users with an app-MFA factor stay unaffected.

## 6. Step-up flow in action

The first time the user tries to approve a request, they'll see:

1. SPA opens the request detail → clicks **Approve**
2. SPA `POST /requests/:id/approve` → api returns `401 step_up_required` (session is MFA-stale)
3. SPA's global step-up interceptor opens the step-up modal
4. User picks their factor, TOTP code or tap their security key
5. SPA `POST /auth/mfa/verify` → api stamps `last_mfa_at` on the **same session row** (cookie unchanged) → `204 No Content`
6. Modal closes → user re-clicks **Approve** → 200

The "cookie unchanged" invariant is critical, see [Authentication → Step-up ceremony](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#step-up-ceremony). Your audit chain stays continuous; the session ID never changes.

## 7. Back-channel logout

Authentik supports RFC 8417 back-channel logout. To wire it:

1. In the provider settings: enable **Back-channel logout** and set the URL to:
   ```
   https://secrets-bridge.example.com/api/v1/auth/oidc/backchannel
   ```
2. Authentik will POST a `logout_token` to this URL when the user signs out of Authentik (single sign-out across applications).
3. The Secrets Bridge api verifies the token signature + audience + the `events` claim, then revokes **every** server-side session for the user's `sub`. The user is signed out of Secrets Bridge immediately.

## 8. Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| "OIDC routes don't appear on /login" | `SB_OIDC_ISSUER` is empty; SPA probes 404 and hides the button. Check the api logs for the `oidc disabled` line at boot. |
| "Login succeeds but I have no permissions" | The user's `groups` claim doesn't include any mapped group, OR the role name in `groupMap` doesn't exist in the role catalog. Check the `auth.oidc.role_reconcile` audit row, `metadata.added` will be empty. |
| "User has admin BUT shouldn't" | An admin-assigned grant exists for them (`granted_by != 'system:oidc'`). The reconciler can't see it. Revoke via `/admin/assignments` or `DELETE /api/v1/user-roles/:id`. |
| "Tier 2 ops still step up after I enabled WebAuthn" | The `amr` claim doesn't contain a strong factor. Run the SQL in §5 to verify. Usually the WebAuthn stage isn't bound to the authentication flow, or it's optional and the user skipped it. |
| "Boot fails with 'SB_OIDC_GROUP_MAP must be a JSON object…'" | The chart was given a non-object groupMap (e.g. a list) OR an entry has an empty role name. Fix the values and `helm upgrade` again. |

## See also

- [Authentication overview](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/), full auth model
- [Bootstrap & first sign-in](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/), local-admin setup before OIDC lands
- [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/), every env var, including the `SB_OIDC_*` set

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/project-environments/

# Project environments

Slice L introduced first-class environments to the Secrets Bridge data
model. This page explains what they are, the `non_prod` / `prod`
distinction that gates direct reveal, and how to wire them up
operationally.

## What an environment is

An **environment** is a lifecycle boundary inside a project: `dev`,
`staging`, `uat`, `prod`, or any other name your team uses. The
schema (`api/pkg/storage/migrations/0001_initial_schema.up.sql`) has
carried environments since v0.1; Slice L1 added three classifying
fields:

| Column | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `kind` | **Hard safety boundary**. `non_prod` or `prod`. The PolicyEngine refuses to honour `direct_reveal_allowed=true` against `kind='prod'` regardless of policy or permission. PROD direct-reveal is impossible by construction. |
| `risk_level` | `SMALLINT 0-4`. Future fine-grain policy knob; today it drives a UI badge intensity only. |
| `description` | Operator notes. No semantic load. |

The existing `type` column (dev / staging / uat / prod / other) stays.
Operators use it as a free lifecycle label that doesn't have to
agree with `kind`. The two are independently mutable for the case
where a staging-labelled env actually carries prod data: set
`type='staging'` but `kind='prod'` and the PROD invariant fires.

## kind vs type, why both

The free-string `type` was useful as a lifecycle label, but it was
also doing double duty as the implicit risk signal. Operators
naturally write `type='uat'` for non-production environments, and a
single typo or rename can silently un-gate a sensitive flow. `kind`
is the hard, two-value classifier that the engine actually consults.

A reasonable mental model:

- `type` is what the env is called.
- `kind` is what the engine treats it as.

Operators who want to demote a prod-looking environment (e.g. a load
test env that mirrors prod schema but holds dummy data) can set
`type='prod'` and `kind='non_prod'`. The PolicyEngine then permits
direct reveal there even though the lifecycle label says prod.

## Backfill rule

Migration `0022_environments_kind_classification` runs the only safe
automatic mapping on existing rows:

```sql
UPDATE environments SET kind = CASE
    WHEN type = 'prod' THEN 'prod' ELSE 'non_prod'
END WHERE kind IS NULL;
```

Anything labelled `type='prod'` becomes `kind='prod'`; everything
else lands in `non_prod`. Operators who labelled a true-prod
environment with a non-prod `type` MUST correct via
`PUT /api/v1/environments/:id` after running the migration.

## API surface

| Endpoint | Auth | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/v1/environments` | admin | Create an env. `kind` derives from `type` when omitted. |
| `GET /api/v1/environments` | session | Flat list across projects. |
| `GET /api/v1/environments/:id` | session | Single env. |
| `PUT /api/v1/environments/:id` | admin | Update `description` + `risk_level` ONLY. `kind` and `name` are immutable post-creation. |
| `DELETE /api/v1/environments/:id` | admin | Hard delete. Cascades through env_id FKs. |
| `GET /api/v1/projects/:id/environments` | session | List per project. |

### Why kind and name are immutable

Once an environment row exists, `kind` and `name` are pinned. Two
reasons:

1. The PolicyEngine caches resolution results keyed by environment;
   flipping `kind` after a policy decision has been audited would
   create a discrepancy between the audit log and the live
   classification.
2. An operator who can flip a `prod` env to `non_prod` after grants
   exist could un-gate the direct-reveal path without anyone
   noticing. `kind` immutability + the PolicyEngine PROD invariant
   are belt-and-braces for the same threat.

Operators who need to change `kind` must DELETE + recreate. The FK
cascade through `access_requests` / `secret_wraps` / `project_secrets`
ensures no orphaned bindings survive.

## Operational checklist for new environments

1. Create the env via `POST /environments`:
   ```json
   {
     "project_id": "<uuid>",
     "name": "uat",
     "type": "uat",
     "kind": "non_prod",
     "risk_level": 1,
     "description": "Pre-production staging for the billing team."
   }
   ```
2. Bind the secrets the env should expose via
   `POST /projects/:project_id/secrets` with the new
   `environment_id` field set (Slice L3). The legacy
   `secrets.labels.Env` label is no longer the authorization key.
   `project_secrets.environment_id` is.
3. Add a `policy_rules` row scoped to this env that picks the right
   workflow. See [Policy templates](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/policy-templates/) for the
   canonical shapes.
4. (Optional) Grant the `secret.reveal.direct` permission to the
   `developer` role (it's seeded by default; revoke if you want a
   stricter baseline). See
   [Authentication, direct reveal permission](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#direct-reveal-permission-slice-l4).

## Related

- [Policy templates](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/policy-templates/), non_prod / prod policy
  rule examples.
- [Authentication](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/), `secret.reveal.direct`
  permission + the L4 dev endpoints.
- API reference: `GET /users/me/projects` returns each project with
  its environments inline (Slice L4).
- [Cross-team requests](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/cross-team-requests/), Slice N split between
  the **target** (team / project / environment that provides the value)
  and the **destination** (provider connection + secret_ref where the
  value lands). Both reference the project / environment model defined
  here.
- [Provider connections](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/provider-connections/), connection metadata
  binds at project ± environment granularity via the
  `project_provider_connections` join table. Project-wide bindings have
  `environment_id IS NULL`; env-specific bindings narrow to one row.
