    although the worker ignores it. With `aws-kms`, give the KMS permissions
    to the api's IRSA role (`api.serviceAccount.annotations`) so no KMS
    credential sits in the shared Secret. With `vault-transit`, the Vault
    token in the shared Secret still reaches the worker's environment.

5. **Keep the Gateway sweepers on.** Check that
   `worker.config.gatewaySweepers.enabled` is `true` in your values. If you
   set `SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED` in the env Secret before the
   upgrade, move it to this value: the chart now renders the variable, and
   the rendered value (`false` by default) wins over the Secret. The interval
   values are listed in the
   [configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#worker).

6. **Set each environment's observation source to `gateway`** once a Gateway
   is bound for it
   ([step 8](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#8-switch-the-environment-to-gateway-observation)).
   Environments the migration moved to `none` stay unobserved until you do.
   The source is read when a request reaches `executed`, so requests executed
   before the switch get no tasks.

7. **Use the console as it is now.** Admin → Integrations and its Argo CD
   endpoint and app-mapping pages are gone. Argo CD is configured on the
   Gateway (Admin → Gateways). On a project's **Environments** tab, the
   **Observation** dialog offers **Gateway** and **None**; an environment with
   no stored source shows **None**.

## Rollback

Redeploying an older api does not restore the control-plane path. The Argo CD
tokens and the endpoint and mapping tables are gone, and the down migration
restores the schema only: no token comes back and no environment returns to
`control_plane`. There is no setting that turns the poller back on.

Until a Gateway runs and its environment is set to `gateway`, observation shows
as unavailable or unverified: requests carry no Argo CD state, or their tasks
end `timed_out` (`gateway_unavailable`) at the deadline. Neither fails the
request. Both clear once a bound Gateway is running.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/object-storage/

# Object storage

The api can keep media files in an S3 bucket or on any server that speaks
the S3 API, such as MinIO. Postgres keeps only the metadata for each file.

!!! warning "In progress"
    Object storage is implemented in
    [api#255](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api/pull/255) and the chart
    values in [charts#40](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/pull/40)
    and [charts#42](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/pull/42). It
    has not passed QA yet. See [Product status](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/).

## What is stored there

Only media. Today that means the project and team logos served by
`GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/logo` and `GET /api/v1/teams/{id}/logo`. New
media fields added later use the same store.

Never stored in object storage:

- secret values, wrapped or unwrapped;
- tokens, credentials or wrap bodies;
- audit records. Audit events for logo changes record metadata only
  (sha256, byte length, dimensions), never image bytes or URLs.

### Object keys

Each object is keyed by the sha256 of its content:

```text
<prefix>/logos/<kind>/<entity-id>/<sha256>.png
```

| Part | Value |
|---|---|
| `<prefix>` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX` |
| `<kind>` | `project` or `team` (singular, lower case) |
| `<entity-id>` | The project or team id |
| `<sha256>` | Hash of the re-encoded PNG. It is also the `ETag` the api returns. |

For example, with `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX=secrets-bridge` a project logo
lives at `secrets-bridge/logos/project/<project-id>/<sha256>.png`. Without
a prefix the key starts at `logos/`. The api trims slashes at either end
of the prefix.

Uploading the same image twice maps to the same key, so writes are
idempotent. When a logo is replaced, the api deletes the old object after
the database row points at the new one. The row stores the full key, so
changing `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX` later does not move existing logos: they
stay at their old keys.

### How a logo moves through the system

The bucket stays private. The console never talks to it. Every read and
write goes through the api, so the existing authorization rules apply:
reading a project logo needs read scope on that project, a team logo has
the same visibility as the team, and uploading or removing a logo needs
the global `team.edit` permission.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as Console
    participant API as api
    participant OS as Object store
    participant PG as Postgres
    UI->>API: PUT /api/v1/projects/id/logo (PNG or JPEG)
    API->>API: Validate and re-encode to PNG, compute sha256
    API->>OS: PutObject at prefix/logos/kind/id/sha256.png
    API->>PG: Upsert metadata row (object key, sha256, size)
    API->>OS: Delete previous object, if any
    API-->>UI: 200 with logo_version
    UI->>API: GET /api/v1/projects/id/logo
    API->>PG: Read metadata row
    API->>OS: GetObject
    API-->>UI: image/png with ETag
```

If the object write fails, the database row is not changed and the api
returns `503 logo storage is unavailable`. If the row write fails, the api
removes the object it just wrote, unless the current row already uses that
same key, and returns `500 internal error`. If deleting the old object
fails, the object is left behind and the api logs a warning; no row points
at it.

On reads, the api answers `If-None-Match` from the row without reading the
object. A row that still holds its image in the `png` column (before the
backfill, or written by an old replica during a rollout) is served from
those bytes with the same headers and `ETag`. If a row points at an object
that is missing, the api returns `404` and logs an error that names the
key; the key is not in the response body.

The api never sets an ACL on an object and does not issue presigned URLs.

## Configuration

The api reads these environment variables. The full list is in the
[Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/#api).

| Env var | Notes |
|---|---|
| Env var | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET` | unset | Bucket name. Unset, with no other `SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` set, means object storage is off. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_REGION` | unset | Bucket region, for example `us-east-1`. Required when the bucket is set. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT` | unset | Endpoint override for S3-compatible servers or a VPC endpoint, for example `https://s3.example.com`. Plain `http://` is accepted only with `SB_ENV=dev`. Leave unset for AWS S3. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` | `false` | `true` or `false`. `true` for servers that need path-style addressing, such as MinIO. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX` | unset | Key prefix inside the bucket, for example `secrets-bridge`. Slashes at either end are trimmed. Empty, `.` or `..` segments are refused. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE` | unset | Unset or empty sends no SSE header, so the bucket's default encryption applies. Otherwise exactly `AES256` (SSE-S3) or `aws:kms` (SSE-KMS). Case-sensitive. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_KMS_KEY_ID` | unset | KMS key id, ARN or alias. Required with `SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE=aws:kms`, and refused with any other SSE mode. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL` | `true` | Run the logo backfill at api start. Set `false` for the first step of a rolling upgrade. See [Upgrading: moving existing logos](#upgrading-moving-existing-logos). |

Credentials come from the standard AWS SDK chain: IRSA, an instance role,
or `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in the environment. This
is the same chain the `aws-kms` backend uses. There are no
`SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` variables for credentials.

### Boot behaviour

| State | What the api does |
|---|---|
| Not configured (no `SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` set) | Boots normally. `PUT` and `DELETE` on a logo return `503 logo storage is not configured`. Logos still stored in Postgres keep being served. The api never falls back to writing media to Postgres. If inline logos exist, the boot logs a warning with their count. |
| Misconfigured | Refuses to boot with an error. This covers any `SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` setting without a bucket, a bucket without a region, an unknown SSE value, `aws:kms` without a key id, a key id with another SSE mode, a malformed endpoint or prefix, a plain `http://` endpoint when `SB_ENV` is not `dev`, and a `SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` that is not `true` or `false`. |
| Configured, bucket unreachable | Refuses to boot. The api calls `HeadBucket` at start and gives up after 15 seconds. A denied `HeadBucket` (see the [IAM policy](#least-privilege-iam-policy)) fails the same way. |
| Configured and reachable | Logs `object storage ready`, writes and reads logos in the bucket, and starts the backfill unless `SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL=false`. |

When the bucket is reachable at boot but fails later, logo requests that
need it return `503 logo storage is unavailable`. The rest of the api
keeps working.

### Helm chart values

The `secrets-bridge` chart maps `objectStore.*` values to the
`SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` variables on the api:

| Value | Default | Env var on the api |
|---|---|---|
| `objectStore.enabled` | `false` | Turns the settings below on. Off renders no `SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` at all. |
| `objectStore.bucket` | `""` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET` (required when enabled) |
| `objectStore.region` | `""` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_REGION` (required when enabled) |
| `objectStore.endpoint` | `""` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT` |
| `objectStore.prefix` | `""` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX` |
| `objectStore.sse` | `AES256` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE`. `""` renders no variable, so no SSE header is sent. |
| `objectStore.kmsKeyId` | `""` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_KMS_KEY_ID` (only with `sse: aws:kms`) |
| `objectStore.forcePathStyle` | `false` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE`, always rendered as `"true"` or `"false"` |
| `objectStore.logoBackfill` | `true` | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL`, always rendered as `"true"` or `"false"` |
| `objectStore.credentials.existingSecret` | `""` | Name of a Secret with static keys. When set, the api gets `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` through `secretKeyRef`. |
| `objectStore.credentials.accessKeyIdKey` | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | Key in that Secret for the access key id |
| `objectStore.credentials.secretAccessKeyKey` | `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | Key in that Secret for the secret access key |
| `api.networkPolicy.egress.objectStore.enabled` | `true` | Adds a TCP egress rule to the object store when `objectStore.enabled` |
| `api.networkPolicy.egress.objectStore.to` | `[]` | NetworkPolicy peers that narrow the rule. Empty allows the port to any destination. |

The chart's default for `sse` is `AES256`, while the api on its own sends
no SSE header when `SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE` is unset. Only the api gets these
variables; the worker does not read media.

The chart does not take credentials in values. On AWS, use IRSA through
`api.serviceAccount.annotations`. For an S3-compatible server, use
`objectStore.credentials.existingSecret`. Static keys cannot be combined
with `kms.backend=aws-kms`, because the SDK prefers them over IRSA and the
KMS client would sign with them.

The chart refuses to render when object storage is enabled and `bucket`
or `region` is empty, `sse` is not `AES256`, `aws:kms` or empty,
`sse: aws:kms` has no `kmsKeyId`, `kmsKeyId` is set with another `sse`,
the endpoint is not `http(s)://host[:port]`, the endpoint is plain
`http://` with `env=production`, the prefix has an empty, `.` or `..`
segment, `logoBackfill` is not `true` or `false`, or static keys are
combined with `kms.backend=aws-kms`.

The egress port comes from `objectStore.endpoint`: its explicit port, else
443 for `https` and 80 for `http`, and 443 when no endpoint is set (AWS
S3). To manage the rule yourself, set
`api.networkPolicy.egress.objectStore.enabled: false` and add it to
`api.networkPolicy.egress.extraRules`.

## AWS S3 with IRSA

1. Create a bucket, for example `example-bucket`, in the same region as
   the cluster. Keep the defaults for Object Ownership (ACLs disabled) and
   Block Public Access (all four settings on).
2. Turn on default encryption. See [Encryption at rest](#encryption-at-rest).
3. Create an IAM role for the api ServiceAccount with a trust policy for
   your cluster's OIDC provider, and attach the
   [least-privilege policy](#least-privilege-iam-policy) below.
4. Annotate the api ServiceAccount and set the values:

```yaml
api:
  serviceAccount:
    annotations:
      eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/secrets-bridge-api
objectStore:
  enabled: true
  bucket: example-bucket
  region: us-east-1
  prefix: secrets-bridge
  sse: aws:kms
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
```

If the api role already has access for the `aws-kms` backend, you can add
the S3 policy to the same role.

To keep S3 traffic inside the VPC, add an S3 gateway endpoint to the
cluster's route tables. The api needs no extra setting for a gateway
endpoint.

## S3-compatible servers (MinIO)

For MinIO or another S3 API, set the endpoint and turn on path-style
addressing. Static credentials come from an existing Secret, never from
values.

Read the keys at silent prompts (paste each, then Enter) so they never
reach a command line, the shell history or the process list. This works
in bash and zsh:

```bash
read -rs SB_S3_KEY_ID
read -rs SB_S3_SECRET
kubectl -n secrets-bridge create secret generic secrets-bridge-objectstore \
  --from-file=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<(printf '%s' "$SB_S3_KEY_ID") \
  --from-file=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<(printf '%s' "$SB_S3_SECRET")
unset SB_S3_KEY_ID SB_S3_SECRET
```

```yaml
objectStore:
  enabled: true
  endpoint: https://s3.example.com
  forcePathStyle: true
  bucket: example-bucket
  region: us-east-1
  prefix: secrets-bridge
  sse: ""                  # no SSE header; see the notes below
  credentials:
    existingSecret: secrets-bridge-objectstore
api:
  networkPolicy:
    egress:
      objectStore:
        to:
          - namespaceSelector:
              matchLabels:
                kubernetes.io/metadata.name: minio
```

The keys in the Secret above match the default
`credentials.accessKeyIdKey` and `credentials.secretAccessKeyKey`, so
those don't need to be set. Deliver the Secret with External Secrets,
sealed-secrets or a similar tool. The `to` block is only needed when
MinIO runs in the cluster and you want to narrow the egress rule.

Notes for MinIO:

- Create a MinIO user with a policy limited to the bucket and prefix, in
  the same shape as the IAM policy below. Do not use the root user.
- Use `https://`. The chart refuses a plain `http://` endpoint with
  `env=production`, and the api refuses it at boot unless `SB_ENV=dev`,
  including when the settings come from `secrets.existingSecret`.
- `region` must match the region the server is configured with. MinIO
  uses `us-east-1` unless you set another one.
- `sse: AES256` needs server-side encryption configured on the MinIO
  server (for example with MinIO KES). Without it, uploads that request
  SSE fail, so use `sse: ""` and let the server's own settings apply.

For local development, the api repository's `docker-compose.yml` runs a
MinIO service and creates the bucket. See
[Running locally with docker compose](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/docker-compose/).

## Least-privilege IAM policy

Grant object access only under the prefix, and `s3:ListBucket` on the
bucket itself. Replace `example-bucket` and `secrets-bridge` with your
bucket and `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX`. Without a prefix, use
`arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/logos/*` for the object statement.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ObjectsUnderPrefix",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:PutObject",
        "s3:DeleteObject"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/secrets-bridge/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "BucketCheck",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket"
    }
  ]
}
```

`s3:ListBucket` is needed for two things:

- **The boot check.** The api calls `HeadBucket` at start, and S3
  authorizes `HeadBucket` with `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket. A
  `HeadBucket` request carries no prefix, so do not add an `s3:prefix`
  condition to this statement: with the condition, `HeadBucket` is denied
  and the api refuses to boot.
- **Missing keys.** With `s3:ListBucket`, `HeadObject` and `GetObject`
  return `404` instead of `403` for a key that doesn't exist, so the api
  can tell a missing logo from a permission error.

The api itself never lists objects.

The policy does not grant `s3:PutObjectAcl`, bucket policy changes or
any access outside the prefix. The api does not need them.

## Encryption at rest

| Setting | `SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE` | Key | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| SSE-S3 | `AES256` | Managed by S3 | Simple setups, S3-compatible servers |
| SSE-KMS | `aws:kms` | A KMS key you control (`SB_OBJECTSTORE_KMS_KEY_ID`) | When you need key policies, key rotation control or CloudTrail records of key use |

Also set the same default encryption on the bucket, so objects written by
other tools (for example a restore job) are encrypted too.

With SSE-KMS, the api role needs these KMS permissions on the key, in
addition to the S3 policy:

- `kms:GenerateDataKey` to write objects;
- `kms:Decrypt` to read them.

Add a statement like this to the key policy, or grant the same actions
in the api role's IAM policy if the key policy delegates to IAM:

```json
{
  "Sid": "AllowSecretsBridgeApiForS3",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {
    "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/secrets-bridge-api"
  },
  "Action": [
    "kms:GenerateDataKey",
    "kms:Decrypt"
  ],
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "kms:ViaService": "s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"
    }
  }
}
```

The `kms:ViaService` condition limits use of the key to requests made
through S3. If you turn on S3 Bucket Keys, the number of KMS calls drops
and the policy above still applies.

You can use the same KMS key as the `aws-kms` backend, but a separate key
keeps media encryption apart from the key that protects wraps.

## Bucket settings

### Private bucket and Block Public Access

- Turn on all four Block Public Access settings on the bucket, and on the
  account if nothing else in it needs public buckets.
- Set Object Ownership to **Bucket owner enforced** so ACLs are disabled.
- Do not add a bucket policy that grants public or cross-account read.
  The api serves every image.
- Optionally add a bucket policy that denies requests without TLS
  (`aws:SecureTransport` is `false`).

### Versioning and lifecycle

Recommendations:

- **Turn on versioning.** A deleted or replaced logo can then be restored
  from a previous version.
- **Expire noncurrent versions** after a retention period that fits your
  recovery needs, for example 30 days. Keys are content hashes, so the
  api only ever rewrites a key with identical bytes. Noncurrent versions
  come from deletes.
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after a short period, for example
  7 days.
- **Do not expire current objects** under the prefix. The api deletes
  objects it no longer needs, and an expired current object turns into a
  `404` for that logo.

Scope lifecycle rules to `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX` if the bucket holds other
data.

## Backups

Media is no longer part of Postgres snapshots. A database restore brings
back the metadata rows, which point at object keys, but not the images.

- Back up the bucket on its own, for example with versioning plus AWS
  Backup for S3, or replication to a second bucket.
- When you restore, restore the bucket and the database to about the same
  point in time. A row whose object is missing returns `404` for that
  logo. An object with no row is unused and can be removed.
- Losing media does not affect secrets, approvals or audit. Logos can be
  uploaded again.

## Upgrading: moving existing logos

Before object storage, logos were stored as `BYTEA` in the `png` column of
`project_logos` and `team_logos`.

### Migration 0040

Migration `0040` changes both tables:

- adds `object_key`, nullable, set by every new upload and by the backfill;
- adds `byte_length`, nullable, the stored PNG's size, so the delete audit
  can report it without reading the object;
- makes `png` nullable. New uploads write `png = NULL`;
- adds a CHECK that every row has `png` or `object_key`.

The `png` column stays for now. A later migration drops it (and the CHECK
that references it) once deployments have run the backfill.

### The backfill

The backfill runs inside the api, at start, in the background. Boot does
not wait for it, because logos still in `png` are served until they move.

- It runs on one replica at a time, under the Redis lock
  `objectstore:logo-backfill`, which it renews while it runs. A replica
  that finds the lock held skips the backfill.
- It pages through rows that still have `png`, checks that the bytes match
  the recorded sha256, writes the object, and then clears `png` and sets
  `object_key` and `byte_length` in one locked, conditional update. The
  update only applies if the row still holds the same image inline.
- A row whose bytes don't match its sha256 is left inline and logged,
  because moving it would change its `ETag`.
- It is idempotent. A second run finds nothing to move, and
  content-addressed keys make a repeated write harmless.
- It also moves rows that old replicas write during a rolling upgrade, the
  next time it runs.
- It writes no audit events, since the logo did not change.
- If it stops early (an error or its 30-minute limit), it logs
  `logo backfill stopped early; will resume at next start` and continues
  on the next api start.

Set `SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL=false` (chart value
`objectStore.logoBackfill: false`) to switch it off. The api then logs
`logo backfill switched off`.

### Rollout

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["1. Create bucket, IAM and KMS access"] --> B["2. Deploy with logoBackfill false"]
    B --> C["3. All replicas new: logoBackfill true, restart"]
    C --> D["4. Verify no png rows are left"]
    D --> E["5. Later release drops the png column"]
```

1. **Prepare storage.** Create the bucket, the IAM policy and, for
   SSE-KMS, the key policy statement, as described above.
2. **Deploy with the backfill off.** Upgrade the chart and api together
   with `objectStore.*` set and `objectStore.logoBackfill: false`
   (`SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL=false`). Migration `0040` runs. Old
   replicas keep reading and writing `png`. New replicas write new logos
   to the bucket and serve both kinds. Until the rollout finishes, an old
   replica serves an empty image for a logo uploaded through a new
   replica.
3. **Turn the backfill on.** Once every replica runs the new version, set
   `objectStore.logoBackfill: true` (the default) and restart the api. A
   chart upgrade that changes the value restarts the pods. The backfill
   moves every inline row, including any that old replicas wrote during
   step 2.
4. **Verify.** Look for the `logo backfill done` log line, which reports
   `moved`, `skipped` and `failed` counts, or check that both queries
   return 0:

    ```sql
    SELECT count(*) FROM project_logos WHERE png IS NOT NULL;
    SELECT count(*) FROM team_logos WHERE png IS NOT NULL;
    ```

    A non-zero count after the backfill means rows were skipped (digest
    mismatch) or failed; the api logs each one. When there is nothing left
    to move, the api logs nothing at the default level.
5. **Drop the old column.** A later migration removes the `png` column.
   Run the queries above before you upgrade to that release, and take a
   database backup first, because the old bytes are gone after it runs.

With a single api replica, or when the short window in step 2 doesn't
matter, deploy with the default (`logoBackfill: true`) and skip step 2.

### Rolling back

- Rolling the api image back to a version from before object storage
  leaves the database at migration `0040`. Rows that were moved, or
  uploaded through a new replica, have `png = NULL`, and the old version
  serves an empty image for them.
- The `0040` down migration deletes the rows that live only in object
  storage, because their bytes cannot be restored into Postgres. Those
  logos have to be uploaded again. The objects stay in the bucket.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/verifying-releases/

# Verifying images and charts

Every container image (`api`, `ui`, `worker`, `agent`, `controller`,
`gateway`) and every Helm chart is signed by the GitHub Actions workflow that built them,
using cosign keyless signing. Each image also carries an SPDX SBOM and SLSA
build provenance. Verify them before you deploy, and pin images by digest
in production, as the charts require.

!!! info "No versioned release yet"
    All repos will release together under one shared version (`v0.1.0`,
    `v0.2.0`, and so on). Until the first release is tagged, the published
    artifacts are the `main` builds: `:dev`, `:main` and `:sha-<short>`
    images and `X.Y.Z-dev.<sha>` charts. They are signed the same way, by
    the workflow running on `refs/heads/main`.

## What is signed and attached

| Artifact | Where | Signed by | Attached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Images | `ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/<api\|ui\|worker\|agent\|controller\|gateway>` | `https://github.com/secrets-bridge/<repo>/.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml@<ref>` | SPDX SBOM, SLSA provenance |
| Charts | `oci://ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge`, `.../secrets-bridge-agent` and `.../secrets-bridge-gateway` | `https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/.github/workflows/chart-publish.yml@<ref>` | none |

`<ref>` is `refs/tags/vX.Y.Z` for a release and `refs/heads/main` for a
`main` build. The image signature covers the multi-arch index and each
platform image in it.

## Verify an image

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/api:0.1.0 \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/secrets-bridge/api/.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml@refs/tags/v0.1.0 \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

For a `main` build, use the `sha-<short>` tag (or the digest) and
`@refs/heads/main` as the identity. Verification fails if the image was
signed by any other repository or workflow.

## Inspect the SBOM and provenance

```bash
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/api:0.1.0 --format '{{ json .SBOM }}'
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/api:0.1.0 --format '{{ json .Provenance }}'
```

The SBOM lists the packages in the image. The provenance records the
source repository, the commit and the build parameters.

## Verify a chart

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/secrets-bridge/charts/secrets-bridge:0.1.0 \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/.github/workflows/chart-publish.yml@refs/tags/v0.1.0 \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

## Release pages

Each release has a GitHub Release in every repo, with the changes for that
version, the exact image or chart digests and these commands filled in.
Release tags are never moved or reused: a broken release is followed by a
new patch version.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/

# Configuration reference

Every environment variable across `api` / `agent` / `worker` /
`controller` / `gateway`. Defaults shown match the source tree as of v0.X.

## api

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `API_ADDR` | no | `:8080` | Listen address |
| `API_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` | no | `15s` | SIGTERM grace period |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | no | `info` | `debug` / `info` / `warn` / `error` |
| `SB_ENV` | no | `production` | `production` or `dev`; anything else fails boot. `dev` allows the `local` KMS backend, seeds three dev users on an empty database and drops the `Secure` cookie flag. Never `dev` outside a laptop. |
| `SB_REQUIRE_MFA_AT_LOGIN` | no | `true`, or `false` when `SB_ENV=dev` | Login-time MFA: every authenticated route needs a session verified with a second factor, and a user with no factor adds one right after signing in. See [Step-up vs login-time MFA](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/authentication/#step-up-vs-login-time-mfa). Setting `false` outside dev logs a warning at boot. |
| `DATABASE_URL` | **yes** |  | `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` |
| `DATABASE_MAX_CONNS` | no | `10` | pgxpool size |
| `DATABASE_CONN_LIFETIME` | no | `1h` | |
| `REDIS_URL` | **yes** |  | `redis://host:6379/0`. Run this Redis with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`: a revoke keeps the agent or Gateway out of the auth cache with a short-lived key, and an evicted key would let a cached credential back in until it expires. |
| `REDIS_POOL_SIZE` | no | `10` | |
| `REDIS_DIAL_TIMEOUT` | no | `5s` | |
| `REDIS_NAMESPACE` | no | `secrets-bridge` | Key prefix |
| `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY` | yes when `SB_KMS_BACKEND=local` |  | base64 32 bytes (`openssl rand -base64 32`) |
| `SB_KMS_BACKEND` | no | `local` | `local` / `vault-transit` / `aws-kms`. `local` is refused at boot unless `SB_ENV=dev`, so production must set one of the other two. |
| `SB_KMS_VAULT_ADDR` | yes for `vault-transit` |  | |
| `SB_KMS_VAULT_TOKEN` | yes for `vault-transit` |  | |
| `SB_KMS_VAULT_KEY` | yes for `vault-transit` |  | Transit key name |
| `SB_KMS_VAULT_MOUNT` | no | `transit` | |
| `SB_KMS_AWS_REGION` | yes for `aws-kms` |  | |
| `SB_KMS_AWS_KEY_ID` | yes for `aws-kms` |  | Alias / ARN / key id |
| `SB_KMS_AWS_ENDPOINT` | no |  | LocalStack / VPC endpoint override |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` | recommended on first boot |  | See [Bootstrap](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/bootstrap/) |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | recommended on first boot |  | |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USER_ID` | optional |  | Opaque user_id for pre-OIDC role assignment |
| `SB_PUBLIC_URL` | no |  | The install's public address, for example `https://secrets.example.com`. Sign-in redirect URIs are built from it, never from request headers. When set, the console shows it read-only; unset, an admin saves it under Admin → Sign-in. Must be `https`, with no user info, query or fragment; plain `http` only for `localhost` or a loopback address with `SB_ENV=dev`. An invalid value stops the api at boot. See [Sign in with Google](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/#1-set-the-public-address) |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_BUCKET` | no |  | Bucket for media (logos). Unset, with no other `SB_OBJECTSTORE_*` set, turns object storage off. See [Object storage](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/object-storage/) |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_REGION` | yes with a bucket |  | Bucket region |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT` | no |  | `http://` or `https://` endpoint override for S3-compatible servers such as MinIO, or a VPC endpoint (`https://s3.example.com`). Unset for AWS S3. |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` | no | `false` | `true` or `false`. `true` for path-style addressing (MinIO) |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_PREFIX` | no |  | Key prefix inside the bucket. Slashes at either end are trimmed |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_SSE` | no |  | Unset or empty sends no SSE header. Otherwise exactly `AES256` (SSE-S3) or `aws:kms` (SSE-KMS) |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_KMS_KEY_ID` | yes for `aws:kms` |  | KMS key id, ARN or alias. Refused with any other SSE mode |
| `SB_OBJECTSTORE_LOGO_BACKFILL` | no | `true` | Move logos still stored in Postgres to the bucket at start. `false` for the first step of a rolling upgrade |

!!! note "Object storage behaviour"
    Without object storage the api boots, but logo uploads and deletes
    return `503 logo storage is not configured`, and logos still stored in
    Postgres are served. With any setting invalid, or a bucket that fails
    `HeadBucket` within 15 seconds, the api refuses to boot. Credentials
    come from the standard AWS SDK chain, as for `aws-kms`; there are no
    object-storage credential variables. Object storage has not passed QA
    yet. See [Object storage](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/object-storage/).

The dev-only switches the api also reads are listed under
[Insecure switches](#insecure-switches-dev-only).

## agent

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SB_CP_ENDPOINT` | **yes** |  | `https://api.example.com` |
| `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT` | no | `false` | Dev only: allows `http://` to the control plane. See [Insecure switches](#insecure-switches-dev-only) |
| `SB_CP_CA_FILE` | no |  | Pin a private CA (replaces system roots) |
| `SB_CP_TLS_SERVER_NAME` | no |  | SNI override for private DNS |
| `SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR` | no | `/etc/secrets-bridge/agent` | Read-only directory with the files `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` (base64 of the 32-byte X25519 key), written from `secrets-bridge-agent enroll` output. Every file is required; a file with group write or any bit for others (`mode & 0o037 != 0`) refuses the start. The agent never writes here. See [Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/) |
| `SB_CLUSTER_NAME` | **yes** for discovery |  | Stamped on every discovered secret. Use the `--cluster-name` given to `enroll` |
| `SB_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | |
| `SB_CLAIM_INTERVAL` | no | `5s` | |
| `SB_CLAIM_CONCURRENCY` | no | `4` | Worker pool size |
| `SB_LOCAL_ADDR` | no | `127.0.0.1:8090` | Listener for `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics` only. The `agent` Helm chart sets `0.0.0.0:8090` so kubelet probes can reach it; the chart's NetworkPolicy denies all ingress to the pod. |
| `SB_VAULT_ADDR` | yes for Vault |  | |
| `SB_VAULT_TOKEN` | yes for Vault token auth |  | |
| `SB_VAULT_KUBERNETES_ROLE` | yes for Vault k8s auth |  | Alternative to token |
| `SB_VAULT_NAMESPACE` | no |  | Vault Enterprise namespace |
| `SB_AWS_REGION` | yes for AWS SM |  | |
| `SB_AWS_ROLE_ARN` | no |  | Cross-account AssumeRole |
| `SB_AWS_ENDPOINT` | no |  | LocalStack / VPC endpoint override |

The agent reads its credential and key only from `SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR`.
There is no environment variable for either. Name, provider type and region are
flags of `secrets-bridge-agent enroll`, not runtime settings.

**AWS credentials** are read from the standard AWS SDK chain
(IRSA, instance role, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`,
shared profile). The agent deliberately does **not** add new env
vars for AWS credentials, that would invite operators to mix
sources.

## worker

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | **yes** |  | Same Postgres as the api |
| `REDIS_URL` | **yes** |  | Same Redis as the api |
| `SB_DISCOVER_TARGETS_JSON` | no |  | Periodic discovery targets (admin API tracked) |
| `SB_WORKER_LOCAL_ADDR` | no | `127.0.0.1:8091` | Local listen address |
| `SB_WORKER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` | no | `15s` | |
| `SB_WORKER_WRAPS_EXPIRED_INTERVAL` | no | `1m` | |
| `SB_WORKER_SECRETS_STALE_INTERVAL` | no | `5m` | |
| `SB_WORKER_SECRETS_STALE_AFTER` | no | `24h` | |
| `SB_WORKER_AGENTS_STALE_INTERVAL` | no | `1m` | |
| `SB_WORKER_AGENTS_STALE_AFTER` | no | `5m` | |
| `SB_WORKER_JOBS_RECOVERY_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | |
| `SB_WORKER_DISCOVER_INTERVAL` | no | `1h` | |
| `SB_WORKER_REVEAL_SESSIONS_EXPIRED_INTERVAL` | no | `5s` | |
| `SB_WORKER_CROSS_TEAM_FILL_EXPIRED_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | |
| `SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_URL` | no |  | Generic webhook. Also turns on the waiting-account message, which goes to this webhook only |
| `SB_WORKER_WEBHOOK_SLACK_FORMAT` | no | `false` | Wraps payload in `{text: ...}` |
| `SB_WORKER_USERS_PENDING_INTERVAL` | no | `1m` | How often the `users-pending` sweeper posts about accounts waiting for approval, at most one message per run. At least `30s`, or the worker refuses to start. See [Sign in with Google](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/#notify-admins-from-the-worker) |
| `SB_PUBLIC_URL` | no |  | Same variable as the api's, used for the link in the waiting-account message. Unset, the address saved in the console is used. An invalid value stops the worker at boot |
| `SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED` | no | `false` | Turns on the four [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#9-turn-on-the-worker-sweepers) sweepers below. Off, the worker never reads the Gateway and observation tables. In the `secrets-bridge` chart, set `worker.config.gatewaySweepers.enabled` (and the intervals under `worker.config.gatewaySweepers`); the chart always renders this variable, so a value in the env Secret is overridden |
| `SB_WORKER_OBSERVATION_LEASES_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | Tick of `observation-leases`, which puts tasks whose lease ran out back in the queue. At least `5s` |
| `SB_WORKER_OBSERVATION_DEADLINES_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | Tick of `observation-deadlines`, which closes open tasks past their deadline as `timed_out`. At least `5s` |
| `SB_WORKER_OBSERVATION_BATCH_SIZE` | no | `200` | Tasks per statement. A tick runs up to 10 batches. 1 to 1000 |
| `SB_WORKER_GATEWAYS_STALE_INTERVAL` | no | `1m` | Tick of `gateways-stale`. At least `10s` |
| `SB_WORKER_GATEWAYS_STALE_AFTER` | no | `2m` | An `active` Gateway with no heartbeat for this long turns `stale` (four missed 30s heartbeats). At least `1m` |
| `SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_REPLICAS_PRUNE_INTERVAL` | no | `1h` | Tick of `gateway-replicas-prune`. At least `1m` |
| `SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_REPLICAS_RETENTION` | no | `24h` | Replica rows not seen for this long are deleted. At least `10m`, the api's replica-limit window |

Every duration is a Go duration (`30s`, `5m`, `1h`) and must be greater than zero, or the worker refuses to start. The Gateway values must also be at or above their floors. The floors are checked even while the Gateway sweepers are off, so a bad value stops the boot with an error naming the variable.

The worker has no KMS settings. It does not read `SB_KMS_*` and needs no
access to the KMS key; the api is the only component that uses it.

## Retired settings

These settings are no longer read. If one is set, the component logs its name
at startup, never its value, and carries on. No value turns the old behaviour
back on, and a value that used to fail validation no longer stops the boot.
Remove them from your env Secret. The `secrets-bridge` chart no longer renders
them, and its old `api.config.gitopsEnabled`, `worker.config.gitopsEnabled` and
`worker.config.gitops*` values were removed; delete them from your values
files.

| Env var | Component | What it used to do |
|---|---|---|
| `SB_JWT_SECRET` | api | Signed the login bearer token. Sign-in is cookie-session only |
| `SB_JWT_TOKEN_TTL` | api | Lifetime of the login bearer token |
| `SB_GITOPS_ENABLED` | api | Turned on the control-plane Argo CD integration (endpoints, app mappings, poller). The Gateway is the only Argo CD client |
| `SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_ARGOCD_ADDR` | api | Allowed `http://` Argo CD endpoints on the control plane |
| `SB_WORKER_GITOPS_ENABLED` | worker | Turned on the control-plane Argo CD poller |
| `SB_WORKER_GITOPS_POLL_INTERVAL` | worker | Poller tick |
| `SB_WORKER_GITOPS_TIMEOUT_INTERVAL` | worker | Poller timeout sweeper tick |
| `SB_WORKER_GITOPS_BATCH_SIZE` | worker | Observations per poll |
| `SB_WORKER_GITOPS_HTTP_TIMEOUT` | worker | Per-call ceiling for Argo CD requests |

The Argo CD settings were retired when the control plane stopped talking to
Argo CD. See [Gateway cutover](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway-cutover/).

## controller

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `KUBECONFIG` | for out-of-cluster runs |  | In-cluster uses the projected SA |
| `LEADER_ELECTION_NAMESPACE` | no | controller's own | |
| `METRICS_ADDR` | no | `:8080` | Prometheus exposition |
| `WATCH_NAMESPACE` | no | "" (all) | Limit reconciliation scope |

## gateway

The [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/) binary. Each variable also has a flag
(`gateway -h`); a flag overrides its variable. A malformed value stops the boot
instead of falling back to the default. The
[`secrets-bridge-gateway` chart](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/charts/blob/main/gateway/README.md)
sets these from its values, and the
[gateway README](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/gateway#configuration) is the
source for this table.

| Env var | Required | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SB_CP_ENDPOINT` | **yes** |  | `https://cp.example.com`. `https://` only, unless `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true`. No userinfo |
| `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT` | no | `false` | Dev only: allows `http://` to the control plane and to every Argo CD `base_url`. See [Insecure switches](#insecure-switches-dev-only) |
| `SB_CP_CA_FILE` | no |  | PEM bundle that replaces the system roots for the control plane |
| `SB_CP_TLS_SERVER_NAME` | no |  | TLS server name override |
| `SB_GATEWAY_IDENTITY_FILE` | no | `/etc/secrets-bridge/gateway/identity.json` | `{"gateway_id": "...", "gateway_secret": "..."}` from enrollment. Mode `0400`, `0600` or `0440` (what a Secret volume with `fsGroup` produces). Any bit for other users, or group write, is refused at boot |
| `SB_GATEWAY_ID` / `SB_GATEWAY_SECRET` | no |  | Credential pair as env vars. When both are unset the identity file is read. The chart does not use them |
| `SB_GATEWAY_LOCAL_ADDR` | no | `127.0.0.1:8091` | `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/metrics`. Must be a literal loopback IP; `localhost` is refused |
| `SB_GATEWAY_CONNECTORS_FILE` | no |  | JSON list of locally bound connectors. Empty binds none. The chart renders it into a ConfigMap |
| `SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS` | no | `false` | Binds the Release 2 `eso` and `rollout` kinds. Not supported for production: the Gateway logs a WARN at boot while it is on. When off, a connectors file that names either kind is refused. The chart never sets it |
| `SB_GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` | no | `15s` | Half is spent waiting for passes in flight, then unfinished tasks are released |
| `SB_GATEWAY_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` | no | `30s` | Used until the control plane suggests an interval |
| `SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_INTERVAL` | no | `5s` | Base claim interval, jittered between half and one and a half times |
| `SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_IDLE_MAX` | no | `30s` | Longest claim interval after empty polls. Not shorter than the claim interval |
| `SB_GATEWAY_CLAIM_CONCURRENCY` | no | `1` | Observation passes in flight per replica, 1 to 16 |
| `SB_GATEWAY_LEASE_MARGIN` | no | `3s` | A pass stops this long before its lease expires |
| `SB_GATEWAY_PASS_TIMEOUT` | no | `30s` | Upper bound for one pass |
| `SB_GATEWAY_CP_UNREACHABLE_AFTER` | no | `2m` | The Gateway turns not ready when no heartbeat has been accepted for this long |
| `SB_GATEWAY_PRIVILEGE_RECHECK_INTERVAL` | no | `5m` | How often every connector self-check and every Argo CD can-i probe runs again. A value under `1m` refuses the start. The chart does not set it |
| `SB_LOG_LEVEL` | no | `info` | `debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error` |

The Gateway ignores `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` for every connection, so a
bearer credential never reaches a proxy.

Each entry in the connectors file has a `name` (a DNS label the control plane
binds to), a `kind` and `settings`. For `argocd` the settings are `base_url`,
`token_file` (an absolute path), optional `ca_file`, `tls_server_name` and
`timeout` (1s to 60s, default 10s), `allowed_projects` (at least one AppProject)
and `applications` (at least one `{id, name, app_namespace?, uid?}`). `uid` is
the Application's `metadata.uid` as a lower-case UUID. An `id` must not start
with `d-`, which is reserved for discovered targets. Unknown fields, unknown
kinds and duplicate names are refused at load.

## Secret material, naming convention

| Material | What it is | Where it lives | Rotation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY` | Master key for the `local` KMS backend | api env / K8s Secret | **Don't use in production**, use Vault Transit or AWS KMS |
| `SB_KMS_VAULT_TOKEN` | Vault token for the `vault-transit` backend | api env / K8s Secret | Lease-tracked; refresh via Vault rotation |
| Agent identity (`agent_id` + `agent_secret`) | Per-agent credential, sent as `X-Agent-Secret`. The control plane keeps only its SHA-256 | Your secret store (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) or a K8s Secret, mounted read-only into `SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR` | Revoke the agent and enroll a new one with a new token |
| Agent wire key (`private_key`) | X25519 key generated by `secrets-bridge-agent enroll`; the control plane seals values to its public key. Not a TLS client certificate | Same Secret as the agent identity. Never leaves your boundary | `rotate-key` with a rotation token, then restart the agent. See [Rotate the wire key](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/#rotate-the-wire-key) |
| Agent enrollment token | One-time token from `POST /api/v1/provider-connections/:id/agent-enrollment-token` | Used once from the operator's workstation, on stdin or from a file. Never stored in the cluster | Single use; expires after 15 minutes by default |
| Gateway identity (`gateway_id` + `gateway_secret`) | Per-Gateway credential, sent as `X-Gateway-Secret` | An existing K8s Secret, mounted read-only as `SB_GATEWAY_IDENTITY_FILE` | No rotation in Release 1: revoke the Gateway, create a new one, enroll it and update the Secret |
| Gateway enrollment token | One-time token from `POST /api/v1/admin/gateways/:id/enrollment-token` | Used once from the operator's workstation, never stored in the cluster | Single use; expires after 15 minutes by default |
| Argo CD token for the Gateway | Read-only token of a local Argo CD account (`applications, get`) | An existing K8s Secret, mounted as a file per connector | Update the Secret; the Gateway re-reads the file |
| `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | Seed admin password | api env at first boot | **Rotate immediately after first sign-in** |

None of these should ever appear in:

- Git history (use a K8s Secret, sealed-secret, or external-secrets-operator binding)
- CI logs (mask via the CI's secret-masking facility)
- Docker images (env vars in `Dockerfile ENV` are baked into layers)
- Application logs (the api strips them from all log lines)

## Insecure switches (dev only)

!!! danger "Never set any of these in production"
    Each switch below turns off a security control so a laptop dev loop
    works without TLS, a real KMS or MFA hardware. All of them default to
    the safe value. If you find one set on a shared or routable
    deployment, treat it as an incident.

| Switch | Component | Default | What the unsafe value does | Guard |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SB_ENV=dev` | api | `production` | Allows the `local` KMS backend and `SB_MFA_DEV_ALLOW_PWD`, seeds three dev users with logged passwords on an empty database, and drops the `Secure` flag from session cookies | Unknown values fail boot; WARN log at boot |
| `SB_KMS_BACKEND=local` (with `SB_WRAP_MASTER_KEY`) | api | `local` | Keeps the storage-envelope master key in the api's own environment, next to the data it protects | api refuses to boot unless `SB_ENV=dev`, so an unset backend fails closed in production; the `secrets-bridge` chart refuses `kms.backend=local` with `env=production` |
| `SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_HEADER_AUTH=true` | api | `false` | Accepts an `X-User-Id` header as the caller's identity when there is no session cookie. Anyone who can reach the api can act as any user. | Not tied to `SB_ENV`; WARN log at boot |
| `SB_ALLOW_DIRECT_AGENT_MINT=true` | api | `false` | Re-enables `POST /api/v1/agents`, which creates an agent and returns a long-lived `agent_secret` outside the enrollment flow | No boot-time WARN. While off, the route answers `403 direct_agent_mint_disabled` |
| `SB_ALLOW_INSECURE_VAULT_ADDR=true` | api | `false` | Accepts `http://` Vault addresses on provider connections | WARN log at boot |
| `SB_ALLOW_UNSEALED_WRAPS=true` | api | `false` | Hands wraps to an agent with no X25519 public key on file as plaintext over TLS, and accepts a plaintext `value` when an agent posts a wrap. Only for an agent that predates wire-envelope sealing. | WARN log at boot. While off, a keyless agent gets `409 agent_public_key_required` before the wrap is consumed and a `value` post gets `400 envelope_required`; both are audited |
| `SB_PROVIDER_CONN_REJECT_SECRETS=false` | api | `true` | Turns off the check that rejects secret-shaped values (AWS keys, Vault tokens, JWTs, OAuth tokens) in provider-connection scope. Credential-shaped key names are still refused. | WARN log at boot |
| `SB_MFA_DEV_ALLOW_PWD=true` | api | `false` | Treats every live session as MFA-fresh, so step-up-gated actions (approve, reveal, role and provider edits) need only a password sign-in | api refuses to boot unless `SB_ENV=dev`; WARN log at boot |
| `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true` | agent | `false` | Allows a plain `http://` control-plane endpoint, so the agent credential and job traffic cross the network unencrypted | WARN log at boot; the `agent` chart refuses an `http://` endpoint unless `cp.insecureTransport=true` |
| `SB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true` | gateway | `false` | Allows plain `http://` to the control plane and to every Argo CD endpoint, so the Gateway credential and the Argo CD token cross the network unencrypted | WARN log at boot; the `secrets-bridge-gateway` chart refuses an `http://` URL unless `insecureTransport=true` |
| `SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS=true` | gateway | `false` | Binds the Release 2 `eso` and `rollout` connectors, which read the Kubernetes API. Not supported for production | WARN log at boot. The Kubernetes self-check still refuses any access to Secrets. The gateway chart never sets it |

The [hardening checklist](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/#hardening-checklist-before-exposing-to-anyone)
checks each of these before a deployment is exposed.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

## Common failure modes

### "Failed to load …" on every page

Likely the api isn't reachable. Check:

```bash
curl -fsS http://localhost:18080/readyz
```

If 503, the api can see Postgres or Redis but one of them isn't
ready, the response body lists which:

```json
{"status":"unready","checks":{"postgres":"ping failed: dial tcp ..."}}
```

### Login returns 401 with a valid password

Check the audit log:

```bash
JAR=...  # a cookie jar from an admin sign-in (see Bootstrap: curl -c "$JAR" on /auth/login)
curl -fsS "http://localhost:18080/api/v1/audit-events?action=auth.login" \
  -b "$JAR" \
  | jq '.[] | select(.status=="denied")'
```

The `metadata.error_kind` tells you what's wrong:

| `error_kind` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `user_not_found` | Email doesn't exist (case-insensitive). Check `SB_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` |
| `wrong_password` | Password mismatch |
| `user_disabled` | `local_users.disabled = TRUE` |
| `missing_fields` | Body shape wrong |

### Google sign-in refused

A refused Google sign-in always lands on `/login?error=sso` with "You
couldn't be signed in with that account.", whatever the reason, so the page
can't reveal which emails have accounts. An admin with `audit.read` finds
the reason in the audit log:

```bash
curl -fsS "http://localhost:18080/api/v1/audit-events?action=auth.sso.callback" \
  -b "$JAR" \
  | jq '.[] | select(.status=="denied") | {time:.occurred_at, kind:.metadata.error_kind, purpose:.metadata.purpose}'
```

The browser isn't signed in yet, so these events have the actor
`anonymous` and no email. Match them to a person by time.

| `error_kind` | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `hd_not_allowed` | The ID token has no `hd` claim (a personal Google account) or a Workspace domain that isn't allowed | Use a Workspace account, or add its domain under Admin → Sign-in |
| `email_domain_not_allowed` | `hd` is allowed but the email's domain isn't | Add the email's domain too |
| `email_unverified` | Google didn't mark the email as verified | Verify it at Google |
| `email_has_account` | The email already belongs to an account here, which hasn't connected Google | The person signs in with their password and uses Connect Google on their profile |
| `account_disabled` | The account was declined or disabled | A declined account can't be re-enabled from the console |
| `provider_disabled` | Google is turned off, or `SB_OIDC_ISSUER` is Google | Turn it on, or use the env-var provider |
| `no_public_url` | No public address is set | Set `SB_PUBLIC_URL` or save one under Admin → Sign-in |
| `exchange_failed` | Google refused the code exchange, usually a wrong client ID or secret | Check the client in Google Cloud Console, replace the secret, run Test |
| `id_token_invalid`, `claims_invalid`, `nonce_mismatch`, `missing_sub` | Google's answer couldn't be verified | Check the client ID, then Test |
| `iat_invalid` | The ID token was too old or dated in the future | Check the api server's clock |
| `no_code` | The person cancelled at Google, or Google returned an error | Try again |
| `state_cookie`, `state_unknown`, `state_mismatch` | The round trip took longer than 5 minutes, or finished in another browser | Try again in one browser |

Two other events explain refusals that aren't in `auth.sso.callback`:

- **`user.pending_refused`**: the [waiting limit](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/google-sign-in/#the-waiting-limit)
  was reached. Approve or decline waiting accounts, or raise the limit. The
  events are aggregated per 10-minute window, with `count`, `first` and
  `last`.
- **`sso_provider.default_role_refused`**: approval is off, but the default
  role now holds a privileged permission, so the account was created
  waiting for approval instead. Fix the role or pick another default.

**Test** runs the same checks and shows the reason to the admin who ran it,
which is the quickest way to check a setup.

### Google shows "redirect_uri_mismatch"

Google stops on its own error page and never comes back, so nothing is
audited. The redirect URI registered on the OAuth client must match the one
Secrets Bridge sends exactly:

```text
https://secrets.example.com/api/v1/auth/sso/google/callback
```

Copy it from **Admin → Sign-in → Google → Redirect URL**, and add it under
**Authorized redirect URIs** in Google Cloud Console. The scheme, host,
port and path must all match. If you change the public address, update the
redirect URI at Google too.

### No "Sign in with Google" button, or Turn on fails

- **No public address.** The login page doesn't offer Google while neither
  `SB_PUBLIC_URL` nor a saved address is set, and Turn on answers
  `409 provider_not_ready` with `missing: ["public_url"]`. Set one of them.
- **Missing secret or domains.** `missing` also lists `client_secret` or
  `allowed_domains`.
- **The env-var provider is Google.** With `SB_OIDC_ISSUER` set to
  `https://accounts.google.com`, the console provider is never offered
  (`409 env_provider_is_google`). Use one or the other.
- **The api won't start** after setting `SB_PUBLIC_URL`: the value is
  invalid. It must be `https`, with no user info, query or fragment, and
  plain `http` only for `localhost` with `SB_ENV=dev`.

### Agent job fails immediately ("agent reported failure")

Read the agent's log:

```bash
docker logs secrets-bridge-agent-1 | grep -iE "job|error|fail" | tail
```

The most common cause is **agent provider settings**. For Vault:
the agent's `SB_VAULT_KV_MOUNT` (default `kv`) has to match the
provider connection's `mount`, otherwise the job fails with a
`kvMount` error. For AWS Secrets Manager: the agent needs
`SB_AWS_REGION`.

For a deeper trace, set the agent's log level to debug:

```bash
SB_LOG_LEVEL=debug docker compose up -d agent
```

### "Wraps card shows 'No wraps issued yet'" after the agent ran

Two possibilities:

1. **You're signed in as the wrong user.** The Wraps card only
   fetches when the viewer is the requester. Sign in as the user
   who submitted the request.
2. **The agent failed before posting the wrap.** Check
   `GET /audit-events?correlation_id=<request-uuid>` for the full
   chain, you should see `wrap.create` events on success.

### "Failed to load audit events"

Likely `audit.read` permission missing. The seed admin role has
it; if you're a different user, an admin needs to grant you the
`audit.read` permission via a role.

```bash
# As admin:
curl -fsS http://localhost:18080/api/v1/audit-events \
  -b "$JAR"
```

Expected: 200 with an array. If 403, your role doesn't carry
`audit.read`.

### Agent stays "stale" forever

Two things to check:

1. **The agent's heartbeat is reaching the CP.** From the agent's
   network, run:
   ```bash
   docker exec secrets-bridge-agent-1 wget -qO- http://api:8080/healthz
   ```
2. **The agent secret is correct.** A wrong secret returns 401 on
   heartbeat (generic message; the audit log records
   `error_kind=unauthorized`). A revoked agent gets the same answer.
3. **The key matches.** A `409 agent_key_mismatch` on every heartbeat
   means the loaded key isn't the bound one; see
   [Requests fail with `409 agent_key_mismatch`](#requests-fail-with-409-agent_key_mismatch).

### Vault read returns "permission denied"

The agent uses the credentials in `SB_VAULT_TOKEN` or via the
configured Kubernetes auth role. Check that they have read access
to the secret path:

```bash
docker exec secrets-bridge-vault-1 sh -c \
  'VAULT_ADDR=http://127.0.0.1:8200 VAULT_TOKEN=devroot \
   vault kv get secret/<path>'
```

If that works but the agent gets denied, the agent token has less
scope than the dev token. Adjust the policy in Vault.

## Agent

Onboarding steps are in [Agent onboarding](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/). Start with the
pod log (`kubectl -n secrets-bridge logs deploy/secrets-bridge-agent`) and the
audit log, which records why a request was refused (`error_kind`) without the
token, secret or key.

### The agent exits at start: a credential file is missing

The agent reads `agent_id`, `agent_secret` and `private_key` from
`SB_AGENT_CREDENTIALS_DIR` (`/etc/secrets-bridge/agent` in the chart) and stops
before it contacts the control plane when one is missing, empty or malformed.
`private_key` must be the base64 of exactly 32 bytes.

- `kubectl -n secrets-bridge get secret secrets-bridge-agent` must exist in the
  release namespace. A pod whose Secret doesn't exist stays in
  `ContainerCreating`; `kubectl describe pod` shows the mount error.
- The Secret must have the three keys. List the key names, not the values:
  `kubectl -n secrets-bridge get secret secrets-bridge-agent-identity -o jsonpath='' | jq 'keys'`.
  When your store uses other names, set `identity.keys.agentId`,
  `identity.keys.agentSecret` and `identity.keys.privateKey`.
- With ESO, check the `ExternalSecret` status
  (`kubectl -n secrets-bridge get externalsecret`). A `SecretSyncedError` means
  ESO couldn't read the store entry, usually a missing `GetSecretValue` or Vault
  `read` grant, or a property name that doesn't match the bundle.

### The agent refuses its credential files as too open

The agent refuses a credential file with group write or any permission for
others (`mode & 0o037 != 0`), checked on the file the symlink resolves to.
Owner and group read (`0440`) is accepted.

The `agent` chart mounts the Secret with `defaultMode: 0400` and requires
`podSecurityContext.fsGroup`; kubelet shows the files as `0440 root:<fsGroup>`,
which passes. A mount that is wider than that usually comes from a pod spec
patched outside the chart (a different `defaultMode`, or a projected volume
with its own mode). Without `fsGroup` the files stay `0400 root:root`, and the
non-root agent can't read them at all: that shows up as a permission error, not
as too open. Outside Kubernetes, `chmod 0400` (or `0600`) the files.

### Requests fail with `409 agent_key_mismatch`

The fingerprint of the key the agent loaded doesn't match the key bound to the
agent on the control plane. The audit log has `agent.key.mismatch`, rate limited
to one event per agent per minute.

- After a [key rotation](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/agent-onboarding/#rotate-the-wire-key) the running
  pod still has the old key. Check that the Kubernetes Secret has the new
  `private_key` (ESO synced it), then `kubectl rollout restart` the Deployment.
- The Secret holds another agent's `private_key`, or the bundle from an
  enrollment that was later replaced. Compare the `public_key_fingerprint`
  stored with the bundle (or printed by `enroll` or `rotate-key`) with the one
  the console shows for the agent. If they differ and no rotation is open, write the right bundle to the store, or revoke the agent and
  enroll again.

### Enrollment is refused

`secrets-bridge-agent enroll` gets a generic error, and the audit log
(`agent.enroll` with `denied`) has the reason:

- `401 enrollment_rejected`: the token is wrong, expired, already used or
  revoked, or the challenge didn't match. Tokens expire after 15 minutes by
  default and work once. Create a new one.
- `401 enrollment_rejected` with the right token: `--cluster-name` or
  `--provider-type` doesn't match the token's expected values.
- `400 invalid_public_key`: the key isn't 32 bytes of base64 for `x25519`, or
  is a refused value (all zero or a low-order point). The CLI generates a valid
  key, so this points at a modified client.
- `400 unsupported_schema_version`: the CLI is older than the control plane's
  enrollment API. Use the `secrets-bridge-agent` release that matches the
  control plane.
- `429`: too many attempts. Wait and retry.

When `enroll` reached the control plane but the write to your secret store
failed, the token is spent and the bundle is gone. Revoke the new agent and
enroll again with a new token.

## Gateway

Install steps are in [Gateway](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/). Start with the pod log
(`kubectl -n tenant-a-uat logs deploy/secrets-bridge-gateway`) and the detail
view (`GET /api/v1/admin/gateways/<id>`), which shows each replica's last
heartbeat and each connector's health.

### Gateway pod is not ready, or exits at boot

Check the log for the first error:

- `identity: ... has mode ...`: the identity file can be read by other
  users or written by its group. The Gateway accepts `0400`, `0600` or `0440`.
  The chart mounts the Secret with mode `0440` and `fsGroup`; a hand-written
  manifest with `defaultMode: 0444` is refused. Fix the mode, and rotate the
  Gateway secret (revoke, create, enroll) if other users could read it.
- `identity: ... does not exist`: the Secret uses a key other than
  `identity.key` (default `identity.json`). A pod whose Secret does not exist
  at all stays in `ContainerCreating`.
- `identity: ... is not a valid identity JSON object` or `... is missing
  gateway_id or gateway_secret`: the file must hold exactly
  `{"gateway_id": "...", "gateway_secret": "..."}`. Unknown fields are
  refused, so storing the whole enrollment response does not work. The
  `jq -ce '{gateway_id, gateway_secret}'` step in the install pipeline keeps
  only those two fields.
- `refusing to start: connectors: self-check could not prove the credential
  cannot read secrets: connector "<name>"; failed check <resource> <action>:
  <kind>; ...`: at boot, Argo CD could not be reached, the token check
  (`GET /api/v1/session/userinfo`) was refused, or a can-i question did not
  complete. The pod exits and restarts (`CrashLoopBackOff`). The named check
  says which: `failed check session userinfo: unauthorized` points at the
  token Secret, `unreachable`, `timeout` or `tls` at `base_url`, the
  connector's `egress` peer or the CA, and any other check (for example
  `failed check exec create: bad request`) at that can-i question. Once
  Argo CD answers, the next restart passes; see
  [Release 1: an Argo CD outage at boot is a crash loop](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#release-1-an-argo-cd-outage-at-boot-is-a-crash-loop).
- After boot, the same failures do not restart the pod. It stays up and not
  ready, stops claiming, and turns ready once a recheck passes.
- `connector kind is not enabled in Release 1`: the connectors file names
  `eso` or `rollout`. Release 1 binds `argocd` only.
- No heartbeat accepted within `SB_GATEWAY_CP_UNREACHABLE_AFTER` (default
  `2m`): the control plane is unreachable. Check `cp.endpoint`, the
  `cp.egress.cidrs` NetworkPolicy peer and, for a private CA,
  `cp.caExistingSecret`.
- `catalog upload failed` with `http 400`, again on every heartbeat: the
  control plane refused the catalog. If the api was not upgraded before the
  Gateway, it does not know the catalog `identity` field that the Gateway
  sends for an Argo CD target whose uid it knows. Upgrade the api; see
  [Application identity](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#application-identity).
- `invalid connector settings: ... applications.id: must not start with "d-"`:
  a target `id` in the connectors file uses the prefix reserved for
  discovered targets, and the Gateway refuses to start. Rename the target.

### Gateway refuses to start: over-privileged

A log line `refusing to start: connectors: credential is over-privileged:
connector "<name>"; failed check <resource> <action>: can-i yes; ...` for an
`argocd` connector comes from the Argo CD can-i probe: Argo CD answered `yes`
to the question named in the line, one of those in
[Argo CD privilege checks](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#argo-cd-privilege-checks). For example
`failed check logs get: can-i yes` means the token may read pod logs. The line
names the resource and action, not the AppProject or the object, so check
every policy line that applies to the Gateway's account or role for that right,
on the allowed AppProjects and on each configured Application. Remove the
extra right from the Argo CD policy of the Gateway's account so that only the
[minimal policy](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#the-minimal-policy) is left, and check
`policy.default` in `argocd-rbac-cm` too: `role:readonly` grants `logs, get`
and trips this check. The pod restarts until the grant is gone. When a recheck
finds a grant on a running Gateway, the replica turns not ready, reports
`over_privileged` in a heartbeat and stops. The control plane then pauses
dispatch for that connector until the report is 10 minutes old, so after the
fix, tasks can wait up to 10 minutes before they are claimed again.

For an `eso` or `rollout` connector, the same message comes from the
Kubernetes self-check. Those Release 2 connectors need
`SB_GATEWAY_ENABLE_R2_CONNECTORS=true`; a Release 1 Gateway built from the
chart has no Kubernetes access and never runs it.

The Kubernetes self-check refuses to start when its service account can use
any verb on `secrets`, or any write verb on a resource a connector reads, or when a review
call fails. There is no override. Remove the grant from the RBAC bound to the
Gateway's service account. When a recheck finds such a grant on a running
Gateway, it reports `over_privileged` in a heartbeat before it stops, and the
api records a `gateway.over_privileged` audit event.

### Connector advertised but nothing is bound

The Gateway reports its connectors and targets in the catalog, but an
advertised connector does nothing until an admin approves it and binds a
target. In the detail view, check the connector's `status`:

- `advertised`: approve it with
  `POST /api/v1/admin/gateways/<id>/connectors/<connector-uuid>/approve`.
- `approved` but no entry under `bindings`: create a binding with
  `POST /api/v1/admin/gateway-bindings`.
- `missing`: the Gateway no longer advertises this connector. Check the
  connector `name` in the chart values.

A binding request that fails answers with a closed code. `target_not_advertised`
means the `argocd_target_id` is not an application `id` in the connectors file,
and `target_stale` means the Gateway advertised it once but no longer does.

### Observation error `target_identity_changed`

The Application under the target's name is not the object the Gateway pinned:
it was deleted and recreated, so it has a new `metadata.uid`. The Gateway
reports nothing about the new object. If the change is expected, read the new
uid (`kubectl get application -n <namespace> <name> -o jsonpath=''`),
set it as `applications[].uid` and upgrade the release. Without a `uid` in the
values, restart the Gateway. The Gateway then advertises the new identity, so
the control plane marks the target `identity_changed` (`identity_status` in
the detail view) and suspends its bindings. A platform admin then re-confirms
it with
`POST /api/v1/admin/gateways/<id>/connectors/<connector-uuid>/targets/<target-id>/confirm-identity`.
Re-confirm only after the Gateway runs with the new uid, because the
re-confirm accepts whatever identity the Gateway advertises at that moment.
See [Application identity](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#application-identity).

While the target is `identity_changed`, its tasks are not dispatched, a result
for it is refused with `target_identity_changed`, and a new binding on it gets
`409 target_identity_changed`. A result for a pinned target that carries no
`identity_digest`, or another one, is refused with `identity_digest_missing` or
`identity_digest_mismatch`. Each refusal is audited as
`observation.evidence.rejected` with that reason.

### Gateway gets 401 from the control plane

The log shows `control plane refused this gateway; claiming stopped, staying up
and not ready until restarted`. The pod stays up and not ready on purpose, so it
does not restart-loop. The api records `gateway.auth.rejected`.

The usual cause is a revoked Gateway (`status: "revoked"` in
`GET /api/v1/admin/gateways`). There is no rotation in Release 1: create a new
Gateway, mint a token, enroll, replace the identity Secret and restart the
Deployment. A `disabled` Gateway gets the same `401`: enable it again
(**Enable…** on its detail panel, or `PUT /api/v1/admin/gateways/<id>/enabled`)
and restart the Deployment. If the Gateway is still `active`, the Secret holds a credential
that does not belong to it, for example from an earlier enrollment.

### Observation stays pending, or shows "No observation configured"

Check the request's observations first:

```bash
curl -fsS -b "$JAR" "$CP/api/v1/requests/<request-id>/observations" \
  | jq '{observation_source, rollup, tasks: [.tasks[] | {gateway_name, state, verdict, attempt_count, deadline_at}]}'
```

`rollup: "none"` means no task exists. Check `observation_source` and the
audit events with the `correlation_id` of the job that executed the change:

- `observation_source` is `none`: the environment is not set to `gateway`, so
  no task was created. `none` is the default, and environments that used the
  retired control-plane poller were moved to it at the
  [cutover](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway-cutover/). With `none`, the audit log has
  `request.observation_skipped` with reason `source_none`. The source is read
  when the request reaches `executed`, so switching it later does not add tasks
  to earlier requests. See
  [Switch the environment](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/gateway/#8-switch-the-environment-to-gateway-observation).
- `request.observation_skipped` with reason `no_gateway_binding`: no enabled
  binding covers the secret in that environment, or the binding's Gateway is
  revoked or disabled, or its connector is not approved.
- No skip event and no task: the binding exists, but the Gateway no longer
  advertises its target (`target_stale`), so it was skipped.
- `scope_not_resolved`, `request_type_not_observed` or
  `provider_type_not_supported`: only patch and cross-team requests on
  `aws-sm` or `vault` secrets in an environment are observed.

`rollup: "pending"` with a task in `queued` that never moves:

- **Not yet claimable.** The first claim is allowed 10 seconds after
  `executed`, and a result that left the stage `not_observed` reschedules the
  task 15, 30, 60 and then 120 seconds later. Argo CD that stays
  `Progressing` or `OutOfSync` keeps the task in that loop until the deadline.
- **The Gateway is not claiming.** Check its status in **Admin → Gateways**. A
  `stale` Gateway has missed its heartbeats; check the pods and their route to
  the control plane. A Gateway pauses claiming while the control plane is
  unreachable, its catalog is not accepted or a connector self-check fails
  (see [Runtime behaviour](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/components/gateway/#runtime-behaviour)). A
  Gateway that has never had a heartbeat accepted gets `204` on every claim.
- **The connector or binding changed.** A task is claimable only while its
  binding is enabled, its connector approved, its target not
  `identity_changed`, and no replica of the Gateway seen in the last 10
  minutes last reported the connector, or itself, `over_privileged`.

A pending task never fails the request. At its deadline it ends `timed_out`.

### Observation timed out with `gateway_unavailable`

The deadline passed and the Gateway had not been seen since the task was
created, or was not `active` (stale, disabled or revoked). Check the Gateway's
status and its pod logs. A task is never handed to another Gateway, so the
request stays `timed_out`; the next change to the secret gets a new task.
`deadline_reached` instead means the Gateway was up but the stage was not
observed in time.

`timed_out` is not a failure of the request or of the deployment. Without the
worker sweepers (`SB_WORKER_GATEWAY_SWEEPERS_ENABLED`), an overdue task is
closed only when someone opens the request.

### Result rejected with `attempt_superseded` or `task_closed`

The Gateway log shows `result dropped: attempt superseded`, `result dropped:
lease expired` or `result dropped: task closed`, and the api records
`observation.evidence.rejected` with a `reason`:

- `attempt_superseded` (`stale_attempt`, `unknown_attempt`): the attempt is
  not the task's current one. Its lease ran out and the task was claimed again,
  it was released, or the Gateway was disabled or revoked while it held the
  lease. The newer attempt carries on. Frequent cases mean the Gateway works
  past its 60-second lease; check Argo CD latency.
- `task_closed`: the task is already closed. A later change to the same secret
  (`superseded_by_later_write`), a source change (`source_changed`), a deleted
  binding (`binding_removed`) or the deadline closed it first.

Neither needs action on its own. The verdict comes from the result that was
accepted, or from the reason the task closed.

### Claim answers `429 inflight_limit`

The Gateway already holds `max_inflight_tasks` live leases (default 20), or the
replica asking already holds one, which is the limit per replica. The Gateway
backs off for the `Retry-After` time. Raise `max_inflight_tasks` when you create
the Gateway, or add replicas, if tasks wait too long. The claim rate limit
(2400 a minute per Gateway) answers `429` too.

## Useful queries against the audit log

### Find every action for one request

```bash
curl -fsS "http://localhost:18080/api/v1/audit-events?correlation_id=<uuid>" \
  -b "$JAR" | jq '.[] | {time:.occurred_at, actor, action, resource}'
```

### Find every login failure in the last hour

```bash
SINCE=$(date -u -d '1 hour ago' +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
curl -fsS "http://localhost:18080/api/v1/audit-events?action=auth.login&since=$SINCE" \
  -b "$JAR" \
  | jq '.[] | select(.status=="denied")'
```

### Find every wrap retrieval (who saw which value when)

```bash
curl -fsS "http://localhost:18080/api/v1/audit-events?action=wrap.retrieve" \
  -b "$JAR" \
  | jq '.[] | {time:.occurred_at, actor, resource, status}'
```

This is the SOC2-friendly query, every plaintext reveal across
the platform, append-only, with the actor and timestamp.

## Reading the metrics

The api and worker both expose Prometheus metrics at `/metrics`.
The interesting ones:

| Metric | What |
|---|---|
| `worker_scheduler_runs_total{task,outcome}` | Per-sweeper success / failure / skipped_lock counter |
| `worker_scheduler_run_duration_seconds{task}` | Sweeper latency histogram |
| `worker_scheduler_lock_skipped_total{task}` | Leader-election losses (expected for N-1 of N replicas) |
| `redis_call_timeouts_total{site}` | api Redis calls that hit their deadline: `auth_cache` (agent and Gateway auth, revoke, 300ms) and `rate_limit` (500ms). A rise means Redis is slow before it is down: limiters start failing open, and revokes may answer `503 revoked_cache_unconfirmed` |

For HTTP-side latency, log-derived metrics are the source today;
a future PR adds explicit histograms.

## When in doubt

- Check the audit log first (`GET /audit-events`)
- Then the api logs (`docker logs secrets-bridge-api-1`)
- Then the agent logs (`docker logs secrets-bridge-agent-1`)
- Then Postgres (`docker exec -it secrets-bridge-postgres-1 psql -U secrets_bridge`)
- File an issue at
  [`secrets-bridge/.github`](https://github.com/secrets-bridge/.github)
  with the correlation_id and the audit chain

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/

# Reference

Catalogues + tables. Look here when you need the exact name of an
endpoint, a permission, a provider, or a KMS backend.

These pages list what the control plane and the agent accept today: the
routes the api serves, the secret providers the agent can reach, the KMS
backends behind envelope encryption, and the permission strings that
RBAC checks. The [Operations](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/) pages explain how to
use them, and the [Configuration reference](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/operations/config/) lists
every environment variable.

- **[HTTP API endpoints](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/api-endpoints/)**: every route grouped by area
  (probes, sign-in, agents, Gateways, access requests, cross-team requests,
  reveal sessions, admin, audit, provider connections and policy rules),
  with the auth each one needs, such as `public`, a session, a session
  plus a permission, or an agent's or Gateway's own secret header.
- **[Providers supported](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/providers/)**: the provider types the agent
  dispatches to. HashiCorp Vault (KV v2, token or Kubernetes auth) and AWS
  Secrets Manager (the standard AWS SDK credential chain) ship. The
  `gcp-sm`, `azure-kv` and `kubernetes` resolvers are placeholders, and
  Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager are on the
  [roadmap](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/overview/product-status/). The page also lists the
  credential-shaped keys each resolver refuses and how a new provider is
  added.
- **[KMS backends](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/kms-backends/)**: the envelope-encryption backends
  selected with `SB_KMS_BACKEND`. `local` is for dev only; `vault-transit`
  and `aws-kms` are for production. Covers their settings, setup, key
  rotation and how to choose between them.
- **[Permissions catalog](https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/permissions/)**: the permission strings that
  `auth.Require(perm)` checks, the seed roles that carry them, which
  permissions are meant to be narrowed by scope, and how to add a new one. The
  api also serves the live catalog at `GET /api/v1/permissions`.

---

Source: https://secrets-bridge.io/latest/reference/api-endpoints/

# HTTP API endpoints

Every route the api exposes today. Auth column shows what's
required to call it.

| Auth | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `public` | No auth, open route (probes, login) |
